The Clerk said the Council had to consider whether it would be to their benefit to have a water cart which, it was suggested, would save expense for the up-keep of the roads. The County Council said they could not spare their cart off the County roads at Stockton Heath. It was decided that the special Highways Committee, with the addition of Messrs. Mounfield, Whitley and Hallows, should consider the matter. This Conncil held its fortnightly meeting at Dutton NORLEY WATER SUPPLY. A CYCLIST'S COMPLAINT.

The Chairman read an extract from the cycling notes in Monday's "Manchester Guardian" in which it was complained that the navvies laying the new pipe from Lake Vyrnwy to Liverpool had made "a positively horrible mess" of the road approaching Delamere station from the direction of Norley chapel. The Surveyor was instructed to give the matter his attention.

HEALTH OF 'ItHE DISTRICT. Dr. Adams reported that during the fortnight, two cases of scarlet fever had been notified from Stockton Heath. It was interesting to note that each of the patients' although only about seven years of age, had had the disease twice. In consequence of an outbreak of measles he had recommended the closing of Norley schools for three weeks commencing on the previous Monday. There was also a measles outbreak at Whitley but he did not at present consider it necessary to close the schools. It was a matter of deep regret to him that owing to the Local Government Board inquiry at Nor. ley he was prevented from attending the ceremony of laying the foundation stones of the new isolation hospi- tal at Dutton. He felt it was particularly hard on him, as it was a matter on which he had thought and felt strongly and deeply for fifteen years. The report was adopted. CASTNER-KELLNER COMPANY'S APPLICATION. The Castner-Kellner Alkali Co. Ltd., Weston Point, wrote stating that they wished to put up a small electric motor for certain purposes connected with their business on land of theirs on the other side of South-road, Weston Point. This would necessitate crossing the roadway with a wire to carry the current, and they would be glad to have permission to do so. The Surveyor said he was informed that the wire would be placed under the roadway and would be pro- tected with cast iron pipes. The Council granted the company the necessary per- mission, provided that there are proper safeguards. THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE MIDWIVES' ACT. The Northwich Urban Council sent copies of resolu- tions upon the proposals of the County Council with regard to the administration of the Midwives' Act, 1902. The great increase in the county expendi- ture had somewhat influenced the Council in its decision regarding the fee proposed to be paid to District Medical Officers of Health. The resolutions were as follows :—" The Urban District Council of Northwich is strongly of opinion that the Act would be more satisfactorily administered by Dis- trict Councils acting as sub-committees for their res- pective districts." That failing such an arrangement, the Council consider the fee of £1 Us. Gd. proposed to be paid by the County Council to the district Medical Officers of Health for each qualified midwife on the register (with a minimum fee of £5 55.) is excessive as a continuing annual payment and is of the opinion that in each case after the first year, the fee should be con- siderably reduced." The Chairman said that at present he did not consider it desirable that the District Councils should have the work of administration placed upon them. He was not prepared to go fully into the proposals of the North- wich Council,and he would like to have time to consider the matter before committing himself to further sug- gestions. The Clerk remarked that in Rural districts the fee to medical officers would probably not be considered ex- cessive. The Chairman said he wanted to know the duties which would have to be performed. If the medical officer had to make special journeys over the whole district and receive £1 us. Gd. for each journey, he (Mr. Woodward) wOuld say the fee was not excessive by any means, because the doctor might be mulcted in a great deal of expense. Dr. Adams explained that the fee was only Li us. 6d. for each midwife per year. The duties would include inspection of the house at least once a year and there would also have to be inspections without warning. It was really a system of medical police. The Chairman intimated that. he would consult with Dr. Adams and report at a later meeting.

ADMIRAL PARRY PROPOSES AN ALTERATION. Admiral Jones Parry moved the rescinding of the Council's recent resolution that the whole Council be constituted the Highways Committee. He contended that• it would be in the interests of efficiency and economy to leave highway matters in the hands of a special committee Mr. Pilling seconded as he did not believe in very large committees. Mr. Spruce contended that the alteration would debar many members from speaking on highway matters. Mr. Hallows thought each councillor should be on the Highways Committee. ,He should certainly object to Stockton Heath being shut out from that committee. On a vote being taken. Admiral Parry's motion was defeated by a large majority.

div.head: WATERING OF STOCKTON HEATH ROADS.
div.p: THE WATERING OF STOCKTON HEATH ROADS.

The Council then discussed the resolution of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee asking them to consider the advisability of purchasing a water cart for use on the district roads in Stockton Heath and the immediate neighbourhood. The Parochial Committee it was estimated, would be prepared to contribute to- wards the cost. Mr. Iktllows said the County Council had a water cart for use in the district. At Stockton Heath it was known as the "weather cart "because when it appeared it was a sign that there was going to be some rain. (Laughter). The County Council rotftis were not half watered. He suggested that arrangements could be made with the County Council to hand over their water cart to the Rural Council together with the amount it cost to water the County roads, and the Rural Council would then water botb the County and District roads. The Chairman said he was informed that the County Council would not entertain the idea of negotiation on the question. They would still hold to the manage- ment of their own roads, and they would not consult the District Council as to what they should do with them. Mr. Hallows then moved that a water cart be pur-

a Good! Why, there's Captain Jan Crawson, as lives in the big hoose yonder, and he was a fisher lad i' Cullercoats, and we've heard naught but good of him. the canny and man. An' there's Ebert Broon, wha's 'left the fishin" to gan on uve river, and wha's a constant pilot nooadays, as rich as ye please. An there's--" But Gilbert Jack's wife, feeling that she had no skill in argument, heard the child cry in the kitchen, and at once abandoned the contest. Nevertheless, the feeling that she could not defend was the one that most generally prevaiied among her neighbours. Bella Wakeman would have had a gayer wedding had she married a fisher lad who had kept to the fishing. As for Bella herself, she was too full of satisfac- tion with the world and her own good fortune to have any idea of what the neighbours said, or any care about it if she had known. Her heart was carolling delightful song all day, and her only trouble was how to get Reuben Taylor to play the violin at her wedding. Reuben kept as far as "possible out of her reach in those days. But she met him onto as he was coining from the boats. "Let's give ye a hand with the creels.. Reuben, ma lad, it's many a day sin' ah did that, isn't it, noo ? " "Ah want nae help, Della." "Mebbe no. Yet ah'd like to help ye for auld sake's sake, Reuben.", "An' for what else?" Asked Reuben, throwing a quick glance at her face. "For ye maim want something mair than to give me a hand with the creels when ye come canoodlin' after this auld- fashioned way." "Dinna be uncanny," said Bella, as she laid a hand to one side of the baskets while he took the other. "An' yet Ale! not tell ye a lee, Reuben. Ah dee want something from ye. I want ye to play at the weddin'. So there,*noo!" Reuben dropped his side of the creel, filled partly with lines and partly with fish. He had drawn a long breath before he said: "And why shouldn't I? We were children together—you and Will and Me. Bella, I hoped— But I wivvent say- that. I trust you and Will may have many a happy year together; and if there should be any bairns liy-and-bye I will be Uncle Reuben to them. Ah, yes; Ah'l come and play at yo'r weddin'. But leave me non, Bella. Ah'l put the creel here, and gan up to the Point and look at the old winter boat." _
He left her to spend his bitter hour lying beside the old boat, and looking out to sea; and then he went and played at the wedding after all.

News came that the Paramatta had foundered in the Southern seas. • Part of the crew saved itself in the boats ; but Will Simmons, first mate by this time, was not among those who made their way to shore. The evidences of his death were even too strong for his wife to resist; and yet she kept saying to others, what she dare not say to her own heart, that Will Simmons was alive somewhere, and that, in God's time, he would come back to her. A hope without belief to sustain it: a pretence that died out whenever she looked at the cradle in the chimney-corner, and then clutched her child to her breast with the cry: "Oh, ye poor fetherless bairn! " _

Years passed and the child was able to toddle to the beach and watch the fishermen putting off or coming home, which it always did with wide, wondering, sympathetic eyes. Then, as it grew, it would wave its infantile farewells at evening time, or shout its joyous welcome in the morning to those who had made it the child of the village.
- Its chief favourite was Reuben Taylor, who would place it in the bow of the old winter boat on the Point, and play his violin to it as long as it cared to listen. _ _ _
white breakers and into the darkness until nothing could be seen of it but the flare, which burnt at the stern.

"May the Lord save. my man!" was Bella's incessant, almost unconscious prayer; for Reuben Taylor, to whom she was to be wedded in a few hours, was already "her man," in her own thoughts. and her heart yearned for him as she followed the flare of lifeboat anti! it rendered dimly visible, amid the tumultuous water, a dark, swaying shadow on the long, dangerous rock known as the "Bear's Back."

Bella clung to the rails on the cliff-tops, fighting against the wind. All the folk of the village were there, even the old men, clinging to the railings as Bella was clinging, and with eyes straining like hers at the flare which had begun to look like a distant star.

Everyone there knew that a great fight for life was in progress where that uneasy, feeble, drifting light could be seen. It was not only the men in the wrecked vessel who were in peril. The life- boat had set out for the dangerous Bear's Back at the risk cf almost certain disaster. Husbands, brothers, sons, were in imminent and deadly peril. The Bear's Back was a long, low reef, covered by the sea at high tide. The danger that the lifeboat would be lifted up by some great wave and dashed to pieces by its fall, was actually much greater than that the crew of the wrecked vessel would be washed into the sea. _ .

And so it was that the dim light on the boat, now and again totally obscured by lifting waves or sheets of driving spray, was followed by half- repressed sobs, and by anxious, but muttered, prayers. If the straining eyes of the fisher-folk on shore could have penetrated the darkness through which the rain was swirling so fiercely they would have witnessed a battle in which was exhibited an almost superhuman courage and strength. There had, at long intervals, been wilder storms on that dangerous piece of coast, but never had the services of the lifeboat been called for in circumstances of such supreme peril. 'God help us and save us!" cried one of the weeping women. "But they'll all be drooned." "Nowt. of the sort," said an old fisherman, taking off his hat and letting the rain drive at his bald head as lie waved his son' -wester to and fro. "Divrent yer see as they're getten away from the wreck."

And, indeed, the flare-light had swung away far from the Bear's Back, and was already, with a great dip now in one direction and now in the other, clearly making for the harbour. "But they're tornin' back; they're tornin' back!" simultaneously exclaimed almost every member of the eager crowd, and the light on the boat was seen to be once more approaching the wrecked vessel.

Ten minutes more of agonised suspense, and again the flare-light was coming harbonrwards. There was a rush of the women down to the shore to help the rescued men ; but Bella Simmons swooned into the arms of a neighbour and recovered only to hear Reuben Taylor saying in a voice hard, calm, and apparently emotionless: "Here, Bella, I've brought him back—have brought yo'r man." VI.
The peril of that brave and determined rescue made talk in the village for many a year to come. "It was a chancey thing, that night o' the wreck of the Hector," a fisherman would remark. _ .

Tie leant his back against the fence, his violin well under his chin, his eyes looking wrapt and far away, his firm touch making the instrument croon, and wail, and plead. Behind him the Links—patches of sand and groups of flowering gorse, and little nests of wild flowers, and towering plumes of rank grass—made a foreground to a calm sea, and to a sky whose clouds were catching the first golden reflections of the sunset.

He was a yellow-haired, bronze-featured young fellow, in the guise of a fisherman, and with the I face of an artist. Two or three yards away from his feet lay a girl with hair like his own, and with the spotted calico bodice, and the many-tuckered, blue linsey-woolsey petticoat of the fisher lass. She had locked her hands behind her head as she lay backwards to listen to the, violinist, and the rays of the descending sun fell upon her features, and made her gloriously radiant and beautiful. "Reuben," she said, as the music ceased for a while and the musician looked in his dreamy way across the inland landscape, stretching over waste spaces to distant purple hills, "ah hard ye in th' chapel last night." "Aye, lass," said Reuben, withdrawing his far- away vision "ah saw ye there, and I had eyes for naught but ye." "Ye played beautifully, Reuben. It was as ifs there was naught but yo'r fiddle in all the quire. I wunnered if there could be anything more beauti- ful in Heaven than music like yo'r's." "It's graun' to hear ye speak like that, lass; not that there's much in ma playin'," said Reuben, with a modesty that he did not wholly feel. "If ye wad let me play to ye elwis, Bella, how graun' it wad be. I'll tell ye what I felt last night in the chapel. I felt that I wis playin' to ye mair than to the Almighty Himself. Ye filled ass' the place for me. It was you that I saw, Bella; it was you that I played to. If I could play to you elwis, Bella, and to none but you! Just to play to you whenever you liked or when I liked mysel' to play," and he thrust his violin under his arm and stepped passionately towards the listening girl. "Gude sakes ! • What's that Reuben ? " she said, as she rose and escaped from what looked like a threatened and compulsory embrace. Reuben Taylor "went to the fishing," as all his forbears had done. That seemed to him the life for which lv had been designed by Providence. The thount never dawned upon him that other careers wcr:t foln. He had no sort of desire out- side the calilp to which he he,4l been bred, except, as he ...vae, won' to say, "to :o4;17 the fiddle weel. ' But to Will Simmons the .f.ore fishing, so far from presenting attractions, was e,etestable, as a limited, monotonous, flavourless kind of life, with no outlook in any direction whal-soever. And so, sickening of the sea-boots, and cite basket of bait in the evening, and the dragging of the cobles ashore in tle morning, he took an ,arly opportunity of running! away to sea, which opportunity was available e.iough, indeed, seeing that the port of Shields was only two miles away. Had ho itayed at home to woo Bella Wakeman, the fiddle of Reuben Taylor might have put his plans to rout; but when Bella's mind could follow him over sea it dwelt with him far more frequently than with Reuben and his fiddle, surrounding him with a halo of admiration and love.

She thought, too, of what he might become. Why, a "knowledgable" man at sea might becorna almost anything, and Will Simmons was certainly "knowledgable." He was the smartest, liveliest, most eager lad that the village had turned out for many a year. Such as Will, if they took their fate into their own hands, as he had done, came back as mates and even as skippers, in a few years' time. Bella Wakeman, almost without knowing it, became proud of Will Simmons because he had run away to Fen. • ------

Then she began to think of what her own future might be if he turned out well. - There was a saying, in the village that a girl should never marry until she could "keep a Man," and keeping a man meant baiting his lines, and selling his fish, and doing his household work when she came home after a weary day of carrying her creels on her back from door to door in the nearest large town. It had never struck Bella Wakeman to revolt against this order of things until Bill Simmons went off to Shields and took ship. Then she said to herself, not knowing why: "Alt shall nivver keep a man. Should all ivver have a man at all, that man shall keep me." And so, though neither Bella knew nor Reuben knew, there was a constantly widening barrier between the fisher lad who had learnt to play the violin so beautifnlly and the fisher lass in whose heart had unconsciously grown up a dislike of the hard life and the mean living of her kind. "Divvent speak to me aboot luv," she would say to Reuben when they had both grown up and he became pressing. "Ah wivvent hear a word Of it. Play on yo'r fiddle, lad. I dearly like the fiddle. Jnst piny on that, and be friends as we've elwis been, and ahl come wiv ye on to the Links at night whenever ye like to play." Wherefore, because Reuben kept silent, knowing how inadvisable it would be to speak, they remained "chums," as in the old days, Reuben only bringing himself to the point of speaking on. that tender, soft, sunlit evening when the syren of the Paramatta sounded so suddenly out of the purple and gliden haze.

div.head: EARLESTOWN LOVE LETTER CASE. "Private Communication " from Gaol..
div.p: THE EARLESTOWN LOVE LETTER CASE. "Private Communication " from Gaol..

At the sitting of the Lancashire Court of Chancery in St. George's Hall on Monday, Vice-Chancellor Hall referred to the case of William Lundy, who was com- mitted to prison some time ago for disobeying an order , of the court restraining him from publishing love letters which had passed between other persons at Earlestown. His Honour said Lundy wrote to him, but the letter was returned by his clerk with the intimation that he refused to receive private communications fromAitigants. However Lundy had since been writing to the Home Office. He did not seem to like being in prison and he wanted to come out. Had be given up the papers and , paid the costs, or had he done anything at all? Mr. Mather (who represented the plaintiffs in the action) said he had no definite instructions but he understood Lundy had done nothing. The Vice-Chancellor said he would hand Mr. Mather ' the petition. He gathered that there was no urgency , about the matter. Lundy suffered from insomnia and I things of that kind, but his health was sound, so he was I not disposed to let him out after so short a time, until he had done what he ought to do—that was, deliver up I the papers and obey the orders of the court. Otherwise he would stop where he was, as far as the court was I concerned. Mr. Mather had better look at the petition , and see what it said.
ACCIDENT AT THE WILD WEST SHOW.

An unfortunate accident occurred during the perform- ance of Buffalo Bill's Wild West Show at IVlansfield,near Nottingham, on Monday afternoon, when Carter, the cow-boy cyclist, sustained concussion of the brain. Carter's item is a bicycle leap through space in which he jumps on his cycle across an open space of 56 feet, covering a distance with the plunge of 171 feet. On Monday afternoon he covered the first distance safely, but in his flying leap he apparently slightly swerved and crashed into an arc-lamp, falling to the ground with much force. Doctors who were summoned pronounced him to be suffering from 3oncussion of the brain. He was also bruised, and had his face cut with the broken glass.

A CHURCH STRUCK BY LIGHTNING. lAfter morning service at St. Nicholas Church, King's Lynn, on Sunday, the congregation were detained by a thunderstorm, accompanied by a deluge of rain. A deafening crash caused much alarm,the lightning having descended by four stove-pipes which pierced the roofs and ran across the floor from one end to another. No damage was done to the fabric, but the pipes were somewhat deranged, and a panic was caused among the school children. Some ladies fainted, and one chorister I felt a shock.

! 'Mere was a marriage, of course. Will Simmons had returned as third mate. lie was shortly to go :up for examination for a second mate's certificate. Certainly there was no prospect that , Bella Wakeman would ever have "to keep a man." Yet her own joy over the wedding found but a poor reflection in the village. The fisherfolk had an almost equal antipathy to those who came to the fishing from other employments and to those who , left the fishing for the larger career of the open

seas. "It's all reef, mebbe,'' said Gilbert -Jack's wife, "but a lass should marry among her amn folk:" am n folk, hinny ?" said Ernstie Mellin. "But surely, mah god woman, Will Simmons is one of us ? " • • , "Wis one of us, Ernstie ; but boo do we. knaw what blood's in him. ills mother wasn't one o' the best, as nh kea. Oor own lads sticks bi the village, an gans as their tethers did, an' as - their grandfet hers did for ivver se many generations before them, and what die we knaaw aboot those as dis any ither way, except dint they gang off and we hears little tuair good of 'nn?"

_ When the first infantile complaint attacked it the mother was distracted. Then; too, it cried for Uncle Reuben and his fiddle. What was she to do in suCh a case ? The plaints of the Child directed her. Reuben had again taken to playing his violin in the solitude of the Links since the little girl had become di—to playing it just where he had played it to the mother in days gone by—and Bella, hearing those strains, followed them to a well- known spot and said: "0 Reuben, the bairn wants ye so much. Ah think she'll die if ye divvent come." It was a great moment for Reuben when this was said. This was what he had been hoping and longing for. His heart thumped in his breast with tenderness for the child and rove for the mother.,

What it was in his mind to say on the moment was: "I'll come an' stay with the child all my life if you'll let me, Bella." But he shrank from a declaration like this, on a second rapid mental survey of things, as if he had been contemplating a blow at the face that he loved before all other faces in the 'world. So he said: "She wants me, Bella ? "
"Aye, she minis ye an' the fiddle." Reuben's heart dropped a little when he per- ceived that the violin was considered to be the most necessary part of himself. Nevertheless he said:

"Well, I'll come." And the first visit was the beginning of many, and the child recovered rapidly enough. And the playing of the violin at night became one of the daily ceremonies of the household, until at last Reuben plucked up heart to say: "Bella, isn't it time that we were wed ?"

Whereupon Bella disolved into a aood of tears, thinking of Will Simmons and the death he had died, and of the days when they -were children together, and of how Reuben had nearly won her heart one quiet, beautiful night when he was playing his violin on the Links. But then the cry of the steamer's syren had come to tell her that Will Simmons had first place in her affections. And, having cried her fill, Bella said: "I will nivver marry until my Will has been dead seven year." "And that will be 1i two months' time," said Reuben, putting his violin under his arm; "and so I'll go off and get th' cottage ready for you, Bella."

The sea had been "calling," as the fisherfolk said, for two days past, and the night preceding the day on which Reuben Taylor was to be married was one of terrible and methorable storm. The waves broke in the bay with the sound of continuous thunder ;• the water wqs, white as far as the eye could reach through the driving rain ; the wind was of such force that the fishermen at the look-out had, at brief intervals, to turn their backs to the hurricane in order to 'draw.:a free breath.

But Reuben was taking no note of the storm outside. He was calmly and perfectly happy, for he had brought Bella round to inspect the cottage which was in a few hours' time to become her own. He had lavished all his savings upon it, and all his desire was to please one whom he had loved from his boyhood, and for whom be had waited as Jacob Waited for Rachel. "e like it, Bella ?" _ _ _

"It's just lovely, Reuben," and she looked upon him gratefully and admiringly, with pride in the manliness of his face and the bright youthfulness which seemed likely to endure into middle age. The old love was dead and buried; and now Bella felt for Reuben Taylor such a quiet and tranquil affection as Will Simmons had never inspired in his day. "Ye'd like a tune on the fiddle before ye go?" said Reuben, inquiringly. "Aye, that I would, just for aad sake's sake," Bella responded. And so Reuben took his violin from its case, and leant against the new mahogany sideboard, and struck into the first bars of a merry tune which was to be the expression of his delight in the realisation of .a long-delayed happiness. • But just then the report of a gun rang out above the noise of the tempest out of doors, and Bella sprang up with a white face, knowing well what that sound portended. "There's a ship on, Bella," said Reuben, casting his violin down as if it had suddenly become of no value; "I mann go and- take my place in the boa t. " , Fishermen, clanking along in heavy sea-boots, were already running past the door. "Come alang, Reuben, lad," said one of -the men, lifting the latch and thrustinc, his head into the ; cottage. "She's on the Bear's Back!" Reuben had already donned his oilskins and his sou'-wester ; and now lac took Bella in his arms, and gazed at her with a calm, resolute face that had suddenly hardened in the presence of an • emergency which was also a duty. "0 Reuben," she said, "this is nae night for the lifeboat to gan oot. The Lord save us, but yell all be drooned !" "I must gan, lass. W'hatever happens, I must gan," and he kissed her passionately, and then almost flung her away from him as he ran out of the door and into the storm. "6 Oh, hear us when we cry to Thee For those in peril on the sea,'"

moaned Bella Simmons, as she sank down on her knees and burst into heavy weeping. Was the cruel sea to claim her lover for the second time? Well, then, she would see the last of him, what- ever befell; and she wrapped her shawl round her head and went out into the pitiless rain, and watched the lifeboat as it plunged through the

"Aye, and the chanciest thing of all," his mate would rejoin, "was when we thowt we had gotten them all aboard the boat, and Reuben Taylor wad have us torn back because, be said, there was anither man on board, calling oot tiv us not to leave him. And so there wis, for sure, one as had been doon below packin' up suvverins in a belt. An' ye ken who that wis weel enough. It wis Reuben as saved him; an' Ah think if Ah'd bin Reuben, Ah should have left him where he wis, to droon or owt. But, after all, one nivver knaws. A life's a life, and one maim save it if one can, by God's help." "Ah seed Reuben when he come ashore. He just mounted the bank like a man as wis as much deed as alive; and when he got to the top, he just pulled himself together and walked straight to where Bella Simmons stood. `Aw've brought ye yo'i man,' he said, and pressed her hand once, and then walked away. An' that wis the last Ah seed of him, for mah part." "There wis a sale, I mind, of all Reuben's things, the boat, an' what not. That was after he had gane awa'. Bill Simmons bowt in some of 4-lint furniture, I hard."

"Aye; it was Bella made him do that. She wanted something to remember Reuben by. It wig him that saved ye oot iv the jaws of deeth,' she tent, him when he said oot that he wanted none of Reuben's things. It's not what ye want, it's what I want mysel" she said. 'Ab, if some things could ha' been different ! ' she sighed to ma wife one day; and then bethought her, and that 7-As all she said."
_ 'What would she have had different, think ye ? "
"Ah'll ax ye anither question, Scotch-wise: Divvent ye think that sone ships come hame that or some folks' NA() were better away 2 _ - (Tam END.I

div.head: SCHOOLS QUESTION.
div.p: THE SCHOOLS QUESTION.
CHILDREN RUINED BY EXCITEMENT.

We all admit the usefulness of Education and the goo 4 done by Board and other schools. But the terrible effect of over-excitement and forced work for Examin- ations demands enquiry. Children are everywhere breaking down from this cause. Great numbers, of little girls especially, come under the doctor for St. Vitus' dance and other nervous complaints. Boys grow too thin and weedy to make strong men. The cause is over-excitement in school, Acting on weak constitutions; the cure is nerve-feeding. ff the brain and nerves are properly fed-up, children learn easily and keep their health-. Blood is the food of brain and nerves.. Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people are the food of the blood. It is pale, thin, aniemic children—children with sharp, pinched-looking faces, lips always open, eyes with dark rims, gums pale and bloodless, who break down from too much school. St. Vitus' dance, which used to be a rare disease, is every year getting more common, and doctors find it very difficult to cure. How Dr. Williams' pink pills cure it, by feeding up the nerves and brain with the new, •rich blood, which they make, is well shown by the following example : We have selected one of the very worst cases of St. Vitus' dance. It is that of a young lady who had some of the best medical attention in more than one hospital. This young lady, Miss Harriet Louisa Roberts, resides with her parents at 44. Ada-road, Smethwick, Birming- ham, and it is ten years since the first sign of illness was seen. Mrs. Roberts thus relates the story of her daughter's suffering : " I first noticed that my daughter's hands were unsteady. If asked to carry a plate or basin she would drop it, and I thought it was a clumsy way she had. But she would cry and say 'Oh. mother, I really cannot holp it!' She often cried because she could not do

her lessons. Soon I began to see that she was afflicted with some nervous complaint. I hoped she would grow out of it; but as her nervousness increased, I took her to the children's j hospital as an out-patient for above twelve months, but she grew so much worse in spite of all the skill bestowed on her that she was admitted as an in-patient for a further three months. Appearing a 'little better, she resumed school, but a fortnight after she was away again and for the next two years she was a patient at the Queen's Hospital, and at the general hospital where, after five weeks' treatment as a resident patient,she was discharged, a Sister at the hospital remarking that everything possible had been done for her. I fetched her home thoroughly disappointed. She appeared to me not one bit better than when she entered. "The nervousness had undoubtedly developed into St. Vitus' dance. She couldn't keep still two minutes together. It was impossible for her to do her own hair, and there was a curious jumping way about her. We were obliged to put her bed against the wall lest she should tumble out; and often, on going to her room, I have found her underneath the bed. Her eyes rolled strangely, her tongue stuck out of her mouth, her head would nod, and her hands at one time shook so violently that she could not feed herself. In walking, she would drag her legs after her as if they were useless. "But lam thankful to say," Mrs. Roberts went on, "that she looks very different now, and the reason of it is this : My son called our attention to Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people. He bought us ono box, and. when Harriet had taken these, to the surprise of every- one there was a decided improvement. He bought her another, and then a third. She has started to go to business now. All my neighbours know how she was afflicted and can vouch for the truth of this. I have not exagger4ted the facts in the least." The cure exaggerated St. Vitus' dance by D. Williams' pink pills is purely a case of blood-making, and the same pills have cured amemia(which is simply bloodlessness), comsumption, decline, eczema, and all other diseases of the blood, as well as rheumatism, paralysis, gout, sciatica, and the ailments which women endure in silence. The genuine pills bear Dr. Williams' name,and substitutes should be avoided, as they never cured any- one. Dr. Williams' medicine company,Holborn- viaduct, London, will senda box, pest free for two shillings and ninepence, or six for thirteen and nine, but they can be had at all medicine shops, if purchasers insist on having the genuine.

Choral Service at Wycliffe Church. The members of the Wycliffe Church choir gave a special choral service on Sunday evening, and acquitted themselves admirably in an interpretation of "The Daughter of Jairus," by the late Sir J. Stainer. The soloists were Mrs. R. H. Pearson (soprano), Mr. Arthur Griffiths (tenor) and Mr. Bowman Hibbert (bass), and they sang the several recitatives and airs with feeling and expression. The choruses were especially well rendered, the lady members of the choir distinguishing themselves in the wailing chorus of women, and the men in the chorus of unbelievers. In the conclud- ing trio and chorus "To Him who left His throne," the trio was sung by Miss Knowles, Mr. W. Brown and Mr. J. Knowles. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., was responsible for the train- of the choir, and is to be congratulated upon its present high state of efficiency. Mr. A. Corney conducted the devotional part of the service and also delivered a brief address. He observed that the service of song brought back to them the miracle of Jesus Christ in the raising of the daughter of Jairus to life again. The three miracles of Christ in raising the dead to life were typical, he said, of Christ's dealing with the human soul. The story of the daughter of Jairus was the story of how Christ awakened the soul of a sleeping child. Some doubted whether children had it soul. It was impossible to prove it. It did not admit of proof. You could not demonstrate the immortality of the soul by any process of reasoning. The demonstration was of the spirit and I spirit spoke to spirit. There were great truths of life that could not be .demlnstrsted by any process of reasoning. A man with an artistic taste saw the beauty of a picture, but he could not prove its beauty to a man who had no love of beauty. In like manner there was no other demonstration of the reality of friendship but the spirit of friendship itself. Friendship spoke to friendship, heart answered to heart and soul to soul. The spiritual life must be fed,and the greatest problem was how were they to feed and nurture the spiritual nature. Anything in literature in art, in Paetry,in anything else that tended to poison the springs of manhood and womanhood ought to be put down, for , we lived by reverence, hope and love.

div.head: Baptist Church, Latchford.
div.p: Baptist Church, Latchford.

There was a crowded congregation at this church on Sunday evening to witness the immersion of five candi- dates. The service, which lasted scarcely an hour and a half, was very impressive. The minister, the Rev. J. F. Matthews, gave an exposition and defence of the New Testament position for which Baptists especially stand, and impressed upon the audience the need for personal loyalty toChrist and His teaching.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

I At the meeting of this society on Sunday, Mr. Cross kill presided, and spoke upon the necessity, of every , member doing what he could to extend the work and ' usefulness of the society.—Mr. Moreland, of Man- chester, delivered a thoughtful address on "Prayer." He asked them to live theirprayers, and when making their petitions to know what they wanted, and seek an answer to prayer.—Master Walter Pierce contributed an ; organ solo. Mr. Farrar, hon secretary, extended a • ordial welcome to a new member. I Bold Street Wesleyan Sunday School. I I On Sunday afternoon a special re-opening service was held in this school which has undergone extensive alterations and improvements at the hands of Mr. William Winstanley, by whom the work has teen very creditably done. The painting, decorating and cleaning have effected a wonderful improvement in the appear- ' ance of the room, and the texts introduced into the • panels are very effective. Mr. William Roberts J.P. ' presided at the service and delivered an address full of encouragement. Appropriate and complimentary refer- ences were made to a large number of workers, past and piesent, in the old school in Butter- market-street, and in , the present building, Mr. William Hickman followed with some ob- servations to the parents and friends, teachers and children, his words of advice and instruction being listened to with great interest. The children sang a number of anniversary hymns, and the choir gave an excellent rendering of an anthem, but the chief musical event of the afternoon was the performance of "The Holy City" (Adams), which was a credit to all con- cerned, especially to the organist and conductor, Mr. Frank Hickman. Mr. Albert Perkins, superintendent of the Sunday school, also took part In the re-opening service. The collections, which were in aid of the renovation fund, amounted to is. Bd., and as Mr. George Ashton kindly contributed a similar amount, according to promise, the handsome sum of £lO 15s. 4d. was realized altogether. Mr. Ashton was heartily thanked for his generosity, and a similar compliment was paid to the Chairman and speaker.

div.head: Rev. H. Dunnico and Two Years' Eventful
div.p: The Rev. H. Dunnico and Two Years' Eventful
Ministry. Warrington a " Drink-Ridden, Brewery- Ridden Town." Lack of Public Spirit.

Services were held on Sunday in celebration of the second anniversary of the settlement of the Rev. H. Minnie° as pastor of Golborne-street Baptist Church. There was an exceptionally large congregation at the morning service, and in the afternoon the church was well filled. In the evening the Parr Hall was crowded. Basing his remarks on Romans 1. 16, "For lam not ashamed of the Gospel of Ch?ist ; it is the power of God," the preacher said that in a few minutes he would have completed the second year of his ministry in their midst. That ministry, though brief, had been a very eventful one, and, perhaps, a unique one; at any rate, he (the preacher) had learned many things and un- learned many more. When he decided to settle in Warrington many of his friends told him that if he succeeded in Warrington he would succeed anywhere. Well, . his ministry had be en success- ful beyond even his highest expectations, but he gave God the glory. He had found out that Warrington was a drink-ridden and a brewery-ridden town, but by the grace of God they hoped to alter that ere long. He must also confess that so far as he could sea therewas a lack of public spirit in the town, and that very few of their leading men were giving either their money or their service in its behalf. Chivalry patriotism, and unselfishness were conspicuous by their absence. So far as the people of Warrington were con- cerned he loved them more to-day than ever. They ad- mired boldness and respected frankness, even when they differed with a man, and with capable leaders the,g would be second to none. Proceeding to discMss the Sunday evening ser- vices, first in the Royal Court, and afterwards n the Parr Hall, Mr. Dunnico said that at the outset even some of his frionds ventured to suggest that for once he had outreached himself, but when they remem- bered that five months had passed away, and that only on two or three occasions had they had less than 1,000 people present, even his critics must admit that they had not entirely failed. That fact had proved two things first, that men and women would attend religious ser- vices when they could meet on equal terms,and secondly that the old Gospel had still power to draw men and women together in away that nothing else coull. They were told by some people that Christianity was played out, and that the Gospel had had its day, and if they took a superficial view of things they might even be tempted to believe that &there was some truth in the statement. Some of the mightiest intellects of the day had hurled all the force of their intellects against it,but all in vain. As the seagulls dashing themselves against the lighthouse failed to extinguish its light, and lay bruised and helpless on the rocks below, so these men dashed themselves against the Light of the World all in vain, for the Light continued to shine across the dark and angry waters of sin. Again and again during his short ministry he had been called upon to deal with three of the most stupendous facts of history, viz., sin, sorrow and death, and he had found again and again that no message save the Gospel of Jesus was of any use. If there was one thing more than another his ministry had taught him, it was this : that a purely ethical and social gospel was impotent and helpless to deal with the appalling evils of the times. Only a week or two ago one of the most conspicuous Socialists in Warrington stated in his own church that the " social gospel " preached by them was not based upon the teachings of Jesus, and that Jesus was not a Socialist. If that was true, then it was worthless ; it was a waste of time to listen to it. The only Socialism that could .ever be successful was that of Jesus Christ. No one had worked harder or with a more sincere motive on behalf of working Er en than he had; no one was more convinced than the present social order of self- interest, greed, and avarice must come to an end. How this re-adjustment would come he did not know, but when it did come it would come on the basis of Christ's perfect law. The socialism of Jesus, or "Christian Socialism," was broad, universal, international broad as the love of God. He did not talk about "Britain for the British," "Let the Armenians look after themselves," "Foreigners not admitted." The Socialism of Jesus did not include such a word as " foreigner " in its vocabulary; it taught us that all men throughout the world were brothers. The Socialism that would drive out the foreigner from our shores simply because he was a foreigner, and, perhaps in some cases, a better work- man, was a bastard Socialism. It u-as the Socialism of Jesus that made John Wesley term all the world his parish- that sent William Carey to the perishing multi- tudes of India; that sent Father Damien to his lonely grave on that leper isle; David Livingstone to his lonely death in the African desert, and brought the Son of Glory to the agony of the cross. He urged his hearers to consecrate their lives to this higher service. The choir and children rendeted anthems and hymns at all the services, Mr. 'P. Brough being the conductor, and Mr. Albert Trow organist.

A SILVER BEDROONI SUITE. It is stated that one of the most extraordinary order?. ever received in Sheffield has been booked by a firm of well-known silversmiths in Sheffield. The order is for a suite of bedroom furniture in sterling silver. Amongst the articles are a bedstead, a cabinet, a dressing table, a dozen chairs, three foot baths, three hot water cans, and other bedroom requisites. The moulding of the room and other ornamentation will also be of sterling silver. The order has come from an Eastern country.

div.head: KING'S BIRTHDAY ?HONOUR!.
div.p: THE KING'S BIRTHDAY ?HONOUR!.

The Birthday Honours' list this year was a tzery long one and, as usV.l, svery 'interesting, but no new peerages were created. Mr. 'Charles Booth, Colonel Kenyon Slaney, and 1.1. r. Parker Smith are the new Privy COl3ll- - and the first-named is a particularly P°Pular and well-deserved honour, the •out- Ceme of years of public philanthropic work. -The King, in addition, conferred seven baronetcies and a long list of knighthoods. The new baronets are Mr. Alfred !Harms- 'Worth, the founder and proprietor of the baily Mail," and many other papers, Sir Robert Ropner, M.P. for Stockton, who is a 'well-known owner and builder of ships and aS popular as he is well known in Durham -and Yorkshire; Sir Edward Wills, of the Iniperial Tobacco TRist ; Mr. Walter Palmer, of the great Reading biscuit firm and M.P. for Salisbury Mr. Henry Kimber, who has

'rePresented Wandsworth in the House of .Ceinmoils ever since it was made a con stituency on its own account in 1885, and is well known in connection with many big business enterprises; Mr. George White, the tristol millionaire and the pioneer of electric steam traction; and Mr. William Goulding, the chairman of the Great Southern and Western Railway in Ireland. Amongst the neW knights, of whom there are twenty-six, -are Mr. Thomas Barclay, president of the British Chamber of Commerce in Paris; Dr. I.gar, the great composer, who has made himself so famous -with his "Dream of 'Gerontius " ; Professor Dewar, the eminent scientist; Mr_ Doughty, M.P. for Grimsby; Mr- Gray Hill, the president of the Incor- Torated Law Society; and Dr. Stevenson, the allalyst to the Home Office. In addition, there was a long list of C.B.'s and War Office ;arid Colonial Office honours, together with many additions to the Order of St. Michael 'arid St, George and the Imperial Servici "Drder.

div.head: BLOODLESS SURGERY IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: BLOODLESS SURGERY IN SCOTLAND.

A Scotsman who is being much talked about at present is Mr. William Rae, of Blantyre, who has been working some mar- vellous cures by his system of bloodless 'surgery and bone-setting. As a young man 'he studied anatomy as a hobby and soon began to put it to practical account. Many diseases which cripple people he holds are due simply to dis- location, an d his system is to put the joints back into their proper places. So great was his success that twelve years ago he was forced to relinquish hi s work as a col- liery official and devote himself solely to the cure of the diseases he has

made a special- Y of. Now he is inundated with cripples iron' - all over the country, and special ex- •2lirsion trains are being run to Blantyre. -\lany of his cures are reported to be mar- and many poor cripples have left his Ittle ),. cottage rejoicing. Mr. Rae is in no Sense of the word a quack, nor does he Profess to work miracles. He simply applies ,rnimonsense principles to a thorough know- edge of anatomy. So great has been the :111mand for his services of late that he finds unself overworked and in need of a com- .Plete rest, but prior to his holiday, he has 'Promised to come south to the colliery ,Vstricts of Lancashire, making Bolton his eadquarters. His fees are very small, and 111 no case will he take more ,than half a '..(3vereign. Sixty years of age, Mr. Rae is typical Scot : tall and upright; and he lived all his life in the neighbourhood of 'Clasgow.

Mr. Roosevelt was nominated unanimously; and Senator Fairbanks was nominated for the Vice-Presidency on the Republican ticket. The Democratic Convention meets on July 6th ; ' but it is by no means certain whom they will choose to run against the present President. Judge 41ton B. Parker represents the Conservative wing of the Democrats, and Mr. W. R. Hears, of the "New York Journal," the Radical wing: whilst Mr. MacClellan, the Mayor of New York, is in the running. But, should there be a serious split in the party, it is probable that Mr. Grover Cleve- land, the Ex-President may be nominated to run for the Democrats. Mr. Roosevelt's election committee will be run by his secretary, Mr? G. B. Cortelyon, who has been secretary to three successive Presidents and will always be remembered for the part he played when President McKinley was assassinated at Buffalo. For some days the affairs of the nation practically rested in his hands: and •he proved 'himself a man of action. Above all, he is a man of absolute political probity, and Mr. Roosevelt wants his election run on "clean" lines.

div.head: KING AT KIEL.
div.p: THE KING AT KIEL.

It is pleasing to note that the King's reception in Germany was most cordial, and although the visit is being described as having no political significance, it will indeed have served a good purpose if it only restores the reciprocal confidence formerly existing between t h e tw 0 counties
but lost in the course of the
last few years. On arriving at Kiel King Ed-
ward, who was
met by the
Kaiser,
Empress
aboard
Hohenwilern,
and afterwards
paid a visit to Prince Henry
of Prussia. The
gala dinner on
board the Ho- henzollern was a
most
brilliant
function,
and
was attended by PRINCE HENRY OF PRUSSIA, the Crown THE KING'S HOST.
Prince of

• Germany Prince Eitel Frederick, Prince William of Sweden, and the Ministers and Secretaries of State, including Count von Buelow, the Imperial Chancellor, as well as the higher Court dignitaries. The King sat between the Emperor and the Empress and in proposing King Edward's health the Kaiser referred to His Majesty's exhaustive endeavours in the pres.ervation of peace, and the King in reply hoped that the two flags would ,float side by side to the most remote ages, even as to-day, for the maintenance of peace and the welfare not only of our own countries but also of all other nations. The Emperor's toast was accompanied by a salute from the warships, and the British and Gelman National An- thems respectively were played at the con- clusion of each toast. As King Edward left the " Hohenzollern " at the conclusion of the banquet the Kaiser sent up a rocket .1 and almost instantaneously all the warships in the harbour. British and German, were simultaneously illuminated, and presented a most beautiful sight. The "Victoria and Albert "looked particularly •well in a blaze of red, white and blue.

div.head: SIR CHARLES ELLIOT AND THE FOREIGN OFFICE.
div.p: SIR CHARLES ELLIOT AND THE FOREIGN OFFICE.
The resignation of Sir Charles Eliot who

held the post of Administrator of British East Africa, to which Sir Donald Stewart has been appointed in his stead, has caused con- siderable sensation in political circles. The immediate cause was his refusal to grant concessions to the East Africa Syndicate which the Marquess of Lansdowne had • \ promised in his capacity of Foreign Secre- tary. Sir Charles Eliot considered that these con- cessions created an unfair mono- poly and set his face against - • . ...‘ them, thereby falling foul of s4l the authorities . , •-• at home with - the result that his resignation became neces- sary. The full SIR CHARLES ELLIOT. rights and wrongs of the matter are at present shrouded in official mystery, but the whole matter will, as soon as Sir Charles Eliot arrives in England, be thrashed out fully in Parliament. The ex- Administrator's career has been a very dis- tinguished one. Born in 1864, he went from Cheltenham to Oxford, where he carried all before him from Balliol scholarships to the Hertford and Craven and was elected a Fellow of Trinity. In 1888 he went to St. Petersburg as Third Secretary to the Embassy and in 1893 was transferred to Constanti- nople, where he stayed until 1898. In 1892 Sir Charles Eliot was charge d'affaires in Morocco and held the same important post in Bulgaria in 1895 and Servia in 1897. In 1898 he was appointed Secretary to the Embassy at Washington, and a year later he became High Commissioner in Samoa. Then he went oa to East Africa, being knighted in Igo°.

div.head: WEAR WEAR AND TEAR OF CITY LIFE.
div.p: THE WEAR WEAR AND TEAR OF CITY LIFE.

Why do so many of our City men look so sickly? Be- cause they drink too much tea,and when they are fagged out cannot take more substantial and nutritive food. The system thus gradually becomes weakened and debil- itated; theie is no relish for food, no energy for work, and the whole of the physical and mental condition be- comes seriously deranged. One City clerk—Mr. H. W. Elliot, 23, Norfolk Road, Canonbury, N.—writes :—" I work late hours, but I find Dr. Tibbles' Vi-Cocoa a delicious and stimulating drink. My doctor, grocer, and chemist speak very highly of it." And if you use Vi-Cocoa regularly you will speak very highly of it too. Sold in 6d. packets and 9d. and is. 6d. tins everywhere.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
Tweed Suits for the Boys on Sundays.

Mr. A. Brooks presided at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians held on Wednesday morning. There were also present :—Mrs. Clay, Miss Broadbent, Rev. Father Mercer, Rev. T. R. Matthews, Dr. Patterson, Dr. Murray, Messrs. S. Davies, J. Payton, J. Clarke, E. L. Bent, William Hickman, A. J. Jolley, T. H. Ashcroft, J. W. Knowles, William Hough- ton, R. Bolton, W. Flanagan, G. Thompson, It. Forshaw, a Mather, J. Turton, and J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), J. F. Awbery (master) and A. Wright (superintendent).

div.head: WALKING DIY.
div.p: WALKING DIY.

The Schools Committee recommended that the chil- dren take part in the Warrington Walking Day; that their railway fares be paid, and the usual treat and extras be allowed. The minutes also included consideration of a reserved minute, as follows :—" After consideration of the minute of May 17th, which had been referred back for further consideration, it was agreed that tweed suits be provided for wearing on Sundays, and when walking out, for the boys in the homes." _ . _

Mr. MATHER moved the confirmation of the minutes. Mr. WILLIAM HOUGHTON moved an amendment "That the minute of the Schools Committee which was passed at their meeting on June 14th, recommending that a change from corduroy to tweed be made for boys' uniform, confirmation of which was deferred pending special notice being given to the members of the Board be expunged, and that no change be made in the material of boys' uniform for the present." He said he regarded the resolution of the committee as simply getting in the thin end of the wedge,and that in course of time corduroy would be dispensed with. The question of expense hardly admitted of any discussion. At the committee meeting it was stated that 2 suits would have to be provided where one suit Of corduroy now sufficed. That would involve the services of another tailor. The objection to corduroy was a sentimental one, but they could not pay their rates with sentiment. They could not say to the rate collector "I have a sentimental objection to them." (Laughter.) By clothing the boys in the stuff proposed they would interfere with that happy freedom which they enjoyed in their sports and play. Furthermore, it would give a boy a distaste for working clothes and he would object to go into a work- ing suit of clothes. The change had been made on a previous occasion and the material shrank up so much that the boys looked very untidy. He hoped the Board would stick t 4 corduroy. Mr. KNOWLES in seconding, said he felt that pauper children ought not to be placed in a better position than the children of the workingman who was trying to bring up his family respectably on a wage of Ll a week. If the cottage homes at Padgate were to be made into a cheap boarding school, the workingman with a large family would be disposed to play "the old soldier," with a bad leg, so that he might get his children into he cottage homes. There were members of the Board wise enough and far-seeing enough to know that it was not the garment that made the man or the woman' but the gifts that the Almighty gave them at their birth and the manner in which their talents had been developed. The children at Padgate were treated much better than were those in other unions. Mr. HicKm : So they ought to be.

Mr. KNOWLES (contintiingr said it was a dangerous thing to interfere with anything that was doing well. There had been no grumbling outside as to the dressing of the children and it was only a fad of a few Guardians to seek a change. __ •

Mr. MATHEIi: observed that Mr. KnOwles was a mem- ber of the School Committee but if he had attended the meetings of the committee he would not have made the remarks he had given utterance to. He (Mr. Mather) had been a member of the committee for four years, but he had not seen Mr. Knowles at a single meeting. When boys left the schools they were given two tweed suits. The reason assigned for this action was that if they wore the corduroy suits the finger of scorn was pointed at the boys as coming from the Workhouse and it was not good for them. He did not what wit Mr. Knowles said about workingmen's children being dressed in corduroy. He had instituted inquiries at the schools in the town and district, and he had the replies with him. They would take about two days to rd them. (Llughter.) Mr. KNOWLES : We had better take them as read.

Mr. THOMPSON : We don't want the opinions of other people; we want to form our own opinions. Mr. KNOWLES : I must object to the replies beißg read, as the inquiries have not been sent out by the Board.

Mr. 'MATHER (continuing) said the replies showed that out of 1,700 scholars only 55 wore corduroy. He (Mr. Mather)also sent out a circular to all the unions in Lancashire inquiring what kind of dress was worn by the boys, and asking their experience as to the difference in cost between corduroy and tweed. He found that Warrington was the only union in the county that clothed the boys in corduroy. Mr. HOUGHTON: I dispute that. Mr. MATHER : Will you kindly go through the replies. They are here. Mr. KNOWLES : Don't take the other side's docu- ments. (Laughter.) Mr. MATHER : Are we the only Solomons or wise men in Lancashire? Equally wise people will not adopt corduroy. Proceeding to discuss the question ef cost, Mr. Mather said the replies were to the effect that the extra cost of tweed was very little, where corduroy was worn for working and playing in,as was proposed at Padgate. Mr. Houghton came there that morning to oppose the resolution because it was passed by a small majority, hut on a memorable occasion Mr. Houghton gave his vote in favour of a proposal that was carried by a majority on the grouna that the Board had no right to upset the decision of a committee. ' Mr. HOUGHTON: Perhaps it was t Subject of no importance. Mr. MATHER : It was a most important resolution affecting the hospital. Continuing, Mr. Mather said if he thought the expense would be very much greater, he would be against any alteration. Mr. FLANAGAN pointed out that the _resolution was carried by a majority of three. Mr. E. L. BENT thought it was, very uncharitable on the part of Mr. Houghton to interfere with the matter when it had been thoroughly. discussed in committee. The initial cost of intryducing tweed was the heaviest item, but this would not be more than £6O or £7O. Mr. FORSHAW considered that Mr. Knowles had not had sufacient experience of the work at Padgate schools to express an opinion on the subject. His arguments were discounted by a "humorous vein of s.arcasni." Mr. HicRMAN said the Board had changed the girls clothing, and he did not see why the boys should always be obliged to wear corduroy. Mr. PAYTON observed that if Mr. Knowles had lieatd the remarks made last Walking Day with reference to corduroy worn by the boys he would not have remarked that no complaints had been made. Mr. BOLTON said he supported the proposed change not because it was any fad of his. but because he wanted to bring the boys out with more self respect. When the boys came out of the institution, wearing corduroy suits, everyone knew that they were paupers. Some of the boys were very sensitive and walked as if they had done something wrong. He knew a Padgate school lad who was very sensitive respecting corduroy suits and who looked upon his clothes as those of a pauper. 116 Mr. Bolton) had to impress upon the lad the necessity is abusing his mind of any idea of pauperism.

Mr. S. DAVIES hoped the Board would settle once for all this vexed question of clothing. He objected to the extra expense and inconvenience which the charge would entail but he was inclined GO be loyal to his com- mittee and support the proposal. On a vote being taken 10 voted for the amendment. The CHAIRMAN (without taking a vote in favour of the original motion) said the minutes of the committee were carried.
There were 22 members present. The ruling of the Chairman greatly pleased Mr. Mather. Mr. Houghton did not press for a further vote, and the proposed change in the clothing will be made.

div.head: TRAINING OF PROBATIONERS.
div.p: THE TRAINING OF PROBATIONERS.

Meeting on the 24th of June,--tii-e-ifoii-a-e-bommittee considered the necessity for providing more efficient general training for probationers. It was felt that the difficulties of the committee in propounding a scheme were great,as they possessed no resident medical officer but it was pointed out that other infirmaries similar in character and size to Warrington were training their probationers without possessing a medical man, resident on the premises, and that the standard of the proba- tioners was good; the nursing more efficient and the examination results highly gratifying and pleasing to the Guardians. If the Warrington Guardians could base their scheme of better training somewhat upon the successful lines obtainable elsewhere together with a proposal from the Kendrick-street Infirmary for joint amalgamation, a good beneficial efficiency would result therefrom.—After discussion,Messrs. Jolley, Thompson, Mrs. Clay and the Master were constituted a committee to visit the Mansfield and Walsall infirmaries where efficient training was provided by the Guardians and who have no resident medical officer, the deputation expenses to be paid out of the Master's petty cash. It was resolved that the following resolution shouKstand on the Board's minutes :—That on the satisfactory com- pletion of the three years' course of training,the proba- tioners shall receive a certificate of competency pro- vided they have passed such examinations as may be prescribed by the Guardians on the Local Government Board.

Mr. A. J. JOLLEY, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said he felt confident that the minutes relating to probationers would meetwith approval. The method of working at the (infirmary, more particularly under the superintendence of Miss Biggan, had improved mat- ters all round,and he thought the committee saw their way clear to give more efficient general training for probationers without any material addition to the ex- penditure. The Board would be pleased to hear that Mr. Samuel Greenway (tailor), had now sufficiently re- covered as to be able to continue his services.

Mr. FORSHAW seconded the adoption of the minutes. Mr. ASHCROFT did not see the necessity of appointing, four on a deputation to the Mansfield and Walsall infirm- aries. A lot of money had been spent recently on deputations, and he thought unnecessarily. He object- ed to four persons joining this deputation. Mr. THOMPSON said he would be pleased to withdraw his name.
Mr. S. MtVIES observed that he would have voted against it if he had been present.

-Mr. JOLLEY ventured to think that the small expense to be incurred would be mere than saved by the experi- ence which the deputation would gain on such an errand. There were points of information which could not be got by corret,pondence. The nursing question was a very difficult one, and if members would take the trouble to ascertain the cost of advertising for nurses they would find that it had been very expensive. The cost of the deputation would be more than recouped by the information gained, to say nothing of the improved training for probationers. He would regret if Mr. Thompson did not join the deputation as Mr. Thompson's assistance would be of value, seeing that he had served on the Warrington infirmary and Dispensary Committee. Mr. MATHER said they owed it to their nurses that they should do the best they could for them. (Hear, hear.)
The minutes were then passed. A GRATUITY FOR MR. HOLFORD.

The Board then prOCe-ed-e-d—tO-consider the "application by Mr. George Holford, vaccination officer,for a gratuity to him in consideration of the extra services discharged by him during the recent attack of small-pox. The CHAIRM AN said the sub-committee went through the various papers submitted by Mr. Holford, and there was no doubt but that Mr. Holford did a great deal of extra work. There were 2,000 re-vaccinations for which Mr. Holford got no fee. He visited every house where there was an outbreak of smallpox. Mr. Holford would be satisfied if the Board gave him twelve guineas and he (the Chairman) proposed that subject to the approval of the Local Government Board, that amount be paid to Mr. Holford. Mr. BENT seconded.
Mr. KNOWLES asked whether the fees of vaccination officers were not increased understhe last Vaccination Act.
The CLERK said the Act of Parliament threw additional work on the vaccinatiov officer and the fee was raised from Bd.. to is. per case. _
Mr. KNOWLES said there was occasional extra work in all situations. If the situation of vaccination officer became vacant there would be a great many ready to take it.

The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Holford had done the additional work himself. When the epidemic arose, Mr. Holford could have engaged additional assistance and that would have run away with more money. Mr. KNOWLES : Would the Local Governmunt Board have sanctioned it? The CLERK: Yes.

The Rev. Dr. MERCER pointed out that owing to the increase in vaccination, Mr. Holford would receive additional fees this year amounting to £4O. At the same time the 2,000 re-vaccination cases, for which he received no fees, meant a great deal of extra work. If the Board engaged Mr. Holford for the whole of his time he (Dr. Mercer) would have declined to give any extra remuneration, but as Mr. Holford was at liberty to take up other work, he thought it was only fair to give him twelve guineas for extra services during the three months the epidemic lasted. Mr. FORSHAW considered it a reasonable amount.

Mr. THONIPSON pointed out that vaczination was costing the Union .21,300 a year. He thought Mr. Holford and the other vaccination officers ought not to bring pressure to bear upon people to get their children vaccinated by the Union officers. Were it not for this pressure, he thought many people Would get their children vaccinated by their own doctors. The CHAIRMAN That is the Act of Parliament. Mr. ASHCROFT supported the recommendation and it was carried.
THE ACCOMMODATION QUESTION. REPLY FROM THE TARVIN UNION.

The followiniletieiVaW;eild'iiO.,:n the Clerk to the Tarvin Guardians (Mr. H. Grant Bailey) :—Crypt Chambers, 17th June. Dear sir,—My Board are willing to take adult male paupers belonging to your Union into our Workhouse at 7s. per head per week. •We can take 20. I shall be glad to hear from you as to when we may meet. I will come to Warrington to see you if it will be more convenient than you coming here. Mr. FORSHA W moved that the letter lie on the table. There were signs of returning prosperity to Warrington and district, and he did not think there would be any necessity to send paupers out of the Union. It was decided to refer the communication to the House Committee.

div.head: DEPUTATIONS TO THE POOR LAW CONFERENCE.
div.p: DEPUTATIONS TO THE POOR LAW CONFERENCE.
It was proposed that the Chairman and Vice-Chairman and the Clerk represent the Board at any preliminary meetings of the North-Western Poor Law Conference to be held at Manchester.

Mr. ASHCROFT thought the Chairman and Vice- Chairman ought to stand down and let other Guardians go. Mr. KNOWLES : Didn't you go last year? Mr. MATHER said he did not know whether it was advisable for Mr. Knowles to go, as he took so little interest in the work of the Board. The resolution was carried and the Board rose.

div.head: CURIOUS EXCISE PROSECUTION.
div.p: CURIOUS EXCISE PROSECUTION.
St. Helens Farmer's Objection,

A farmer named Taylor, of Eecleston, near St. Helens was charged at St. Helens County Petty Sessions on Tuesday with . keeping a dog without a licence. Mr. Taylor said the dog was only five months old at the time of the charge, and the Excise people had written to him once or twice offering to let him off if he paid ss. Councillor Martin (chairman).—ls this the usual thing for you to say that you will let people off on pay- ment of ss.

Mr. Fleath.—Yes, that is the procedure. If we can get them to take out the licence and pay a fine of ss. we don't bring it into court. The Defendant.—l would sooner pay the full penalty than ss. in this way. The Bench dismissed the case.

div.head: BURTONWOOD'S CHURCH HALL.
div.p: BURTONWOOD'S CHURCH HALL.
Mrs. Lyon Lays the Foundation Stone.

Saturday was a great day at the colliery village of Burtonwood, for it witnessed the laying of the founda- tion stone of the new church hall whifih is being erected by the congregation of St. Michael's. In time it is also hoped to build a handsome church, and the hall is designed as an integral part of the whole group of future buildings. It will be connected by a short corridor with the north transept of the church. The portion now in course of erection and in which the memorial stone is laid comprises the church hall proper, which will be a room measuring 68 feet long by 30 feet wide,, with small bays projecting on either side. There will be a gallery at one end over a spacious vestibule, flanked on one side by a staircase and on the other by the corridor to the church. There are lavatories and cloakrooms on each side. The hall will, it is - estimated, seat 400 persons and will be well adapted, as regards lighting and height, for mission services,. Sunday school purposes, for meetings and entertain- ments or for a gymnasium. The present contract, amounting to .£1,468, incluctes the complete shell of the hall and an additional £220 is required for its com- pletion, exclusive of furniture and appliances, architect's commission and legal expenses. Further buildings con- templated in the near future are a large class or club room in the rear of the hall, with kitchen, Scc., adjoining, which may either be used separately or in conjunction with the large halL The Church Hall fund now totals £1,400, leaving about £3OO to be raised. Mrs. T. Henry Lyon,of Appleton Hall,laid the founda- tion stone. Prior to the ceremony a service was held in the Parish Church, for parishioners and Sunday school children, at which the Vicar (Rev. A. M. Mitchell)- officiated. Afterwards a procession was formed by the clergy, church officers, choir and Sunday school child- ren,who carried all kinds of pretty flags and other bunt- ing, and, headed by the Newton Farm School Band,made its way to the site of the Church Hall, to the accom- paniment of the hymns " The Church's one foundation:* and" Through the night .of doubt and sorrow." On arriving at the site the procession was met by a large gathering.—Mrs. Lyon, who was accompanied by Mr.. Lyon, drove up shortly afterwards, being greeted by the Lord Bishop of Liverpool (Dr.Chavasse), Rev. T. Ellison (Bishop's chapiain), Archdeacon Madden, Canon. Willis and the Rev. A. M. Mitchell. There were also present the Revs. Canon Penrhyn (Winwick), T. R. Mathers and A. Ainley (St. John's Church, Earlestawn), Messrs. R. Forshaw, NV. Fairclough, T. H. H. Gordon.T. Southern S. Driag, and Drs. Valentine and Mouncey. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell, make a short state- ment in respect of the building. Canon Willis then handed Mrs. Lyon a beautiful silver trowel, on behalf of the Vicar and members of the Building Committee. - -

Mrs. -Lyon proceeded to spread the mortar, and as the stone gradually lowered into its place, she said: "To the glory of God and in the faith.. of Jesus Christ, we place this foundation stone, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost," and after tapping the stone gracefully with the ivory mallet Mrs. Lyon said "I declare this stone well and truly, laid in the name of God the Father, God the Son and God the Holy Ghost." A hymn was sung by the choir, during which the general offerings were received by the Bishop, and the- purses containing small amounts collected by school children, were presented to Mrs. Lyon on behalf of the Building Fund. The Bishop of Liverpool delivered an address in which he said that no parish hall was ever built which was more needed than in that 'mist' of Bartonwood. That hall was the result of a great and noble effort on the part of the Vicar. He thought it was a brave attempt they had made in the midst of great difficulties and considerable opposition in carrying out that notable enterprise. He thought they had set their hearts on having a Churcn Hall and a church side by side, and he believed the people of Burtonwood would never rest until on that site neN„t the hall the noble wills of a dignified church stood,' Votes of thanks were accorded to Mrs. Lyon, the Bishop, and the Vicar.

ONE OF THE OLD BRIGADE.
On Monday, Andrew Christie, of Nelson street, Run- corn, died at the age of eighty years. Christie went through the Crimean war in the 42nd Regiment, and ossesses the medals for Alma and In kerman.

div.head: MAN BLOWN THROUGH A WINDOW.
div.p: MAN BLOWN THROUGH A WINDOW.

A hugh vat of naphtha exploded with terrific force at Shoreditch methylated spirit manufactory. The back wall of the factory was blown out, the roof lifted, and a young man blown bodily through a window. He lies- in a precarious condition. VANDALISM IN SNOWDONIA.

Over 1,800 signatures have been received to the petition to the Board of Trade against the vandalism contemplated in Snowdonia in the shape of a proposed overhead electric tramway between Bettws-y-coed and Beddgelert, via Capel Curig and Pen-y-Cwrhyd. They in- clude many eminent names.
