div.head: EXAMINEE,
div.p: THE EXAMINEE,
JULY 2 19C4.
At the end of the THE MORAL OF THE yachting at Kiel, VISIT TO Kra,. Europe seems to be

convinced that it has no political significance. The whole affair has passed off most happily. Whether the idea originated with the KAISER or with the Senate of Hamburg, the KING'S visit to that famous city was an admirable inspiration. Hamburg, by its commercial character, is more in tooth with England than any other part of Germany, and its citizens certainly rose to the occasion when they et eyes oil an aiglish sovereign for the first time. Their level heads,at any rate, were unmoved by the vituperation of this country,which seems still to be the frequent employment of German professors. The pursuit of learning in Germany begets animosity,. against England,:and even so erudite a man as IVlornmsen had his heated moments when he abased us as violently as he abused Cicero. In Hamburg, merchants show a different temper but it would be rash to assume that these repre- sent German opinion. Many German journals strove to represent the KING'S visit to Kiel as a proof that England still felt herself isolated, despite the Anglo-French Agreement, and that she could not feel secure until she had conciliated Germany. The political egotism of the Teutonic mind constitutes a permanent quality of humour which is not otherwise exuberant.

Englishmen are most willing to be on, peaceable terms with Germany; but there is no desperate solicitude for her good grace. Without any vin- dictiveness, we still remember the frenzy of the whole German people against us during the South African war. With the help of their professors, they raked up every historical grievance which memory or imagination could devise. The oatbreak was too startling to be lightly dismissed, and Englishmen can scarcely be blamed if their political relations with Germany are marked in future by the element of caution. King EDWARD'S unfailing tact, however, showed that the rather excited admonitions addressed to him in some quarters before he went to Germany were quite needless. The KAISER'S admirable feeling and good Meuse gave no opening to the speculators, who are always on the look-out for new political combinations. There is evidently a magic quality in KING, EDWARD'S personality which diffuses calm wher- ever he goes. It was only the other day that the KAISER was contemplating the possibility that a bridge over the Rhine might resound with the tread of his legions marching to war. Bat when he spoke again, the colnhig visit of his uncle was in his mind, for he talked about the " solidarity " of European Peace. Unquestionably the reunion at Kiel has minis- tered to that sense of tranquillity which enables Europe to watch the progress of the struggle be- tween Russia and Japan without alarm. Having practically settled her difference with us, France has viewed the episode at Kiel with :sympathetic interest. She is so little disposed to adventure on her own account that even the crisis in Morocco, where a successful brigand has virtually usurped the authority of the Sur.rAN, finds her unwilling to exercise the rights accorded to her by the Anglo-French Agreement. She is undoubtedly disturbed by the revelation of weakness in the Russion armaments. Every Freuchman believed that Russia would make short work of Japan, and the evidence of her incapacity is a disagreeable surprise: Ten years ago it would have spread con- sternation through France; but to-day a well- guarded confidence in her own strength helps her to regard it with philosophy. In Western Europe the influences which make for peace were never stronger than they are now, and it is a matter for congratulation that no man has worked more earnestly and successfully to bring them about than the Statesman who wears the British Crown.

The monthly meeting:of the Town Council will he bold on Tuesday, and judging from the agenda the proceedings should not be protracted to any length. There are very few realty important or debatable matters on the minutes. Undoubtedly i the most interesting item s the election of an alderman to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Alderman Heaton. An aldermanic election always creates a little excitement, even if the order of succession hAs been cut and dried beforehand, and in this case we do not know that it has. A week ago it was suggested that Councillor W. J. Forshaw was a likely candidate from the Conservative side, but we can find no reason to believe that Councillor John Evans' vastly stronger claims will be over- looked. He is next on the seniority list with nine years against Councillor Forshaw's four; he was also the defeated candidate at the last election and this is something in hi favour. Possibly there will be no contest, hut in any case we think a great majority of both Liberals and Tories will vote for Councillor Evans.

Coming Events. The annual sermons in connection with the taptist Church, Latchford, will be preached on Sun- day, July 10th, by the Rev. J. G. Greenhough, M.A„ ex-presi.dent of the BaptiSt Union and the National Pree Church Council. Mr. C. E. Parker will deliver all address at the young people's service, in the after- noon. BASSINETTES AND MAIL CARTS in latest art shades.-1 S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and Z, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. The Warrington Cricket Professional at the Oval. Lynes, the popular Warriagton professional, has this week had an opportunity of showing his qualities before a more critical public than usually assembles , at Arpley. For the first time he figured in the Lan- , cashire second eleven at the Oval on Thursday in the match with Surrey 2nd. In the first innings he had the misfortune to be stumped by Bale without scoring, but yesterday he made amends by knocking up 71 in fine style. He also did good work with the ball, cap- turing four of the Surrey wickets. The Clergy Daughters' School. On Tuesday tilt headmistresses and students, to the number of ninety-one, had an outing to Darley Dale Which is shortly to be the new home of the institution Leaving Warrington at 8.3 G the party arrived at Mat- lock shortly after 10 o'clock, and proceeded to Darley Dale hydro which IV; 11 be the school quarters. They thoroughly explored the place, and were favourably impressed with. it. Afterwards some of the visitors had a walk along the banks of Derwent, whilst others inlpected the church and rambled on the moors. Tea was served in the pavilion at the Whitworth Institute, Mr. Holmes cater- ing. During the afternoon tirs. Willis and Miss lctnnedy (the principal) joined the party. The weather was splendid, and the outing was thoroughly enjoyed by all. The return journey was made by the ,even o'clock train. D3ath of a Formr Warrington Railway Official.

Many Warrington railway employes will regret to bear of the death of Inspector Charles Astbury, which took place a few days ago at Chesterton. The deceased commenced his railway career at Chester, Working himself up from the rank of a porter to that of inspector. About 21 years ago he came to War- 'ington, and was appointed inspector under the Cheshire Lines Committee at the Warrington Central Btaticp, where he acted as chief inspector. Personal. The Rev. A. Inglis, curate at Holy Trinity Church, has accepted the curacy at Winwick Church. We print this week a short story by Mr. Harold Bindloss, eldest son of Mr. and Mrs. Bindloss, Grappenhall Road, Stockton Heath. See page 6. Remanded. - - -

Patrick Smith, a tramp, was remanded at Warring- ton Occasional Court yesterday, on a charge of being drunk and committing wilful damage at Great Sankey on the previous night. He will be brought before the magistrates at the County Petty Sessions on Wednesday. UNDER the CLOCK for GOOD BOOTS.—Advt.

The Manchester Ship Canal Bill. This Bill has been read a second time in the House of Commons. The time for petitioning against the Billlexpired on Wednesday. There are only two petitions against the Bill, one lodged by the London and North Western Railway Company and the other by the War- rington Corporation. We understand, however, that the former petition is lodged merely to obtain protec- tive clauses, and the Warrington Corporation will withdraw their petition, subject to a slight alteration in the clauses of the Bill. It is anticipated that the Bill will go through the House as an unopposed measure.

A Warrington Tanner Drowned. At 1.25 on Sunday afternoon two Warrington boys were walking along the towing path of the Sankey and St. Helens Canal at Dallam, Burtonwood, when they saw the body of a man floating in the water. They informed James Taylor, labourer, Dallam Cottages, who recovered the body with a boat-hook.— An inquest was held by Mr. Brighouse at the Chapel House, Burtonwood, on Wednesday.—Williatu Dagnall, tanner, of 56, John-street identified the body as that of his son, James Darrnall, also a tanner,living with him in John-street. ''The deceased had been missing since the previous Wednesday. A verdict of "Found Drowned" was returned. _ _ _ _

Warrington Ragged School and Mission. On Monday evening, by the kindness of Mr. Roger C. Parr, 150 fatherless children were provided with a supper. The committee desire to thankfully acknowledge donations towards " Walking Day" ex- penses from the following :—Money, Warrington In- dependent Labour Party, £2 12s. 6d.•' anon. (Stockton Heath), 2s. 6d. Other monies have been collected in the town, and in Stockton Heath by authorised col- lectors, hut the total amount cannot be stated until all is paid in. Clothing, Mrs. Richardson, Springfield- street, Mrs. Chantry, Bold-street. A large quantity of children's jackets and other winter clothing have also been sent by Messrs. Lord Bros. A box of sweets from Mr. Joseph Podmore. Several parcels have also been sent anonymously. All clothing distributed is first marked with the stamp of the Mission. Rev. H. Dannico and Insinuations.

An open-air meeting was held at Bridge Foot on Tuesday under the auspices of the Gas Workers 'and General Labourers' Union. There was a large attend- ance. The Rev. H. Dunnico presided, and was sup- ported by Mr. P. Curran (organizer of the Labourers' Union and Labour candidate for Jarrow), Mr. Seddon, of St. Helens, who, the Chairman announced, was on Monday night selected to contest Earlestown in the Labour interest, and Councillor Stott.—The Chairman stated that he had received several letters from anonymous writers who attributed base motives for presiding at that meeting. He treated those insinuat;ous and the people who had'made them with the utmost contempt and scorn. (Hear, hear, and applause).—Cmincillor Stott referred to the question of the wages of the stoker at Winwick pumping station. He had been severely criticized, he aid, for the action he had taken, but he wished to point out that he was fighting for a principle. (Applause.)—Mr. Seddon and Mr. Curran also addressed the meeting on trades union principles generally.

div.head: Sankey Wire Mills Cricket Club.
div.p: Sankey Wire Mills Cricket Club.

On S-aturday afternoon Mr. William Backhouse,who has occupied the position of General Secretary to the above club for the last 13 years, was the recipient of a handsome present consisting of an oak. timepiece, suitably inscribed, from the members. Mr. Councillor James Evans made thepresentation, and in doing so spoke highly of the ability with which Mr. Backhouse had earned out his secretarial duties, and of his gen- eral services to the club. Mr. Frank Taylor, the club's captain, also made reference to the good work which Mr. Backhouse had done for the beneat of his fellow-members, and on their behalf expressed the hope that the club would • continue to enjoy his services for many years. Mr. Backhnlt33 in replying, expressed his gratitude at the mark-of appre- ciation which the members had shewn him, and as- sured them that he would endeavour in the future to perform to the best of his ability the duties which they might entrust to him, and which in the past had al- ways afforded him very great pleasure.

PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER the CLOCK for BEST ROCT3 in LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Shocking Fatality to a Carter. An inquest was held yesterday morning at the Red Lion Inn by Mr. Dobson on the body of Thomas Woods, aged 51, who lodged at 63 Chorley-street. The deceased was a carter in the employ of Mr. Unsworth, contractor, Warrington, and was killed by being run over by a cart of which he was in charge at Stockton Heath on Thursday afternoon.— Evidence of identification was given by his landlady, Mrs. Tatlow.—George Hailwood, 10, Warlsurton- street, Stockton Heath, deposed that about 1-20 on Thursday afternoon he was in Gibson-street when he saw the deceased leading his horse and cart laden with sand from the sand hole. He had hold of the horse with- the right hand. The next thing he saw was the deceased on his back underneath the horse. In trying to rise, the horse's hind hoof caught the deceased on the head or chest and the wheel of the cart passed over his body. Witness thought that deceased was changing hands-with the horse when his feet became crossed in the sand, causing him to fall. He died a few minutes afterwards. Dr. Parker was called and pronounced life extinct.—Acting SergeantAßowyer described the injuries. There were marks of the cart wheel having passed over the de- ceased's body on the left leg and side and three ribs had beedbroken inwardly. The left side of the head was completely smashed in. A verdict of" Acciden- tal Death " was returned. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE 'TONIC IS the KING OF T01,71C5.-63. S ANK EY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. Local Druidism. Bro. David Houghton, D.C.S., who was recently elected Tice-Grand Master of the Order of Druids, paid an official visit to the " Mermaid " Lodge on Saturday evening 'and was introduced to the officers and members present by the Lodge Secretary, P.D.G.M. James Ray. The ordinary business over the members settled down to a pleasant evening. P.D.G.M. Samuel Caldwell proposed the toast of the new V.G.M., and in a few well-chosen words spoke of the pleasure it afforded the lodge and himself to wel- come and honour Bro. David Houghton, who had been so honoured, at the last A.M.D. The V.G.M. respond- ing, said he had to pay many visits, not only in War- rington, but all over the country, and he was sure none could give him a more cordial welcome than "Mermaid" had done. After giving an account of his varied experiences at the A.M.D., held at Oswestry, interspersed by several anecdotes, told in his own inimitable style, Bro David Houghton concluded by declaring it was his intention to work, and to work hard, for the welfare of Druidism throughout the country. He was pledged to innumer- able visits already, and it was his intention, not to disappoint any, where he had promised to be present. P.D.G.M. Bro. George Roughley proposed the toast of Mrs. D. Houghton and family, which was drunk with applause.. P. A. Bro. R. Sudlow said the delegates at Oswestry, by returning .Bro. David Houghton with such an overwhelming majority, had conferred a last- ing honour on the Warrington District, of which Bro. Houghton was such a leading star. P.D.G.M. Henry Kent spoke in similar strains. After other speeches the unanimous wish of the meeting was that Bro. Houghton might be spared to long life and good health to visit the lodge next year with the gold chain of the order, when lie takes his seat as Grand Master. Bro. H. oughton suitably responded, and brought a most en- joyable evening to a close.

Mr. R. Dobson, Caoner, field an inquest at the Stag Inn, Walton, on Tuesday evening touching the death of Anders Fissell, a seaman employed on the Nor- wegian steamer Ling, whose body was recovered from the Manchester Ship Canal on Sunday.—Captain WariLg represented the Canal Company. Deceased was missed from his ship on Wednesday, and early on Thursday morning was seen at Walton by William Ball, a Warrington lamp lighter. He was. under the influence of drink, and Ball directed him towards Acton Grange where the vessel was lying. Nothing was seen of the deceased until his body was recovered from the canal. There were no marks of violence upon it. A coat, supposed to belong to the deceased, was found on the canal bank.—A verdict of " Found drowned " was returned. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS.--63. SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. The Dispute in the Flint Glass Trade. No settlement has yet been arrived at in this dis- pute. which affects a number of men employed at the works of Messrs. Robinson Sons and Company at Bank Quay. The serious depression experienced for some time past in the Lancashire flint glass trade in consequence of foreign competition, led the manufac- turers two months or so ago to give notice to the glass workers in their employ of a reduction of 15 per cent. in the wages of one class, and of 20 per cent. in an- other, no alteration to be made in the wages of the third class of workers. The operatives after consider- ing the question for a month, intimated that they would not accept these terms. but offered to submit to a reduction of is. a week in the two classes affected, which is equal to 21- per cent in one case and 31 per cent. in the other. The masters however, maintained the position they had originally taken up, and, as the other side were equally firm, issued a notice to the men to terminate.their engage- ments pending a settlement of the ques- tion. The result is that all the glass workers in Lan- cashire are for the present out of employment, and, if the dispute is not speedily settled, the glass mixers, mould makers, packers, firemen, general warehouse- men, and the people employed in the other 4rdepart- meats, will also be thrown out of work.

Another Presentation to Mr. G. F. F. White. Mr. George F. F. White, the Warrington magis- trates' clerk, was the recipient of a wedding present from the members of the County Borouglb Police Force on Monday. At the conclusion of the business at the Police Court the Chief Constable (Mr. Luke Talbot) on behalf of the Force, handed to Mr. White a handsome fish service, together with an address which read as follows :—" Dear sir,—We, the members of the Warrington County Borough Police Force, deferentially ask your acceptance of the accompanying fish service as a slight token of the deep respect, esteem, and cordial regard in which you are held by all ranks of our organization. In your approaching union with the lady of your choice we wish you and your intended life partner the choicest blessings which Providence can bestow, and trust that both may live long and happily to enjoy the honour and affection of your almost innumerable friends. Signed on behalf of the P dice Force, LUKE TALBOT, Chief Constable." Mr. White has since written to the Chief Constable as follows :—" Will you please accept and convey to the other members of our County Borough Police Force my best thanks for the exceedingly handsome present, and for the good wishes accompanying same. I may say that I value the present very highly, as having been connected with the force for upwards of 25 years I feel as if I were one of you. It will give me very great pleasure to convey the very good wishes of the Force to, my future wife. Agairi thank- ing you I am very sincerely yours, GEORGE F. F. WnrrE."—The fish service was supplied by Messrs. Eustance and Co., Sankey-street.

At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court yesterday, before Mr. Registrar Ridgway, Joseph Woodward, builder, Bewsey-street, again appeared for his examina- tion.—Mr. Browne represented the debtor, and Mr. F. It. Roberts appeared for a creditor.—Mr. Johnson, assistant official receiver, said the debtor, previous to the last court made certain statements which it was deemed desirable to investigate more fully than had been possible up to that time. Since then the matter had been more fully gone into and the debtor had deleted a statement he made in regard to property at Latchford. He (Ur. johnsm) proposed to read the memorandum to the debtor with the passages taken out, and also the memorandum which We debtor had made saying that the charges were absolutelywithdraWn —By Mr. Johnson (to the debtor) That statement has been unreserVedly withdrawn by you and voluntarily withdrawn ?—The Debtor: Yes.—.llr. Johnson : That is to say without pressure from anyone ?—The Debtor : Yes.—Mr. Johnson informed the Registrar that after careful inquiry the Official Receiver was quite satisfied that there was no evidence whatever in support of the debtor's statement, and so far as he could judge there was no truth in the allegation made. He thought it was only fair to Mr. Roberts to say that. —The examination was closed.—Samuel Finley, formerly carrying on business as a builder at 3, Clarence-street, Newton-le-Willows, now of 94, Rydal- street, appeared for his examination.—lir. Browne represented a creditor, and Ur. Longton appeared for the debtor.—Mr. Johnson said .in this matter the debtor had offered a composition to his creditors which was likely to be accepted. He proposed that the case be adjourned until the next Court.—This course was agreed to. •

and looked the picture of contentment. Without going into details, it may be said that the same idea of grouping was observed by all the schools,the child- ren wearing sashes of various colours. An exquisite floral arch was borne aloft by the children of St. Alban's School, and there was a statue of the Madonna and child embellished with tiger lilies. The effect was heightened by many of the chil- dren carrying wands, tipped with flowers. For picturesque effect, St. Benedict's undoubtedly carried off the palm. There was a magnificent arch of roses and trailing 'greenery, and a lovely harp of ferns and greenery, set off by roses, together with a floral cross of artistic design, excited general admira- tion. The infants carried gilt crosses decked with choice blooms. St. Mary's, Latchford, and the Church of the Sacred Heart, also presented a charming picture. The costumes of the children were tasteful, and floral devices were conspicuous. A statue of the Sacred Heart pleasingly decorated was carried, and several banners depicted the Sacred Heart. ks usual the scholars walked in Indian file and taken as a whole the spectacle fully maintained the reputation of the Roman Catholics in Warrington for charming pageantry. Parents and teachers alike must have gone to a great deal of trouble and expense in prepar- ing the children, but no doubt they felt rewarded in knowing that it was largely through their efforts that a pageant which reflected infinite credit upon the schools passed off o successfully. After traversing the arranged route the scholars proceeded to their respective churches, where there was the Benediction of the Holy Sacrament.

div.head: WALKING DAY AT PENKETH.
div.p: WALKING DAY AT PENKETH.

Walking Day, so eagerly looked foward to by the younger generation, dawned brightly at Penketh and though a boisterous wind caused some discomfort, and dust abounded, the day was fine, and fine weather is of course very necessary for the successful carrying out of this popular function. The scholars of St. Mary's Mission Sunday School were first in evidence, and headed by Messrs. Walkers band, started from the Mission at 1.30. The scholars attending the Sankey Sunday school had marched round to the Mission, and the combined schools made a brave show, with their lovely banners, &c. Lurries and carts conveyed the younger children and the joy of the youngsters was great. The Vicar the Rev. J. R. Jones M.A., was pre- sent, and the superintendants and teachers of each school looked after the order of the procession. The procession went to the" Black Horse " Sankey, turning there back to the Sankey Sunday School, where tea was provided,and the remainder of theevenin,g was spent in the field adjoining the vicarage, where keenly contested sports, and pleasant games passed the time away until dusk when the children dispersed tired but happy. The scholars attending the Wesleyan Sunday school met at the school at 1.30, and shortly afterwards, led by the Penketh Tannery Prize Band, started on their journey. Messrs. C. E. Parker, J. T. Ambler, J. G. Withinshaw, and the class leaders were in charge crf the proceedings, and the muster of the scholars was very large. A pleasing feature is the way the older scholars still rally to the Walking Day procession, and take their place in the day's proceedings. A beautiful selection of bunting and two fine banners were carried, and the carts and lurries brought up the rear of the procession. The route taken was by Warrington-road, Heath-road, Grey- stone-road, Station-road, and round to the school,where tea was provided. A move was then made to the Recreation Ground,where races and games were partici- Dated in, the strains of the band enlivening the proceed- ings at intervals.

div.head: WARRINGTON WALKING DAY.
div.p: WARRINGTON WALKING DAY.
YESTERDAY'S PROCESSIONS.

When Warrington children awoke yesterday they rejoiced to see the sim shining gloriously. The morn- ing.was full of promise, and soon happy children in light holiday attire were to be seen wending their way to the Sunday schools. Once again, Walking Day— the day of days to the youth of the town—had come. Year by year the great Sunday 'school festival is celebrated with whole-hearted enthusiasm, for who would grudge the youngsters a day entirely set apart for their enjoyment ? He would be a bold individual who would attempt to consign Walking Day to the oblivion of byegone events. The youngsters undoubt- edly enjoy the march through the gaily decorated streets—however fatiguing it may be—and the after- noon frolics in the fields afford them genuine delight. The parents, too, always do their best to make the festival a success and many with straitened resources find the wherewithal to obtain some articles of finery for the little ones.

A wet Walking Day would indeed be a dire calamity, and there were doleful faces on Thursday- evening when it wak, feared that the ideal summer con- ditions which had been experienced during the week were at an end. Dull clouds and a smart shower helped to conjure up visions of bedraggled dresses and hasty retreats from sodden fields. It was a relief when. Friday morning broke beautifully fine,a pleasant breeze tempering the heat. The whole town gave it- self over to holiday making, and as the time for the pro- cessions drew near the streets became thronged. Flags fluttered gaily from places of business, and there was bunting in profusion. As usual the main procession was massed on the lawn in front of the Town Hall. Here the schools began to muster about half-past nine, and, bathed in bright sunshine, the scene was one of animation. On the Town Hall steps the Mayor and Mayoress and party had assembed, and from this elevated position a good view of the schools as they. entered the park was obtained. Mr. R. T. Fairclough and Mr. Eric Fairclough under- took the mashalling, and the Chief Constable and his staff rendered valuable service in maintaining order. Shortly after ten o'clock the signal was given br the schools to file through the central arch of the iron gates.Bv this time the Sky had become overcast and rain fell rather heavily, to the discomfiture of the children in their light attire. Fortunately there was soon a change for the better, and to the strains of lively music the children, looking radiantly happy, passed along, many holding aloft banners and floral devices.. The procession left the Park in the following order :- 1. Blue Coat School and Band. 2. Padgate Industrial School and Band. 5. Parish Church and St. Helen's Church, Hollin- fare and Crosfield's Band. 4. St. George's Mission and Lymm Band. 5. St. Clement's Mission and Churca L Os' Brigade Bugle Band. 6._ St. Peter's School and Band. 7. St. Paul's and Ardwick Green Industrial Band. 8. St. Ann's and Walker's Band. 0. Holy Trinity and Walton Baud. 10. St. Luke's. 11. Factory Yard. 12. St. Barnabas' and Preston Brook Band. 13. St. James's and Volunteer Rand. 14. Emmanuel Reformed Church. 15. Buckley Street and P. S. A. Band. 16- Sharpe Street Primitive Methodist. 17. Salvation Army and Band. 18. Ragged School and Drum and Fife Band. As a demonstration of strength the procession was imposing, but there was little attempt at originality and picturesqueness. Some beautiful large banners bearing scriptural illustrations were displayed, and the long ribbons were held by little girls clad in white. Many children carried baskets of choice flowers, and here and there were to be seen infants cosily ensconced in tastefully decorated mail carts. As usual the Blue Coat School had the place of hanour, and the scholars of this old institution looked well in their neat dresses of 33lue serge with collars and and collarettes. The children from Padgate Industrial Schools followed, ill charge of Mr. A. Wright, the superintendent, the boys, wearing the usual corduroy suits. They were accompanied by Messrs. 0- Mather, W. Houghton, and R. Forshaw (Guardians), and Mr. S. Sutton (assistant clerk to the Board). A detachment of the Church Lads' Brigade, looking very soldierly in their smart uniforms, marched at the head of St. Clement's school. -Decor- ated staffs, surmounted with floral devices, made a pleasing feature. The teachers at St. Peter's school are to be complimented upon the exceedingly creditable display which the scholars under their care provided. A contingent of youngsters figured in the familiar Pierrot costumes, the girls jingling tambourines, whilst the boys rattled " clappers." Several scholars wheeled bicycles gaily-decked with flowers. Miss Bee was responsible for this original feature of the procession, which did her great credit. In the forefront of St. Paul's school walked a good muster of members of the Men's Bible Class. The dresses of some of the girls attending this school were ornamented with ivy and roses, and the effect was pleasing. Garlands of flowers and prettily decorated wands were carried in the Emmanuel School proces- sion which though not very strong in numbers looked attractive. The Ragged 'School made a brave show with a handsome new banner, bearing the inscription " Warrington Ragged School and Mission. Founded by James Skelland." A. portrait of Mr. Skelland,who has made the institution his special care, app6ars on the banner,. together with pictures illustrating the rescue work which he superintends. On glancing at them, the spectator. saw how children. had been raised from poverty and squalor to comfort and elevating surroundings through the agency of the mission.

There were numerous lurries drawn by gaily' caparisoned horses, and., beavily laden with infants. Whilst the scholars were assembling in the Park these vehicles waited in .Hanover-street and adjoining thoroughfares, and re-joined the procession as It passed. After traversing the appointed route, some of the scholars' attended service at their re- spective churches, and in the afternoon adjourned to fields in the district ''where they spent a happy time amid pleasant surroundings. At times the clouds gathered threateningly but the rain kept off, and the usual sports Were indulged in. Most of the Nonmformist scholars entrained for country resorts early in the morning. The Wycliffe scholars again journeyed to Dunham Hill. Bold- street Wesleyans and Legh-street Primitive Methodists paid a visit to Lymm, whilst their friends at Silver- street spent the day at Hslsby. The G-olborne-street Baptists had an enjoyable time at Acton Bridge and St. John's Presbyterian scholars went to Frddsham. The Cairo-street school and congregation accepted the invitation of Mr. F. Monks to spend the day at Walton Old Hall. The scholars at the Workingmen's Mission disported themselves in a field at Sankey.

div.head: ROMAN CATHOLIC PROCESSION.
div.p: THE ROMAN CATHOLIC PROCESSION.
A Pretty Spectacle.

Once again the Roman Catholics made a brilliant and striking show, and the charming spectacle excited the admiration of all who witnessed it. Bridge-street was the only thoroughfare in which the procession could be viewed in its entirety, and here .the crowd was thickest. The Police had a difficult task in clear- ing sufficient road spice for the processionists to pass along in comfort, the crowd persisting in pressing for- ward in their eagerness t) obtain a view of the - gaily dressed children and • beautiful banners. The display was on the same lines as in pre- vious years,and it was that superb grouping of scholars and uniformity of costumes which Made it so impos- ing. Then, again, the youngsters marched witkalmost military precision, and whenever there was a Momen- tary halt one could hear the little .feet marking time. Long lines of splendid banners with prettily coloured borderings fluttering in the breeze, formed a veritable panorama of sacred pictures. Some were em- blematic of the Sacraments of the church, whilst others depicted the Blessed Virgin and Saints. Here and there a glittering processional cross attracted the eye, and there 'a re statues of "Our Lady" magnifi- cently decked with flowers.. The place of honour was held by St. Mary's, Buttermarket-street, and. the lead- ir.g banner from this fine church was embellished with a copy of Marino's " Immaculate Conception." Immediately behind it walked a group of tiny tots all clad in white and sashed with blue. The girls carried lovely bouquets, and on their heads were dainty wreaths. All the boys in this section had white sailor hats. Banners of fine texture and workmanship were the most striking feature of this school's display. The .members of the various confraternities and guilds turned . out in strong force, wearing distinctive medallions.. A contingent of infants rode in a landau,

div.head: STATISTICS FOR THE VARIOUS SCHOOLS. How the Day was Spent.
div.p: STATISTICS FOR THE VARIOUS SCHOOLS. How the Day was Spent.
We have obtained the following information regard- ing the schools which took part in yesterday's festival :
Church of England.

BLUE COAT SCHOOL :—Established 1667. Number of scholars on books, 40 boys, 30 girls • number of teachers, 4; governor and head master, Mi.. E. Rose; matron, Mrs. Rose. The children took part in the general procession, headed by the school band and the banner, bearing an illustration of the Bible, the crown and sceptre, and setting forth the injunctions : "Honour all men," "Love the brotherhood," "Fear God," "Honour the King." After the procession, the children attended service in the Parish Church. Parents and guardian 4 were allowed to visit the children at the Blue Coat School in the afternoon. A special dinner and tea were provided. Sports and games were engaged in, in the school grounds. PADGATE INDUSTRIAL :—Established 1881. Num- ber of scholars on books, 115 boys, 93 girls ; average attendance, 200 • number of teachers, 4; Clergy, Rev. W. Pollock Hill, chaplain; Mr. Arthur Wright (super- intendent), and 15 officers. All the children dressed in new suits left Padgate by the 9 o'clock train. After joining in the procession,the Protestants attended service in the Parish Church and Catholics la, for home. A very good tea and treat were provided by the Guardians Mr. J. W. Houghton, Woolston, lent a field for sports. Being the first Friday in the month it was the children's friends' day and many visitors were present. Tea was served in picnic fashion on the field and the children spent one of the happiest days of the year.

NATIONAL :--Established 1833. Number of scholars on books, 325 boys: number of teachers, 25; clergy, Rev. Canon Willis and Rev. G. D. Dickenson; superin- tendents, Mr. James Wood and Miss A. Brown. The children assembled at the schools at 9 o'clock, and joined the general procession headed by Messrs. Cros- field's Band. After parading the town they returned to the church where a special service was held, the preacher being the Rev. Maurice Bell, Vicar of St. Katherine's, Abercromby-square, Liverpool. At two o'clock by the kindness of the Principal, the Training College field was thrown open to the scholars till 8, tea being provided at the various schools. During the afternoon and evening the band played for dancing on the green.

FAIRFIELD :—Established 1810. Number of schol- ars on books, 455 girls; number of teachers, 25 ; clergy, Rev. Canon Willis, Rev. G. W. Dickenson; superinten- dents, Miss Ethel White, and Miss Cicely Willis. The arrangements were exactly the same as for the National school.

ST. GEORGE'S :—Established 1891. Number of scholars on books, 730; boys,3oo ; girls, 430; number of teachers, 30; curate-in-charge, and superintendent, Rev. A. F. White. The children took part in the pro- cessiou headed by Lvmm Blnd,and spant the afternoon and evening in St. Elphin's Park. ST. CLEMENT'S :-1892. Established 1892; number of scholars on books, 700; boys, 300; girls, 400 ; num- ber of teachers, 30: curate-in-charge, Rev. A. S. Cameron ; superintenlents, Rev. A. S. Cameron, Miss Boardman, Miss E. L. Broadbent.. The Church Lads' Brigade marched at the head of the mission procession, and the arrangements for the day were the same as for the National school.

ST. PETER'S :—Number of scholars on books, 228 boys, 309 girls; infants 140; average attendance, 450; number of teachers, 21; clergy, Rev. B. Percival and Rev. D. R. James; superintendents, Captain Langton, C.A., and Mrs. Percival. A brass band headed this school's procession which,as usual,was very attractive In the afternoon the scholars adjourned to a field adjoin- ing the Barracks,where an excellent tea was served. Races and games were indulged in, and the time was very pleasantly spent. st PAUL'S :—Ntunber of scholars on books, 400 boys, 450 girls; average attendance, 60; number of teachers, 50; Rev. W. Bracecamp, vicar: Rev. R. H. Bowen, curate ; superintendents, Mr. A. J. Jolley, boys; Mrs. Bracecamp, girls. Immediately on assembling the scholars proceeded to the Town Hall, headed by the Ardwick Green Industrial School band, and joined in the general procession. After parading the principal streets of the town, the scholars attended a brief service at the church. The afternoon was spent in a field at Bewsey, kindly lent by Messrs. Hatton and Reid. Tea and refreshthents were provided. The band played for dancing. Games were indulged in and prizes were awarded for various athletic achievements. ALL SAINTS' MISSION.—Number of scholars on books. 350; number of teachers, 20; superintendent, Rev. R. H. Bowen. This mission is connected with St. Paul's Church, and the scholars attending it, joined in the procession of the mother church. The afternoon was also spent with St. Paul's sobolars at Bewsey. ST. ANNE'S :—Number of scholars on books, over 500 ; number of teachers, 22 ; clergy, Rev. James Davies, , vicar, Rev. D. Kerrin, curate ; superintendent and other officers, Rev. James Davies (vicar), Miss Davies, Miss R. Bunch; treasurer, Miss M. Rigbey. The scholars assembled at the schools at 8.45 and marched to the Town Hall via Winwick-road, Winwick-street, Horse- market-street and Sankey-street, the music being sup- plied by Walker's Brewery Land. The handsome large school banner was borne at the head of the procession and some of the children carried bannerettes bearing scripture texts worked in various colours on scrolls. On leaving the Town Hall the scholars walked in the general procession as far as Market-gate. On reaching this point they proceeded along Horsemarket-street to the Parish Church in Winwick-road, where service was held. At 3 o'clock tea was partaken of in the schools in Dannett-street. Afterwards the children adjourned to a field (kindly lent by Mr. Robinson, Orford-avenue Farm), at the end of Orford-avenue, where games and Ivarious competitions were provided for the various classes. The prizes were distributed at 7 o'clock, each Ichild also receiving a bun and the children dispersed labout 8 o'clock. ,

HOLY TRINITY.;—Number of scholars on books 140 boys, 150 girls; average attendance, 240; number of teachers, 19 ;clergy, Rev. E. C.E. Carleton, vicar; Rev. A. Inglis, curate. The Vicar 'acts as superintendent, with Mr. J. J. Hesketh as secretary. As usual the scholars paraded the town, headed by Walton band, and carrying numerous banners. They left the general pro- cession at Market-gate and proceeded to the schools. The afternoon was spent on the hills at Frodsham, sports and various amusements being indulged in. ST. LUKE'S :—Number of scholars on books, 436 ; average attendance, 3.50; number of teachers, 26 ; curate-in-charge and superintendent of Sunday school, Rev. H. R. Wild: secretaries, Messrs. T. Sutcliffe and R. Graham. The scholars took part in the procession with Holy Trinity school in the morning and spent the after- noon and evening in a field off Liverpool-road. The usual games were indulged in. FACTORY YARD MISSTON :—Estahlished 20 years ago ; number of scholars on books, 280; 120 boys. 160 girls- average attendance, 250: number of teachers, .11; clergy. Revs. E. C. E. Carleton and A. Inglis; superintendent, Nlrs. Carleton; secretary, Mr. J. H. Halton. The children took part in the procession along with Holy Trinity and St. Luke's schools, and in the afternoon the elder scholars journeyed to Frodsham. The youngsters went to a field at Arpley, kindly lent by Mr. James Bowcock, of Horsemarket-street, and partook of tea in Holy Trinity schools.

Sr. BAR.NABAS:—Established 1879. Number of scholars on books, 242 boys, 227 girls; average attend- ance, 200 bovs,l9o girls; number of teacher's, 24; vicar, Rev. J. IC G. Hollingworth ; superintendents, Air. James,. Mrs. X. H. G. Hollingworth. The children assembled in the church and joined in the procession round the town, preceded by Preston Brook brass band. The large school banner,. bearing a picture of our Lord blessing little !children, was carried, and there were many small flags. Early in the afternoon the scholars entrained for Farnworth, and on reaching the village marched to Pex Hill where games were engaged in. A capital tea was served. • The return journey to War- rington commenced at 8-53., a most enjoyable day having been spent. ST: JAMES' :—Number of scholars on books, 271 boys, 369 girls; average attendante, 544; number of teachers, 22; vicar and superintendent, Rev. H.B. Firth,

M.A.; secretary, 11Tr. James Fargher. The children assembled at the schools at 8.15 a.m., where a well- organized procession was formed by Mr. %V. H. Stans- field,M.A. Headed by the Volunteer band and the banner of St. James', the procession (including three lurries prettily decorated provided for the little ones)traversed round the parish, and then proceeded to the church where a short service was conducted by the Vicar. The procession was reformed and proceeded to the Town Hall to join in the general procession round the town, and then back to the school. The procession was re- formed at 1.30 p.m.,and proceeded to the Brewery Park, Wilderspool, headed by the band, where scrambling for nuts and sweets, and games of nearly all sorts were I greatly indulged in. The band played a selection of music during the afternoon and evening. Tea was pro- vided for the infants on the field, and the older scholars had tea in the schoolroom.

E‘DIANUEL (REFagmEn) E3tablishel 1879 Number of scholars on books, 200 ; average attendance 140; number of teachers' 17 minister, Rev. F. Vaughan; superintendent, Mr. W. Brown; secretary, Mr. J. Lloyd. This school had a pretty procession, many of the children carrying garlands of flowers. At 12.30 the scholars proceeded by train to Daresbury and spent the rest of the day in a field lent by Mr. Milling- ton. Tea was served and the usual games were engaged in.

div.head: Roman Catholic.
div.p: Roman Catholic.

ST. NARY'S :—Established 1874. Numb t; of sciholars on b00k5,404 boys, 451 Girls; average attend- ance, 749; number of teachers, 21; clergy, Revs. Neville Wilson, 0.5.8., Dr. Mercer 0.5.8., and Basil Primavesi 0.5.8. As usual this school had a very prettypageant, which is more fully described in another column. The school children assembled in the schools at 9.30, and the religious confraternities were marshalled in the grounds by the officers of each guild. There were several hundred members of the Guild of St. Agnes, Confra- ternity of Mount Carmel, Guild of the Sacred Heart, and Children of Mary. At 10-30 the procession left the school headed by the League of the Cross prize brass hand. Many beautiful banners were displayed, one bearing a reproduction of Murillo's "Immaculate con- ception." There were banners emblematic of the seen Sacraments, and others with beautiful pictures of Our Lady and St. Benedict. The afternoon was spent in a field off Gorsey-lane, andall the children were provided withteas. The usual games and sports were engaged in.

ST. ALBANS :—Number of scholar, on books 450; average attendance 410; number of teachers, ii: clergy Rev. Father Whittle' Rev. Father Gibbon and the Rev. Father Swarbreck. The school children and members of guilds and confraternities formed into processional order. The Borough Band was in attendance. Some beautiful banners were displayed. In the forefront was one of St. Alban, the martyr, and a large banner of Our Lady, preceded the children of Mary. There was also a double-pole banner of St. Agnes ao2ompanying the Guild of St. Agnes, and a banner of the Sacred Heart for Men's Confraternity of the Sacred Heart. The ensemble was imposing and impressive. A service was held in St. Alban's Church after the procession, and in the after- noon, the scholars and friends disported themselves in a field near the Barracks. Tea was served and the band played for dancing. Games and sports were also engaged in.

ST. BENEDICT'S :—Number of scholars on books, 300 boys, 338 girls; average attendance, 553 ; number of teachers, 13 • priest-in-charge, Rev. J. Baines ; head teachers, Mr. D. fooris, Sister Imelda. This school had an exceedingly pretty pageant. It was headed by Wavertree prize band, and there were many artistically worked banners, the principal one bearing a representa- tion of St. Benedict. The afternoon and evening were enjoyably spent in a field off Gorsey-lane. ST. MARY'S (LarcliFoßD) :—Established 1869 Number of scholars on books, 211 ; 108 boys, 103 girls ; average attendance, 170; number of teachers, 4; clergy taking part in the procession, \Teri Rev. Canon Dallon Craig; Rev. Fathers Thompson. Hennelly, Paul, Donlevy, Chambers, Damien, McGrath, and D'Arcy. The procession included many beautiful and artistic features, and was headed by St. Edmund's band from Runcorn. Pretty emblematic bauners were carried. At three o'clock the children re-assembled, and preceded by the band, marched to the Park, Old Warps, where sports and dancing were engaged in. caußcri OF THE SACRED HEART :—Established 1896; number of scholars on books, 400; Priest-in- charge, Rev. M. Ryan; head teachers, Miss Dinsdale (mixed department), Miss Bonny (infants). The scholars left the schools at 10.45, beaded by the Pioneer band, and proceede. along Liverpool-road, Parker-street, Wilson-Patten-street, to Bridge-foot, where they joined the other Roman Catholic schools. Some eloborately worked banners were carried, the principal ones depict- ing the Holy Family, the S tcr9d Heart of ear Lord, the Sacred Heart of our Lady, and• St. Patrick. `) The after- noon and evening were spent in the Park, Old Warps, where tea was served, and sports were indulged in. Nonconformist.

I, WYCLIFFE (CONGREGATIONAL) :—Established 1818 Number of scholars on books, 243 boys, 214 girls average attendance, 274; number of teachers 38 ministers,Rev. John Yonge and Rev. H. Wall (assistant) ; superintendent, Mr. W. Brown ; deputy superintendent Mr. W. Besnick ; treasurer, Mr. D. Owen ; secretary' Mr. E. Pickavance ; assistant secretary, Mr. G. Ford The scholars assembled at 9 a.m. and preceded by the. school band, marched through the principal streets to Bank Quay Station where they entrained for Dunham Hill. The scholars at once proceeded to a field where sports were indulged in until dinner time. After dinner 'rambles round the district and a visit to Chester by some of the older scholars occupied the time until tea was served. After tea, the prizes were distributed and the band played several selections. The return journey commenced at 8.30, Warrington being reached by 9 WYCLIFFE COCKHEDGE MISSION (CONGREGA- TIONAL) :—Established 1871. Number of scholars on books, 160 boys, 140 girls; average attendance 220' • number of teachers, 15; minister and superintendent, Rev. Harry Wall ; assistant superintendent, Mr. Ben- jamin Hall; secretary, Mr. John Pickton. The children assembled at the mission, Brick-street, at 8.30 a.m. leav- ing at 8.45 in procession • for Wycliffe Church, by way of Fennel-street, Buttermarket-street, Scotland-road and Bewsey-street. Here they joined Wycliffe School and proceeded by Legh-street, Sankey-street, Arpley- street, Wilson Patten-street, Arpley-road, Mersey-street Fennel-street,lliattersby-lane,and Marshhouse-lane, to a field in;Orford-road. Dinner was served at 12, Meat pies &c.' being provided. The afternoon was spent in games and sports for which prizes were given. Tea was par- taken of at 4 p.m. and the rest of the evening was devoted to games &c. SILVER - STREET (WEsLEvAN) : —Number of scholars on books, 400; boys ~.•110, girls 190; average attendance, 354 ; number of ' teachers, 45; minister, Rev. R. Wilkins Rees: superintendents, Mr. J. W. Hayward J.P., and Mr. It. Corbett ; secretary, Mr. L. H. Farrall ; hon. secretary, Mr. E. J. Mitchell. Headed by the Borough Band and the school banner, the chil- dren marched to Bank Quay station and, left by special train at 9.30 for Helsby. The day was pleasantly spent in a field, dinner being provided at 12 o'clock and tea at 4. A number of friends and visitors partook of tea in the Wesleyan Schoolroom at Helsby. BOLD-STREET (WESLE VAN) :—Number of scholars on books, 334; boys 179, girls 155; average attendance. 201; number of teachers, 37 ; ministers, Revs. G. H Carnson, W. C. J. Neville and R. Wilkins Rees; superin- tendent, Mr. Albert Perkins; secretary, Mr. H. B. H. Sander; assistant recretary, Mr. John Osborne. The day was spent at Mr. Winstanley's Dairy Farm, Lymm where games and races &c., were engaged in. The children returned at 8-30.

SANKEY BRIDGES (WESLEYAN) :—Numb3r of scholars on books, 400; boys 220, girls 180; average attendance, 350; number of teachers, 26; superinten- dents, Mr. S. Blythe and Mr. J. Corradine. The scholars met at the school at 9 o'clock and headed by the large banner proceeded direct to the field lent by Mr. Cook at Burtonwood where the day was spent. Dinner was served at 12 o'clock and tea at 4-30. Various games were indulged in and the children returned about 9 o'clock.

ELLESMERE-STREET, (WEsr.EviN) :—Established 1884. Number of scholars on books, 187 boys, 212 girls average attendance, .238; number of teachers, 20; ministers, Revs. G. H. Carnson, W. C. J. Neville, R. Wilkins Rees ; .superintendent, Mr. John Barlow ; assistant superintendent, Mr. John Ellison; secretary, Mr. F. Cox; assistant secretary,Mr. W. Voole.The schol- ars and teachers assembled at 8.30 and at 9.0 proceeded by way of Ellesmere Street, Hall Street, Mersey Street, and Knutsford Road to a field near the Latchford Swing Bridge where the day was spent: Sports took place in the afternoon, various prizes being offered for competi- tion. All the junior scholars were conveyed to and from the field on lurries engaged for the purpose. GOSPEL HALL SUNDAY scacioL (FoRsTER- STREET) :—Number of scholars on books ; 230 boys, 242 girls; average attendance; 400; number of teachers, 25 ; superintendent. Mr. J. Green ; secretary, Mr. J. Miles; treasurer, Mr. %V. Street. The children left the school at 9.30 a.m., and proceeded by Orford-lane, Marshhouse-lane, and Padgate-lane to Mr. Fryar's field at Padgate. Dinner consisting of pies, buns and milk was provided at 12-30, and tea was served at about 4.30 to the scholars and about 100 friends. Cricket, football, and various other games were engaged in. BUCKLEY-STREET :—Established 1873. Number of scholars on books, 250 boys, 350 girls ; average attendance, 350; number of teachers, 20; superinten- dent, Mr. A. Jennings; assistant superintendent, Mr. T. Cook; secretary, Mr. J. Ryan. The scholars formed in procession at the church at 9.15, and marched down Dallam-lane, Tanner's-lane, Bewsey-road, Edgeworth- street, Legh-street, and Sankey-street to the Park, where they joined the main procession. Buckley-street P.S.A. Band supplied the music, and the large school banner bearing pictures of the " Good Shepherd" and the Angel of Mercy watching over two children playing on the edge of thejprecipice, was o.isplayed. On leaving the Park the scholars proceeded along the usual route and then up Winwick-street to the school, where a , capital dinner was served. The meal over, they again formed in procession, headed by the band and marched to a field near the Waggon Works, kindly lent by Mr. S. Plinston. Here cricket, football, and races of all descriptions were indulged in. A substantial tea was partaken of in the schoolroom, and afterwards there was more recreation in the field. To-day the teachers hold their annual pic-nic to Llandudno, and given flue weather the affair promises to be a great success.

GOLBORNE STREET, (RAPTIsT) :—Established 1869. Number of scholars on books, 105 boys, and 129 girls ; average attendance; 210 ; number of teachers, 26; minister, Rev. Herbert Dunnico ; superintendent, Mr. H. Buckby ; secretaries, Mr. T. Longshaw, and Mr. Pepper ; treasurer, Mr. Albert Hunt. The scholars left Bank Quay at 8.10 by special train for Acton Bridge, accompanied by the Paster and officers and many friends, the party numbering 340 mall. Luncheon and tea were provided in the Baptist schoolroom (Milton). The rest of the day was spent in games, races Sr.c., in a. field set apart for the use of the scholars. Others took long rambles in the country. Bugle call for home was sounded at 7.0 p.m. and several hymns were sung. Votes of thanks were passed to the Milton Baptists on the motion of the Rev. H. Dunnico, Mr. Buckby and others, and were responded to by Rev. T. C. Elder. The children reached home about 8 o'clock.

LEGH-STREET (PARTICULAR BAPTIST) :—Estab- lished over a century. Number of scholars on books. 72; average attendance, 50; number of teachers, 6; officers, Messrs. W. Tinton, superintendent; Joseph B Groom, treasurer; John L. Bate, secretary; J. Byfield, hank treasurer; William J. Bate, bank secretary. The scholars met iTt the schoolroom at a quarter to one and then proceeded to a field in Lower Walton, kindly lent by Mr. Weir, where games and refreshments were pro- vided. Tea was served in the schoolroom. - - ---------

--- LATCHFORD (Punt ITT VF: METHODIST) :—Number of scholars on books, 90; boys 40, girls 50; average attendance, morning 40, afternoon 80; number of teachers, 16; minister, Rev. J. Gardharn Reed, B.D. superintendent, R. J. Cotterel ; secretary, Air. Harding; treasurer, Mr. P. Massey. The scholars proceeded in the tramcars to the terminus at Latchford, and thence proceeded to Mr. Joseph Clare's farm where tea was provided and games &c., engaged in. _ _

ST. JOHN'S (PRESBYTERIAN) :—Established 1851 Number of scholars on books, 80; teachers, 8; superin- tendent,:llev. J. L. Milne, M.A.. B.D. ; secretary, Mr. C. S. Barlow; treasurer, Miss Spendelow. The scholars proceeded to Bank Quay Station, and departed by train for Frodsham. A pleasant time was spent on Overton hills, and tea was partaken of in true picnic fashion on the summit.

SHARP-STREET (PruNtrTrvE METBorasT) :—Num- ber of scholars on books, 250; boys 120, girls 130; average attendance, morning 80, afternoon 170; num- ber of teachers, 22; minister, Rev. J. Gardham Reed, 8.D.; superintendent, Mr. J. R. R. Thompson; secre- tary, Mr. J. Jones. The scholars assembled at the Mission Room and walked in procession to a field a- Padgate where the day was spent pleasantly and te freshments were served. LEGIT-STREET (PRrmiTrvE METHODIST) :—Num- ber of scholars on books, 220: boys 90, girls 130; average attendance, morning 50, afternoon 160; number of teachers, 22; minister, Rev. J. Gardham Reed, 8.D.; superintendent, Mr. Bissell; secretary, Mr. J. Landon - treasurer. Mr. 11.11. Matthews. The scholars proceeded by train to Lymm. The school did not join in the general procession but walked through the princlipal streets to the railway station headed by the Legh-street brass band. On arrival at Lymm, the scholars pro- ceeded to a field where they disported themselves. Dinner and tea were served

WORKINGMEN'S MISSION :—Established 1871 ; number of scholars on books, 274 boys, 2i3 girls; average attendance, 450; number of teachers, 36; Mr. Nathan Holigh,president;lVlr.Thornas Dale and 111r.Alfred Tilling, superintendents; Mr. Arthur Gleave, secretary; Mr. James Woolley, treasurer. The scholars :assembled at the school at 9.0 a.m., and formed into processional order. The beautiful banner representing on one side Jesus as the Light of the World, and on the other Jesus blessing little children, was given the place of honour. The processionists proceeded to a 'field lent by Mr. Fairclongh at Skelton's-lane, Penketh. Here the scholars were provided with a good dinner and tea. Sports as usual were engaged in, and the scholars returned from the field at 730 tired though happy. On reaching the school each child received some nuts and an orange EBENEZER CHURCII SUNDAY SCHOOL : Established 1886; number of scholars on books, 60 boys, 62 girls ; average attendance, 80; number of teachers, 10; superintendents, Mr. J. W. Roberts and Mr. E. L. Jones secretary, Mr. T. Hughes ; assistant secretary, Mr. H. Dutton. The children assembled at 8.45, and walked in procession front the school to a field lent by Mr. J. Newton. The large banner bearing the name of the school an the texts "Search the scriptures" and 1" The Lord is my Shepherd," with suitable pictures, was carried. Dinner and tea were served in the field, and games were indulged in, a very pleasant day being spent.

BRICK-STREET AND FRIARS'-GREEN:—Estab- lished 1803; number of scholars on books, 550 ; average attendance, 350; number of teachers, 2;a superinten- dents, Messrs. E. Howard, John fludsonVilliam Evans, and Councillor Thomas Barton; secretaries, Mr. Cannell and Mr. John Woods ; assistant secretary, Mr. F. Scragg. The procession left Friars'-green headed3by the school brass band, along Suez-street, Palmyra-square, Parker- street, through the Park, Sankey-street, Buttermarket- street, to Brick-street school. fhe children were then conveyed on lurries to a field at Padgate belonging to Mr. Fryer, where dinner and tea were provided. During the afternoon sports wete held, and cricket and football were indulged in. ,The school band played selections of music.

BRICK-STREET MISSION :—Established 1893. Number of scholars on . books, 200 boys, 250 girls; average attendance, 403; number of teachers, 21; superintendents, Messrs. J. Shaw and T. Riley; secre- tary, Mr. A. Kay; treasurer, Mr. J. Thornilev. The procession left the school at 8 45 headed by f he Nlission band, and proceeded along Lythgoes-lane, Hayduck-st., Winwick-st., Horsemarket-st., Buttermarket-st., and Church-st., to thelfield at Padgate. The day was spent in games and other amusements, including a cricket match between young men and married men. Dinner was served at 12 30 and tea at 4 30. The young children were conveyed to and from the field in four lurries. CAIRO-STREET (UNITARIAN) :—Established 1788. Number of scholars on books' 145 boys, 125 girls • num- ber of teachers, 21; minister, Rev. Charles Harve/Cook ; superintendents, Messrs. Charles A. Pemberton and Frederick %V. Purse. The children were conveyed in 'busses to the grounds of Walton Old Hall which had been kindly placed at their disposal by 'Mr. F. Monks. Lunch and tea were provided, an,the usual sports helped to while away the time agreeaby. Undenominational. RAGGED SCHOOL.—Number of scholars on books. 350; (boys .150, girls 200); average attendance, 250; number of teachers, 20; James Skelrand, superintendent; F. J. Owen, assistant-superintendent and hon. treasurer; Messrs. Hand T. Wright, school secretaries; John W. Howarth, financial and organizing secretary. rife scholars took part in the general procession, with the Drum and Fife band iv attendance. A new silk banner, bearing an original design, and supplied by Messrs. Slingsby and Son, of Nuneaton, occupied the place of honour. The use of the new banner for the first time was commemorated by a photograph, the officials, teachers and scholars being grouped round the banner. A quantity of miscellaneous clothing was given to the boys. The committee ,aish to thank all those who have sent in parcels of clothing for this object. After the procession, the children marched to a field at Grappen- hall Hayes, kindly lent by Mr. J. Charlton Parr. The youngsters were conveyed in lurries kindly lent by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company. Refresh- ments consisting of pies, buns, cakes, tea and lemonade were served. Cricket, football, sports and other games were engaged in.

SALVATION ARMY :—Established 1884. Number of scholars on books, 56 boys ; 60 girls; average attend- ance, 100; number of teachers' 15. The local officer of the army are: Adjutant and Mrs. Everness, Sergeant Major Ferguson and Miss Lily Dickenson, treasurer. As usual the,lmem‘)ers of the local organisation pat forth commendable efforts to enable some of the poorestichil- dren in the town to spend a happy time on Walking Day. All the poor children that came along were accepted and it was computed that something like 1,28 a joined in. The procession was headed by the Army band and the large banner. The usual games WiL5 after- wards indulgcd in on the Recreation ground at the Park by kind permission of the authorities. Dinner and tea were provided and the proceedings concluded about 9 p.m.

div.head: PADGATE WALKING DAY.
div.p: PADGATE WALKING DAY.

Favoured with beautiful weather, Walking Day at Padgate passed off with great success on Saturday. That village was brightly decorated with flags and bunting, and wore quite a festive appearance. At 1.30 the scholars of the Church and Wesleyan Sundtry schools assembled at their respective sz,-hools and were after- wards joined by the children of the Cottage Homes. The children of the Church of England Sunday school led the procession, and were preceded by the band of the Cottage Homes. The route followed was by way of Padgate-lane qfi far as the finger-post, returning thence to Fearnhead fl.koss, where a halt was made. From here the children of the Wesleyan school and those of the Industrial school returned to their different schools,but before dispersing the scholars and teachers joined in singing the National Anthem. The Church of England school scholars then proceeded to Cinnamon Brow Farm, where Mr. George Mather placed a field at their dis- posal, and those attending the Wesleyan school were invited to the grounds of Mr. Henry Thornton, "The Laurels," where photographs of the groups were taken, after which they marched to a field in Padgate-lane. The procession was marshalled by Mr. George Mather. The remainder of the day was spent in a most enjoyable manner, the sports held at Cinnamon Brow Farm proving a great attractiom. The prizes were distributed by Mr. Henry Hoult. The prize winners in the committee race weret—l, Mr. E. Gorton 2, Mr. Pocock; 3, Mr. Vaughan. A display of fireworks completel a very successful Walking Day.

Poles and Englishmen at Loggerheads. At the Newtou-le-Willows Police Court on Thursday morning, a Russian Pole named Poorjunus, was charged with unlawfully wounding another Pole named Anthonis Szitkanckas on Friday week at Hay- dock. On the date in question there was a pitched battle between Poles and English at Haydock, during which the defendant ran out of his house and dealt the complainant a severe blow on the head with a poker, causing a nasty lacerated wound. Defendant denied the offence. He was ordered to pay costs.

The second eleven did well in averting defeat, for at the close the odds were certainly in favour of Bolton. Going in first, the Bolton men declared their innings after compiling 203 for the loss of 7 wickets. A splendid stand by E. Redford and S.Altham resulted in 58 being scored for the first wicket. The finest batting perform- ance was given by G. G. Altham who ran up 68. The Warringtonians fared rather badly, and compiled 93 for the loss of 6 wickets. To J. Thompson and T. Houghton belongs most of the credit for saving the game their figures being 20 and 42 respectively.

A draw was the result of the encounter between Sankey Wire Millsand Hough Green, but Hough Green lnd the best of matters. They were all dismissed for 102, and 8 of the Wire Mills wickets were down with only 55 scored when play ceased. The feature of the Hough Green innings was Martindale's fine display for 43. Taylor (14) was the highest scorer for Sankey. Woodcock did good work with the ball, taking six wickets for 17 runs.

Crosfield's visited Arley Park and made short work of the villagers, running up a majority of 44. Their most successful batsman was T. H. Ford, who knocked up 34, and T. Whitfield contributed a capital 21.

Warrington police accomplished a smart performance in defeating Cheshire Lines Engineers by 36. P.C. Jones was in fine form with-the bat. whilst P.C. Holland was the destructive agent, capturing 6 wickets for 9 runs.

Appleton and Stretton had to bow the knee to St. Helens Cable Co., who triumphed by a 56 margin. G. Peacock (21) and H. Dutton (19) did acceptable work for the victors, but not one of the villagers reached double figures.

Warrington Grammar School mule a poor show against Hulme Grammar School. They were all out for 41, and their opponents responded with 126 with only 7 wickets down. Burgess (21 not out) was the only Warringtonian who did himself justice.
St. Paul's entertained Sankey, and gained a creditable victory,J. Bate tting vell for his 21 not out.

There was an exciting match between Latchford Baptists 2nd and Stretton and Appleton 2nd, the Baptists winning by a couple of runs. Penketh had little difficulty in disposing of Fairfield, their best bats- man being Hobson who placed 16 to his credit.
Grappenhall were fortunate in beating Lymm by 5, W. Banks (16) and W. Watson (12), doing good work for the victors.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

It was little wonder that with such ideal weather con- ditions interest in the local bowling competitions on Saturday should be fully maintained. The end of the works contests for the Finlayson cup is now in sight, Saturday witnessing the completion of the third round. Three matches were decided and the tit-bit was undoubt- edly the defeat of the cup holders, L.& N.-W. Railway, by Rylands No. L The railway men have not main- tained their usual high standard this season, but still one can hardly help sympathising with them. They had such provokingly hard luck in being beaten by six points. Each team made a bold bid for victory, and matters had reached a crucial stage when T. Horrabin (the railway captain) and T. Hum- phreys entered upon their game. Rylands had the lead by 127-119; but Horrabin went to work with a will and at the sixteenth end was ahead by 12-7. He had therefore to prevent Humphreys scoring again, to give London and North Western the victory, and the hopes of the railway men were encouraged? Humphreys, however, was on the alert, and scored a single from the next end. This he follgwed with a double and two singles, and the victory was with Rylands's, although Horrabin had won his game by 15-13. Naturally the wire-workers were elated at their success, and their opponents were just as disappointed.

An exciting game_ was that in which A. Peters figure against R. Knight. Peters started well and placed three to his credit against his opponents' one. Knight soon turned the tables, and at the seventh end had the advan- tage by 5-3. Peters gradually gained upon him, and at length led by 9-6. Two doubles in succession fell' to Knight, making the position 10-9 in his favour. Peters showed superior skill in the two succeeding .3nds and got in front by 1240. Then Knight had two singles, and the trundlers were level with 12 each. Knight made the best of the next end, and the score was 14-12. Peters was fortunate enough to s3cure a single and a double, and ran out winner of a fine game by 15-14.
Woods, thecaptain of the victorious team, was in great form and defeated W. Bridgen by 15-9. Bridgen soon fell behind,and his scores came very rarely.

Pearson and Knowles No. 1 did what was expected of them, and triumphed over Smith's Wire Works by the handsome majority of 54. They won nine of the twelve ganCes, and there was a dearth of exciting contests. The closest was between Thomas Davies aad T. A. Thorniley, the last named claiming the victory by 15-12. The contestants several times drew level,and the detailed scores -are interesting : 7-7, 7-9, 8-9; 9-10 10-10, 10-11, 11-11, 12-11, 12-12, 13-12 15-12. George Ball, the forge captain, had to admit de- feat at the hands of Henry Daintith, the opposing cap- tain, who ran up a majority of 15-11. Daintith speedily showed that he meant to win, and held the upper hand throughout.

The expected again happened in the encounter between Houghton's Wire Works and Cockhedge Factory, the wire workers demonstrating their superior skill by a 60 points majority. They were victorious in nine games, but the contests were not all runaway affairs. E. Unsworth made a good stand, and was beaten by G. Harrison by a solitary point. R. Savory won his g•tme with James Jennings by 15-12, and J. Firth (the Factory captain) defeated. William Foster by 15-11.

Bowlers, like most other working-class people will no doubt give themselves up to holiday-making to-day and consequently no works competition matches are down for decision. The draw for the semi-final took place on Monday evening, and the result is that the following matches will be played next Saturday : Houghton's Wire Works v. Cheshire Lines; referee, Mr. George Ball. Pearson and Knowles No. Iv. Etylands N 3.1 ; referee, Mr. Tom Ellison.
Both these matches should be verfclose, but I fancy Pearson and Knowles' and Houghton's will prove the finalists. The ;games will clammence at 3.30 and 2d. will be the admission charge.

Saturday, July 16th, will be a great da3, for the final will then be decided. The committee have decided to divide the proceeds between the Nurs- ing Association and the Infirmary—bwo deserving institutions which greatly need support. The cup and medals will be presented immediately after the match. On the following Saturday the cup winners will meet a team selected from the various teams which hay figured in the competition, and the proceeds on this occasion will also go to thelnfirmary and Nursing Associ- tion. The price of admission to the green on each date will be threepence.

There were three matches in connection with the Warrington and District League on Saturday, and the most interesting was undoubtedly that between Penketh Park and Cemetery. The contest was very keenly fought, although Cemetery had a slight lead through- out. In the end they triumphed by 4 points. There were Several very close encounters, W. Hill defeating J Grahamand S.Shave beating LB elton by the margin o

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. Warrington Borough Police Court. Minor Cases.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. Warrington Borough Police Court. Minor Cases.

SATURDAY.—Before Mr. Birchall (in the chair), Alder- man Bennett, Councillor Wilkinson, and Messrs. R. T. Fairclough and E. Woods. FOUND VIM Johnson,of no fixed residence, stood charged with being drunk and begging in Buttermarket-street at a quarter past eleven the pre- vious night.—Superintendent Monaghan said he 'observed the prisoner, who was drunk, accost several people and ask for alms. A few minutes later he walked up to till superintendent and told him he was out of nark. "Well," was the Superintendent's rejoinder, "‘ I'll find you lodgings," and without more ado handed him into the custody of P.C. Hesp.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for fourteen days.

.MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Francomb and Sme hurst, Councillors Tinnion and Thornton, Messrs. Birchall, Hayward, Wright and W. Roberts. DISGILkCEFIIL CONDUCT AT ARPLEY.—Joseph Clancy, •of 23, School Brow, Andrew Clancy, Walsh ard, and Joseph Grady were charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Arpley on Sunday afternoon. The brothers Clancy were further charged with assaulting Police Constable Clarke.—The Chief Constable said the case arose ovt of serious complaints made by several gentle- men about the disorder which went on in Arpley fields on Sunday afternoon and evening, and of •considerable damage being done. He had had occasion to put several officers on plain clothes •duty in the neighbourhood. and unfortunately the com- plaints were very well founded.—P.C. Clarke said he was passing the Cricket Ground when ha heard a -"terrible noise" behind the boards. Eight or ten men, including the prisoners, were in the field with a stone jar of beer. They were drunk and rolling all over the ground. He ejected them from the field and asked for their names and addresses, but they would not give them. The brothers Clancy set upou him and kicked and butted him, throwing him to the groflud. P.C. Johnson ,came upon the scene, and prisoners were taken to the lock-up.—P.C.'s Corbett and Johnson gave evidence—The brothers Clancy denied the assault—Mr. C. H. linsworth •secretary of die Wtrrin4ton Cricket Club, said it was .quite unknown to the committee or officials that the prisoners got on the ground. They must have climbed over the fence. The committee did their best to keep the ground as private as possible. and prisoners had no 'business there. The club would certainly prosecute -trespassers in future.—Prisoners admitted climbing over the boards—Grady was fined ss. %nd the brothers Clancy were each fined 10s. and costs, with the option • of fourteen days' imprisonment.

• FRlDAY.—Before Mr. Alderman Smethurst (chair- man, Mr. Councillor Tinnion, Mr. Councillor John Roberts, Mr. George Piling and Mr. L. W. Reynolds. THREE MONTHS FOR STEALING LE A D.—WillißM Blanchard, labourer, Guardian street and Joseph Ashton wire-worker, 5 Chapel street,were charged with stealing '2cwt, lqr. 121bs of lead, of the value of 305., from the works of Messrs. Pochin and Company. Bank Quay, sometime between June 16th and June 30th.—Superin- tendent Monaghan said he would withdraw the charge against Ashton in order that he might call him as a witness. In detailing the circumstances of the case, :Superintendent Monaghan stated that the prisoner worked at Messrs. Pochin and Company for about six months, but left about a fortnight ago. 'On the 16th inst stuck was taken of the lead and it was then all right. The police received information on Thursday morning respecting some lead having been buried in a ditch in Arpley fields -and covered over with grass. P. C. Sweeney was placed on duty there in plain clothes and at 9.45 the prisoner, Ashton and another man came on the • scene with a handcart. They commenced to load the lead and had got ten pieces on the cart when P.C. Sweeney arrested the prisoner and Ashton. The other man got away.—Joseph Ashton on being called as a witness said the prisoner and another man came to his house and asked him to hire a handcart. He thought it was to remove furniture, hut when he got to Arpley fields the prisoner told him he had "a bit of crooked • stuff to remove. Witness refuse 4 to have anything to •do with it.—The prisoner was committed to prison for three months with hard labour.

div.head: PEN KETH.
div.p: PEN KETH.

FIRE.—An exciting time was experienced on Wednesday evening, the cause being a fire broke out in a large hay- shed on the premises of Mr. Walter Kelsall, Bank House farm. The alarm was quickly given and word dispatched to the Penketh Tanning Company's Brigade who turned out with commendable promptitude, and quickly got to work. A stand pipe to the main was the method adopted as the pressure of water was very low, and it is fortun- ate that there was no danger of the flames spreading, as the supply of water would have been quite inadequate to cope with a serious conflagration. The contents of the shed consisted of shaw, which was very dry owing to the hot weather, and soon blazed furiously. The t*ber on the shed was also fired and had there been wooden posts instead of iron pillars, the structure would soon have been totally demolished. The damage to produce is not heavy, but the shed consisting of three large bays is a wreck. The firemen were on hand from 5 p.m. until 7.30, when the mastery was obtained. Large crowds watched the fire, but admirable order was main- tained, P.C. Houghton being pr.nt during the course of the fire.

div.head: New Methodist Hymn Book.
div.p: The New Methodist Hymn Book.

The Rev. R. Wilkins Rees preached on "The new Methodist Hymn Book," at Bewsey-road Wesleyan •Glhurch on Sunday evening. He made a general reference to the Methodist Hymn Book, and specially referred to the edition just issued.

div.head: LIKE THEM? RATHER!
div.p: LIKE THEM? RATHER!

It was " Nacural Fruit Jellies "prepared from Brown • & Poison's "Patent" Corn Flour and the juice of stewed fresh fruit, that called forth these remarks. The young housewife had sent for Brown & Poison's booklet of "Summer Dishes," and her first try to make the jellies had met with most gratifying success. To quote an old saying, these natural fruit jellies aro as full of good- ness as an egg is full of meat—cooling, agreeable sweets, ; and so wholesome, because absolutely free of artificial preservatives or condiments. The recipe is given in Brown & Poison's booklet," Summer Dishes," a copy of which will be forwarded to all ladies sending Id. stamp to Brown & Poison, Paisley. Send at once, your ;memory may fail you.

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, July 2 1904

Horse and Jockey disposed of Sankey Chapel House somewhat easily, as the 64 points majority indicates. The closest game was that in which T. Harrison accounted for J. Sparks by 15-14. Horse and Jockey won no fewer than eleven games.

Liberal Club tasted the sweets of victory, their opponents being Fearnhead. The Liberals were victor- ious in ten games, and secured a majority of 53. Some of the games were very well contested, the margin of 3 giving the victory to E. A. Saunders against James Roberts, and J. Sankey against W. Andrews.

The following is the league table up to date : P. W. L. For Agst. Pts. Cemetery Chapel House Horse and Jockey 8 ... 5 ... 3 ...1253 ...1000 ... 10 Bull's Head Brooklands Fearnhea,d Penketh Liberal Club 8 ... 2 ... 6 ...1106 _l2lO ... 4 There will be no league matches to-day.

The semi-final for the Allison Cup presented to the Cemetery Club commenced on Monday evening when W. J. Kay beat A. Vernon by 21-15. The game between Boardman and Antrobus had to be postponed until Wednesday next, Boardman having met with= accident.
