div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

"Ladies' Day" was the Warrington Cycling Club's fixture for Saturday, but only three mEmbers of the fair sex journeyed to Lower Pe,3ver. No doubt the threatening weather of the morning was to some extent responsible for the small muster. Eleven members put in an appearance, and the outing proved very enjoyable.
Tea was provided at the Warren de Tabley Arms and the ride home was made under grand weather conditions.

Beautiful weather favoured Ttiesday evening's run to Lymm and thirty members turned out, this being the largest attendance of the season. Several games of bowls were played on the Plough Hotel green, and the homeward journey in the moonlight was a splendid close to an enjoyable evening.
On Wednesday evening the first bowling main was brought to a close at Sankey Chapel House, and after some exciting games, IVIr. Frank Redfern ran out winner.
To-day's run is to Chester and on Tuesday evening the club goes to Bucklow hill.
LIGHTING-UP TIME. To-night Sunday Monday 9.40 Tuesday. % 9.40 Wednesday Thursday

div.head: Water Polo.
div.p: Water Polo.

There was a large attendance at the Legh-street Baths on Tuesday evening to witness Warrington second's encounter with South Hill. The Warringtonians showed very indifferent form, and in the first half were thoroughly outplayed. Only once did they pierce the visitors' defence, and that was when J. Warren sent the ball through at the top corner. South Hill attacked vigorously and when half time was called had registered four goals. The scorers were W. White (2), W. Haddon, and L. Foschi. On resuming the Warringtonians played more briskly, but failed to score again. It was unfortunate for the home team that J. Rathbone and W. Warren were ordered out of the bath for some breach of the rules. Bailey effected several fine saves, but White again scored and the game ended in a victory for South Hill by five goals to one.

The Warrington team was as follows :---Warrington : G. Raney, goal; S. Walker and W. Warren, backs; R. Allen (capt). half back; J. Rathbone, right wing ; C. Turner, centre; J. Warren, left wing. Mr. Snowden;of Liverpool, was the referee.

The works squadron competition promises to be a great success. The first round was decided on Tuesday evening, and aroused much interest. Houghton's (Sankey Wire Mills) accounted for Richmond's, and Pearson and Knowles defeated Post Office No. 1. The Co-operative Stores triumphed over the Post Office No 2, but Crosfields only just. managed to beat Monks Hall

div.head: Angling.
div.p: Angling.

The first match of the season in connection with the Black Bear Angling Society was duly decided in the waters of the Bridgewater Canal at Grappenhall on Sat- urday last. There were nineteen competitors, and though sport was not of a brisk nature, yet an enjoyable match resulted. The following were the winners of the prizes in the order named: Messrs. J. Cook, W. Dakin, J. Bradshaw, J. Clarke, F. J. Emson, T. Nixon and A. Bate. The arrangements for the match were satisfactorily carried out by the Secretary, Mr. Sam Grindley. The next match will be decided on Wednesday evening, July 6th. at Grappenhall.

At the meeting of the Latchford Angling Society held on Monday, detailed arrangements were confirmed as to the first match of the season which will be fished at Northwich on July 9th. The Secretary, Mr. Alfred Starkey, reported that several tue•nbers had already re- corded some excellent specimens of course fish from the Bridgewater Canal.

The Rope and Anchor Cycling Club held a contest at Hunt's Lock, Northwich. The following were the prize winners :—J. Bothwell, 4 ozs. (three fish) ; J. Hackney, 3 ozs. 14 drs.; J. Atherton. 3 ozs. 5 drs.; A. Bradley, 3 ozs. 4 drs.; .1. Nicholson, 3 ozs.; W.Clare, 1 0z.12 drs.; F. W. Berry, 14 drs.

div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.

The Gordon Bennett race is over; the coveted Cup has gone from Germany to France, and despite a little natural regret that Jenatzy, the former holder, should have lost it—for the loss was by a few minutes only— Thery's victory has proved a popular one. England was hopelessly out of it; but, notwithstanding the spasms of patriotism and plrtissnship which have prompted a few journalists to predict that we stood an excellent chance, no redly practical motorist enter- tained the faintest hop 3 of th 3 Cup returning to our shores.

Thery's victory Ills been the more popular because it was gained by consistent good work throughout the whole of the course, and was not attributable to better drivers and their cars being deleted through unavoid- able accidents. There is nothing much to be proud of when the best engines havg been put out of the running through some fearful a cident, a second-rate car driven by a less skilful driver wins by the merest fluke. Indeed, this is not winning in the best sense of the word, for there is no questioa of beating others. Before now, accidents, arising through no defect in mechanism or want of skill on the driver's part, have utterly spoiled the chances of the best cars entered for some event, as a perusal of the records of past racing will show. Tbery won on his merits as a driver of a good car, and no true sportsman will grudge him the victory.

Although a broken-down motor car is not the common object of interest by the roadside that it WAS hut two or three years ago, there is no doubt that many break- downs occur which are really of the most trivial nature and could be readily put right by even the most amateur of amateur drivers, did he but know how to locate the trouble.

In the event of a sudden &nd apparently unaccountable stoppage of the engine, first look to the ignition, and ,if this appears to be all right, next pay attention to the petrol. The chances are that it is one of these two departments that the cause is to be found.

• The ignition may have failed through a variety of causes. The accumulators may have run down, for instance, the sparking plugs may be cracked or dirty, or there may be a short circuit. •:Test the accumulators with a voltmeter; if the reading is 4 volts the fault is not here. Take out the sparking plugs and clean 'the points; if a crack is discovered here is the root of the mischief.

More likely, the engine has been over-oiled, in which case there will be a film of partially burned oil on the porcelain. This can be removed with petrol. Before replacing the plug, take a rag dipped in petrol, and with it clean away as much oil as possible from the orifice in the combustion chamber in which the plug is screwed.

Providing that the ignition is all right, it is most likely that there is somqh.ing wrong in the petrol department. Perhaps the spirit is not getting through properly, owing to wchoked carburetter; or, probably, the tank is practically empty—and the best petrol car ever made will not run without spirit. In nine cases out of ten, the temporary but. unlooked-for stoppages of an engine are due to some simple cause; in the tenth the cause may be slightly more difficult to locate ; but more often than not common sense and possibly a spanner will put the matter right.

div.head: TIIE FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: TIIE FREE CHURCHES.
THE LICENSING BILL.

The strong feeling which the introduction of the Licensing Bill has Caused in. Free Church circles has by no means abated. Everywhere Free Church Councils are taking the matter up. The National Free Church Council is co-operat- ing with the Committees responsible for the various demonstrations, and is taking an active part in the opposition. Thousands of copies of a pamphlet explaining the Act have been sent down to the local Councils, and memorials against the Bill have been extensively adopted.

It was a still, cool night late in the fall when two men, clad in ragged blue canvas and jackets of deerskin stained With green stains by glacier clay, came plodding down a trail which winds through the ranges of British Columbia into the wilds of Caribou. Forty years ego that trail was worn deep by the feet of a multitude pressing feverishly north- wards in search of gold, and the bones of dead men and horses were strewn along it. To-day the forest has reclaimed much of its own, and portions of the road are covered with willows, for the alluvial diggings are worked out now, and the precious metal is won in a few places by hydraulic monitors whose owners are joint-stock companies. Still, men of experience say there is more treasure yet hidden in the wilderness between Quesnelle and the. Peace River than ever was taken out, and at intervals detachments of the unfortunate go up in search of it. Some come back with a little, and some never come back at all. Carson, the Englishman, and Cedar Crossing Lee had, however, been unusually successful, and now, with shoulders aching under their burdens, trudged behind the weary pack-horse on their homeward journey. By the next nightfall, if all went well, they should reach a log-built settlement from which a waggon road led to the post where a stage would bear them swiftly south to civilisation again, and for this reason they had determined to cover at least another league before they camped. Carson's feet were bleeding, and the straps brd eaten raw wounds in his shoulders; but these were minor discomforts, for the treasure of the north is not to be lightly won, so he whistled odd snatches of English ballads while the stately pines loomed up out of the dimness and vanished again behind. On either hand the huge, tapered trunks rose like mighty columns, their great branches meeting as though they were arches of the groined roof above, while stray shafts of moonlight filtering through cast patches of shimmering radiance athwart the trail ahead. Also, as usual in that region, the boom of a glacier-fed river rose from unseen depths below, and in places framed by festoons of whispering needles there opened up before him a majestic vista of everlasting snow. He halted for a moment to adjust his burdens, two blankets, an axe, and a heavy packet in wrappings of hide, while the moonlight beat down upon his bronzed face with the long hair •falling about it, and keen, fearless eyes. "We might hold out for another hour, but that's the most," he said. "The poor Cayuse is dead beat, too. I don't know why, but up there I hadn't a care, while now I feel strangely anxious to make the settlement. Well, no one can march for ever, and we'll start with sunrise." Lee, of Cedar Crossing, who was similarly caparisoned, laughed as he smote the horse's flank, and there was a clattering of shovels, axes, tin pans, and kettles as the tired beast blundered on again. He was a forest rancher, who, like others of his kind, spent much of his time wandering through the wilderness in search of minerals which he did not often find. "I guessed you were getting jumpy," be said. "One usually feels that way towards the end of a lucky journey, especially if he's young. Thinking of that girl in the old country, say? Well, you've enough to go home and see her. I'm too old for such fooling even if I hadn't Eliza. Going to start a store at the crossing and indent for a post-office instead." He started, for as if in answer a weird, unearthly laugh rang out of the stillness, and changing into a mournful wail died out far up in the silence of the black hillside; then smiled feebly as he said: "Only a loon. Never liked to hear it. That blamed distressful bird seems to know when there's trouble coming. Guess we'll get on a last rustle." They quickened their pace, brushing through the dewy coolness while the scent of pine and cedar hung heavy in the air, but Carson hardly noticed it. Already in fancy he breathed the fragrance ,of English roses, while the sombre conifers gave place to sunny meadows ridged with whitening bay. Also the faces of his kinsfolk rose up before him, and among them one which was not that of a relative smiled at him wistfully with tear-dimmed eyes, as it did the day he turned his back on the Mother Country. Now he could go back and see them all, while even after that his share of the gold would enable him to seize upon one of the openings which present themselves to the adaptable man with a few dollars in the seaboard towns. He was entitled to a space of leisure, he thought, after four weary years of disappointment and ill-paid labour in the Dominion, and he had won it hardly enough, facing snow-slide, starvation and death in the northern wilderness. Then he shook the reverie from him when the trail wound along the edge of a slope of shale which dropped steeply to the river whose roar reached them more hoarsely. White mist curled up towards them from below, and on the other hand the climbing pines seemed spires of blackness, while the 'moon, which now hung over their shoulder clear of the trees, cast lone shadows down the trail. Caution was needed here, and Carson wished his comrade had not talked so freely before the loungers in the store of the first outpost of civilisation where they had slept two nights earlier. It stood at the branching of the ways where one trail led north-west towards the desolations of °easier, and sometimes desperate, broken men who had lost their all came back at that season along it. Still, he knew the most part of the free prospectors were honest as the day, and tried to forget. his growing uneasiness as he listened to the calling of the river and the whisper of the pines, until Lee, grasping the Cayuse's rein, stopped suddenly. "Stand fast!" said a hoarse voice. got you covered. Hold your hands lip!" Then Carson, who set his teeth, staring into a thicket of sal-lal and withered fern, saw the end of a rifle barrel that glinted under the moon. He was by no means a timid man, but he knew that sudden death would overtake him at the first move, and clenching his fingers hard raised both hands above his head. "That's better," said an 4 unseen man, ironi- cally. "Thought you were going to be too late with it. Don't want any useless unpleasant- ness, and we'll be satisfied with what you have got with you. Now, one at a time; the short man first. Slip the straps off your shoulders and let those packages go. You .can unbuckle the sling of the rifle, too." Lee growled something which was not a blessing, but his Winchester fell clattering on the trail, and the hide package followed with a thud. Mean- time Carson, whose nerves were tingling with the effort to restrain himself, moved one foot softly into the shadow that crept towards him. Another few inches and he would be out of the hateful moonlight., when there mieht be a chance for a bold dash for liberty. Already balancing himself on the other heel he prepared for a spring, and then the tension on his muscles slackened again, for a second voice said: "Stop right where you are. Another move and you won't know what's hurt you. l'm watching you." The sprays above a low cedar branch rustled, and Carson, who canght the dim outline of another barrel turned upon him, did as he was bidden. After this, while Lee stood up unloaded, looking badly ashamed of himself, the first speaker said: "Stand there against. the hemlock while we tend to you. Drop all those things about you—sol The Cayuse ? Guess we've no use for nulling round a camp outfit, and we'll leave him with you. He's branded, with a bite on the off ear, too. Got anything else of value? No! Then march out straight before you, and something will happen to the first who looks behind him." Lee struck the Cayuse pony savagely with his fist, and when he moved dejectedly up the trail Carson strode behind him white-faced with dismay end fury, for the gold they had earned so hardly, floundering through snow-choked passes, and swinging the shovel from early dawn until star- lieht shimmered on the spectral glaciers, lay in the red dust behind. Worse still, the long expected journey home and the chances of a future had gone Where a'really reliable automatic carburetter is used, with it. div.head: BUMMER WORK.
div.p: BUMMER WORK.

During the summer months interest ia religious and social work everywhere tends to flag. Yet there are very many forms of Christian activity which can only be done in the summer time. - The National Free Church Council strongly urges local councils throughout the country to take up the matter of open-air services. There has been considerable success in this branch of work during the past few years, in numbers of towns open-air services being conducted by the council as a whole, and all the denominations joining in. Granted fine weather, it seems probable that this year there will be a larger number than ever to take up the work.

div.head: SEASIDE CONFERENCES.
div.p: SEASIDE CONFERENCES.

Following out the same idea, a very interest- ing series of meetings has been arranged to take place at the seaside. The idea has been to hold great conferences at popular resorts, where there are sure to be a large number of Free Churchmen and Christian workers gathered from all parts of the country. Arrangements have been made for meetings to be held at Scarborough on the 29th and 30th of August, and Blackpool on August 31 and September 1. The Rev. F. B. Meyer, the President of the National Council, will preside at these meet- ings, and will be accompanied by the Rev. Thomas Law and others. On the first night there will be a great Free Church demonstra- tion, and the next • morning there will be a Christian Endeavour Rally at seven o'clock. This will be followed by a gathering of ministers and Christian workers at eleven o'clock, and a Bible Reading in the afternoon. There will be an informal conference over tea on Girls' Guild work, to be followed in the evening by another public meeting, more especially concerned with the deepening of spiritual life.

div.head: MACEDONIAN ATROCITIES.
div.p: MACEDONIAN ATROCITIES.

For the moment Macedonia has rather faded out of men's minds, and the knowledge that fearful atrocities are even now being committed on a defenceless Christian population does not arouse that stern indignation which has fired up at other times. Mr. Setchanoff, a Bulgarian pastor, has just arrived from the scenes of the massacres, and he has a thrilling story to tell of the terrible work of the Turks. Pastor Setchanoff has received the warmest commen- dations of the National Free Church Council and has arranged to speak at Men's Meetings at Westbourne-park, Christ Church, and the City Temple. Pastor Setchanoff ought to, be heard in all parts of the land, and the story he tells should arouse intense indignation, leading to action on the part of our Government.

div.head: GIPSY SMITH IN SOUTH AFRICA.
div.p: GIPSY SMITH IN SOUTH AFRICA.

Gipsy Smith's mission in South Africa is proving a wonderful success. Although on the side of conversions the numbers are unprece- dented, the greatest feature of the mission is the force it has exerted in drawing together 'hitch and Englisht There was considerable, bitterness, the legacy of the late war, in tho minds even of Christian workers, but the mis- sion has done much to dispel this. At a great converts' meeting at the close of the Cape Town Mission some 2000 converts attended, and one of thl leading ministers of the Dutch Reformed Church made a most striking statement of the result of the mission among the Dutch. Gipsy Smith at Kimberley succeeded in filling the Town Hall for a record number of consecutive nights, and accomplished a marvellous mission there. Gipsy Smith is going on to Bloemfon- tein, Johannesburg, Pretoria, East London, and the other principal cities of South Africa. Owing to the great success of the mission, urgent requests have been sent across for an extension of time. The General Committee of the National Free Church Council, feeling how im- portant it is not to hamper the good work, have arranged that, should Gipsy Smith wish it, he may prolong the visit another two months. The life-story of the Evangelist, published by the National Free Church Council, has just gone into another edition, completing 49,000.

div.head: OLD TIME PASSIVE RESISTANCE.
div.p: OLD TIME PASSIVE RESISTANCE.

Passive resistance to the law is by no means a new thing, and was heard of and practised long before the present Education Acts were conceived. Dr. John Brown, the well-known authority on Puritan Times, in the book "From the Restoration of 1660 to the Revolution of 1688," just published by the National Fre• Church Council, gives some thrilling stories of the sufferings of our Puritan forefathers when they resisted the law in obedience to tlie voice of conscience. He tells in a graphic way of the ejectment of ministers caused by the Act of Uniformity, and the wholesale imprisonment of Nonconformists following on the Conventicle and other Acts. His book needs to be read at this time when the forces of reaction are so rampant.

div.head: DR. HORTON'S RECOVERY.
div.p: DR. HORTON'S RECOVERY.

• Although Dr. Horton has returned to his ministry at Hampstead he is only allowed by his doctors to resume his work very gradually. At first he is only to preach once on Sunday and once in the week at his own church, and must not travel or preach elsewhere for at least three months. He is allowed to read and write very little as yet, and in order that he may fulfil his duties next year as President of the Free Church Council it is absolutely necessary for him to be very quiet this year and to har- bour his strength. All our readers will feel great sympathy with Dr. Horton in his con- tinued affliction, and we all hope for his com- plete restoration.

div.head: CLUBS FOR GIRLS.
div.p: CLUBS FOR GIRLS.

The new movement to erect homes or club- rooms for the use of girls of the Free Churches is making considerable headway. The National Free Church Council, through :its Girls' Guild Department, has been urging the establishment of permanent homes in all the large centres of population. In this month's Free Church Chronicle an account is given of the work at Eastbourne, together with pictures showing the Guild Parlour there. There are now quite a number of these permanent homes in all parts of the country and they all seem to be doing a very good work..

div.head: TO NON-CHURCH-GOERS.
div.p: TO NON-CHURCH-GOERS.

From the multitude of articles, itc., that have been written on the reason for abstinence from Church services, the non-Church-goer should be brought by now face to face with his responsibilities. The Rev. F. B. Meyer in this month's Free Churchman writes a striking letter "To one who does not go to Church." He deals with an imaginary objector, and his excuses are handled in a masterful manner. in the same issue, Professor A. E. Garvie, M.A., D.D., writes a learned article on "John Wyclif, the Morning Star of the Reformation."

Author of "In the Niger Country," "A Wide Dominion," "Ainslie's Ju-Ju," "Life and Death in the Delta," "The Kingdom of Courage," &c.

"That's just it!" was the answer. "You couldn't see them; they could see you, and it's no use arguing with the man who's watching you (Ter the foresight with a steady squeeze on the trigger. No; its safer to do just whatever tie asNs you. I'm feeling it, too, and Eliza will talk considerable when I come back again with nothing—and your English shot-gun hanging all the time against the Cayuse's near side, out of their sight but just where I couldn't get it. Say, do you figure on spending all the night here ? " Carson's eyes glittered with a dangerous light as lifting the weapon down he opened the breach. Two cartridges filled the chambers, but these he slipped out, replacing them with others whose wads bore the letters B. B.

"No," he answered, grimly. "You see, I want that gold particularly. As I think I told you, there's a girl in the old country who expected great things of me, and has been disappointed—badly. Somehow, I missed my chances hitherto, and now, for her sake, I'm going to make a last effort. We've had an object-lesson of the fact that the man with his finger on the trigger is master. Well, it's a trick that two can play at, and it's no great matter if it doesn't succeed. I'm tired of being a failure, and it will be better, perhaps, for her." The stalwart axe-man from Cedar Crossing glanced at him with sympathy. "Maybe you're right. I'm coming along,' he said. "They have got my gun, but if I can jump in before I'm expected, I guess this will do." I Lifting the big, double-bitted axe from its resting- place on the saddle, he swept the keen-edged blade, which made flashes in the moonlight, in a hissing circle round his head; and, in the hands of those who can use it, the axe is a terrible weapon.

Carson, however, laughed mirthlessly, as he answered: "I daresay it would, but you would hardly get the opportunity; and this is my particular business. You have your ranch, I have nothing, unless it is a reputation for coming to grief; and it's my gun. However, there's no use getting shot needlessly, and I'm going up on the hillside to stalk them, while, working round by the river, you might run in when I whistled. If you don't hear the signal in half-an- hour, you can go back without me." "Then good luck go with you, partner," said Lee of Cedar Crossing, and his hard fingers trembled as he grasped his comrade's hand. "I don't go back alone, and if I hear nothing I'm coming right in with the axe to look for you." So they parted, and Carson brushed swiftly over the dry needles beneath the towering pines, trusting that as their assailants would hardly expect any attempt at reprisal, by apparently unarmed men, and thr; trail was often untrodden for days together, they would camp, or at least examine their booty there. How many the party consisted of he did not know, though he guessed there were not more than two; and with grim satisfaction he tightened his grip on the twelve-bore gun. In an uncertain light, it was a more reliable weapon than any rifle, and no single bullet could at close quarters equal the effect of one-and-a-quarter ounces of heavy shot. Presently, guessing at the distance, he slackened his pace, and slipped cautiously from tree to tree, growling under his breath each time a dry twig snapped, until at last he halted quivering all through behind a hemlock, for the red gleam of a fire flickered out among some willows perhaps two hundred yards below.

Then Carson felt thankful he had been a sportsman at home, and in British Columbia had stalked the wood deer, as dropping on his hands and knees he crawled nearer, stopping at times to listen, while fortunately the bush was open, for there are parts of the Pacific slope forest which even at noonday no man without an axe could force his way through. He could hear low voices now and then, while occasionally a great trunk hid the light; but moving forward, he found it again, and at last wriggled like a snake among the slender stems of the willows, knowing that any blunder would sign his death-warrant now. Once a few leaves rustled above him, and a branch creaked, and it seemed to his excited fancy that the sound must fill the bush; but still he heard no challenge, only a confused murmuring and the crackle of the fire, and, holding his breath, he' won a few yards more. Then a fallen trunk lay across his way, and, lifting his head above it cautiously, he rested the gun-barrel on the moss, and, while a tiny artery drummed inside his head, stared before him over the twin muzzles.

Under a spreading maple, whose• leaves blazed with gold and crimson where the light touched them, two men sat in the red glare bending over the hide package wherein lay a little pile of what looked like coarse grains of sand, though there were a few larger pieces among them. One was bronzed and stalwart, with little cunning eyes, of a type more common in seaboard cities than the British Columbian, bush. The other was haggard and hollow in face, while something about him which suggested an Englishman seemed curiously familiar. Carson noted all this, and also with exultation that the rifles rested against a hemlock some few paces away. "I'm glad it's over," said the weaker of the pair. "I want the gold, Heaven knows how ninch ; and yet—well, it's no use saying now that I'm almost sorry I ever thought of it. Oh, hang the measure! Take what you think is your share, and then the sooner we part, the better. Before two days are over, we'll have twenty armed ianchers scouring the bush for us. I'm heading west, to come out by the lake trail, if I ever reach it." "No more use for me now ? "said the other, with an ironical grin. "Of course, this kind of thing is way beneath a high-toned man like you. Yes, 1 should say we had better be rustling_; and I'm' contented to strike out for myself. You're not worth much at a hard march, any way." He wrapped up the package tenderly, while the other looked down at the little heap before him with a sombre face and moody eyes; then, as lie turned to stir the embers with the toe of his worn- out boot, faced round with an imprecation. "Hold up!" The stern summons rang sharply through the shadows. "Hands above your heads; now move a finger and it's all over with you and Carson rose upright into the glow of the fire with the twin barrels levelled on the foremost. "it's not a Winchester," he added, grimly; "and I could get both Of you. Drop that packet! It was done, and for the space of a few seconds there was no change in the tableaux. The shadows drew in closer, and opened out again as the red firelight rose and fell,, glinting on the rifles which lay temptingly just out of reach, and shewing the three figures standing rigid and still as though they were carved things, with no life in them. Then the stouter of the robbers flinched as he gazed at the stern face behind the rib of the double gun. He knew that big shot spreads, while as in this case there was no lever to jerk a touch on the second trigger would certainly complete what the first discharge left unfinished. He also glanced towards the rifles sideways out of the corners of his eyes, but it would take several steps to reach them, and said, sullenlY: "Euchred! We give in. You have won the game. Will you shew us the rest of your hand?" "It's a strong one," said Carson, driiy. "Two-and-a-half ounces of shot, while even if it didn't all hit you, my partner's waiting ready with the axe. I want all the gold, your weapons, and one of you to deliver up to justice. We could hardly manage the two. Which it is does not matter; and you can settle it between yon,” "There's no need," said the other Irian. "I am sick of a hopeless struggle and am willing to go. Besides, played out, ; something badly wrong with my lungs. This was my last bid for fortune. 1 lost it, and it's all over now. "Then I'm off," said his comrade. "You won't shoot, stranger ? " and Carson answered: "If you walk straight on through the bush—no." The tramp of feet. grew fainter, and died away, while when the hush of the forest settled heavily down again, and there was only the! sputtering of the fire, Carson looked at his prisoner, wondering uneasily what next to do. Exactly where Lee was be did not know, and felt it might be better to do without him than to hail and get no answer. "What are your orders, Henry Carson ? May I sit down?" asked the man, with no trace of Western accent; and Carson started, for again he was struck, and more strongly, by the resemblance to.someone he had known long ago.
"Open your jacket; no liea-pon I see. You s may, "he answered, coldly. "May I ask how you knew me ? "

_ "Heard your name back at the trail forks," said the other, with a curious smile. "It didn't strike me then, but I went to school with you. You needn't. be afraid: I regretted my share in the proceedings even before we got the gold. and, on my word of honour—if that is worth anything—l'll give you no more trouble."_

(arson dropped the gun-butt between his heels, and stared hard at the pesber. He remembered now, and knew that the man before him had taken high honours at an English college.. He was worn i and bent in frame, dressed n ragged deerskin, and signs were not wanting that as. he said there was something radicallx wrong with his lungs. Carson also devoutly hoped that Lee of Cedar Crossing had for the time being lost .his Way. "I can't compliment you on Your present

occupation," he said, with coldness, ooth there was a time when I envied you; but I wit th for the sake of old acquaintance, I had chosen tf other—man. Do you mind telling we what brougu" you--er—down-to this ? " "It's a simple story," was the answer. daresay von have heard it all before. 3t177 prof Ilion was overcrowded, and 1. emigrated, was mad foolishness—my young English wife Witl me. Professional business seemed even worse orf here, so I invested what little I had in fllll ranch, and building lots in what was to be a rising city. The town-site busted, as they say, and the boomers divided the fragzents between the:, while, as a matter of course, I had mortgaged I e ranch. Fruit failed two seasons, and no would even buy what we had; my wife, poor sor ' broke down under the struggle;_ and as a limier hope I sent her into the city and went up prospect_ ing. We found nothing; but working in tce-wate and sleeping wet through developed a lawnt weakness, and before I met that confound e 8 rascal, my late companion, I knew there could .1;0 no more hard work for me. All I left ill wi must have been exhausted, and I couldn't go bac broken-down and empty-handed, you see." ! Carson said nothing for several moments; then, he answered: "I am not ,a vindictive man, 8/11d, don't set up as judge, while I've got back the gold' All things considered, we have not fared badly' and for the sake of happier days—if a few ounce! are any use to you we could spare them, Thre I'll give you a fair start, and there's the wh° of the forest open to you." "You are very good," said the other busklTY; but I cannot take alms from the man" robbed' It's a romantic delusion, of course; but the thing seemed different some way. In any,, ease, Henry Carson,. I am much indebted to you. "Hallo, partner! Hall!" The crY repeatedly through the silence of the woods, a° Carson said, simply “That is my comrade hailing. You had better go. My offer is still open; but, anyway, take your own goods and rifle with you." The man vanished into the shadows, and Ca",:',./3 waited a space before he answered the hail; wl".“ when Lee, grasping the axe, rushed into the cam]) he stared about him in bewilderment ars• he note the packets of gold and the weapons. "You held them up alone, General Jackson!" I; said, wringino, Carson's hand. "I've. been i ' ° blind state of fear about you; got stalled fl cluster of devil's club, and couldn't get throng"; But where, in the name of thunder, have them gone to? You didn't shoot them both, did yoo •ve "No," said Carson, smiling. "'I cooldnft ta's the pair, so I chose one; and finding he wag, an old friend of mine, I let him go. As a fav°„et to me, I don't want this little affair talked ah°,"ei Lee. Now we'll go on, and the further we e- from this place, the better I'll sleep." Jed In due time they found the Cayuse ponY, through the torrent, and camped on the other while, when when they reached the haunts of men agaje,:, Carson, who changed his share of the dust dollar-bills, took the first train east. div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

June is the month of roses and this year this is no fallacy, for roses and rose-colour figure prominently in the world of millinery and dress. This lovely flower has been made to imitate the natural blossom faithfully by the manufacturers of artificial flowers and in every shade and every graduation of colour it graces the prettiest samples of headgear. Two of the latest shapes in straw hats are the Toreador trimmed by a bunch of small roses or a single large flower tied with a black velvet ribbon, thus gracefully breaking the othervk ise hard round brim, and the resuscitated Marquise in white chip adorned by one or two roses and a bow of silk ribbon at the back. Other charming shady hats which make one think of sunny days are formed entirely of drawn Spanish point lace except for a cown of pink, creamy. or yellow roses. " These form a perfect complement to a dainty white muslin toilette and are eminently suited to garden party wear. They are exceedingly

Simple in reality and are finished at the back either by long drooping ends of the lace or by trails of roses and buds. In the latter case it is generally the small variety of roses which are employed and these, tied together in little bunches, look very charming against the hair. The charming hat sketched is fashioned something in the style of those I have just described only that it is made of string- coloured muslin with an embroidered crown and is trimmed with crimson roses and a fall of lace at the back, the same lace draping the gracefully curving brim. The shape is of the most fashionable mode, shades the face, and is a desirable style, the back of the neck being protected by the lace fall. This is a delight- ful hat for seaside wear and is one which would become any style of face while the shade of the roses could be chosen to harmonize or contrast artistically with the accompanying gown. Linens and muslins are quite the most fashion- able materials for morning or country wear and nowadays these are made in such a profusion of beautiful shades that one is puzzled which to select. There is also the offer open to us of buying these ready-made or of selecting one or other of the many becoming shades and buying the material by the yard to be made up by ourselves or some favourite little dressmaker. The former is, of course, the simplest plan, and by far the least trouble, but the latter, I fancy, will be found the most satisfactory in the long rung
INEN TOILETTEJ

The simple toilette shown in my secona sketch is designed in a brownish shade of linen which, indeed, is of a tone rather difficult to describe but might be termed cinnamon. It is, however, quite light in tone and only a few shades deeper than the holland colour with which we ale all so familiar. It is trimmea with bands of cream grounde,._ linen spotted with tiny dots of dark brown. The style in which it is made is quite simple but very neat and when worn with a rustic straw hat trimmed with a wreath of pink and red roses the result is most taking. The skirt in the gown illustrated trails slightly on the ground, but, no doubt, many of my readers have become so enamoured of the walking• skirt that clears the ground all round that they may prefer to adopt it instead under which circumstances I recommend it to be gauged a little more fully round the hips. Pale green linen is a very pretty cool-looking colour for summer wear, while a misty blue is eminently becoming to a fair-haired girl. Muslins of the old-fashioned clear variety liberally gauged and tucked and adorned with plentiful inser- tions of fine lace are very pretty for summer wear for a young girl but should only be worn by those possessed of a perfect skin and com- plexion for there is something about the clear purity of the muslin that shows up any blem- ishes.

The smart little coat given in my last illustration makes a very dressy complement to alight summer gown. It is of taffetas, and is slightly trimmed with passementerie of the same shade as the silk, namely, a holland colour. A small collar, which should be finished by a chou of silk, is also covered with this trimming. This coat could also be expressed in voile' or a thin canvas over silk and used to complete a costume skirt. Indeed, I would recommend any one in doubt as to what is the easiest gnd best thing to wear to buy a ready-made accordion-pleated skirt of biscuit-coloured voile with either enough material to make up into this little coat or to select, if the skirt is sold singly, some yards ol taffetas of the same shade as the skirt and make it up in the above manner. This coat can be worn over a blouse or not, as preferred, which is a great advantage as sometimes the weather is chilly enough to make a blouse and coat a necessity, while at other times the brilliancy of the summer sun makes one wish to wear as light and cool a toilette as can be arrangedi
COQUETTE.

div.head: FOUNDATION OF PROTECTION.
div.p: THE FOUNDATION OF PROTECTION.
THE EFFECT OF IMPORT DUTIES.
WHO PAYS?

PROTECTION is purely a class policy. It was originated in the interests of privileged classes at a time when nobody thought it worth their while to hide the fact that it was a burden upon the masses. In the old days, when the Government of the country was openly carried on for the benefit of the landed interests, Protection was instituted for the specific purpose of putting up the price of corn as a means of increasing the landlord's rent- roll. If we mil 4 lament the callous indiffer- ence of those days, which prompted men to seek riches by the suffering and starvation of the poor,, we cannot complain that they did so under the guise of benefiting the nation or consolidating the Empire.

Honesty. 13-IIT in these days when men are seeking to return to Protection, although the object may be the same, the avowed reason is not so honest. Now we are told that we must adopt Protection as a patriotic duty in the first place, and in the second place as a means of 'improving trade, increasing employment and wages, and cheapening the cost of living, as well as providing old-age pensions and other benefits. This may be good electioneering for a democratic, age, but we should say it was not honest if it were not so manifestly absurd.

Fa tit ty Fo un dations. THE fact of it is,. Protection can never become a domestic policy, because its results can only benefit a few classes at the expense of the rest of the community. Mr. Chamberlain has, however, tried hard to prove that Protection will not only help the landlord and employer, but that it will benefit the people .at large. The protective duties which he proposes will, he says, be paid by the fonigner. Thus at one and the, same time be is going to protect our industries by keeping, out foreign goods, and decrease the Mwdens of taxation by making the foreigner pay ior the privilege of entering the British market. . This is the foundation of modern Protection, the idea that you can make the foreigner pay a duty upon goods which are brought into this country. Such a foundation is faulty upon the face of it:
1. There is no method of making the foreigner pay. 2. Th only people who pay duties are the consumers. 3. Unless the consumer pays there is no Protection for the manufacturer. Who Pays?

THE idea of making the foreigner pay fot the upkeep of the British Empire may be attractive to some people. At the same time, such people cannot help being troubled by the thought that upon the same line of reasoning; the British public has to pay for the mainte- nance of foreign Governments, if it were possible by putting a tax upon imports to make the people who send us their goods pay a duty upon them, then the people of Great Britain have been paying duties to nearly every foreign nation in the world. But nobody is quite so foolish as to suppose we have been doing anything of the kind. And yet Mr. Chamberlain solemnly assures US he can make the foreigner contribute towards our national revenue by taxing the goods le sends us. If this were possible then every nation would support itself by taxing everybody else, and the country which sent out tile most exports would have to pay the most taxes, not to itself, but to some other nation, while the nation which had the most imports would not have to tax its own people at all. The effect of this would be to put a check upon exports, which, accord- ing to Mr. Chamberlain, would mean disaster. Of course the whole argument is absurd. You can no more make the foreigner pay for send- ing his goods into this country than you can make him send them for nothing.

Taxing the Consumer. A MOMENT'S thought will shew that imports are not brought into any country unless some person living in that country wishes to possess them. Food, materials, and manufactures are only brought into a country when there is a demand for them. No foreign producer can force us to take his goods, neither can we force any other nation to take our goods. Anybody who wants something from another country has to pay not only for the article itself, but for the cost of transit, and also the duty (if any ) which his Government may charge for allowing that article to come in. Every charge which is put upon an article, whether it be the prime cost, carriage, duty, .kw profit, must be ix rue by the• person who purchases the article. Upon no other system could the commer,e 'of the world be conducted.

div.head: Principles of Protection
div.p: Principles of Protection

IT is Mr. Chamberlain's efforts to prove to the consumer as well as the producer that his scheme of Protection will benefit both of them that has led to the strange contradictions which his proposals now contain. He tells the ..Biitish conEumer that as the foreigner will pay the, import duties it will not only not increase the cost of living, but it will relieve the burden of taxation.

He tells the Colonial that a preference over the foreigner will encourage his ccmmerce and increase his profits until he supplies us with all the food we require. He tells the British producer that Protec- tion will keep out foreign competition. Now just let us see what Mr. Chamberlain has promised to do. He will tax the foreign imports without increasing the price of these imports. At the smile time he will .give•the Colonial an advantage 'in our markets, and protect the British producer against foreign competition.

• l•row all these thwe proposals are contra- dictory. If you are to give a preference to the Colonial, you must increase the price of the goods he has to sell by putting a tax upon the foreigner's goods sufficient to increase their cost.

If you are to protect the British producer against foreign competition you must shut out his Colonial rival; and you must put a duty upon all imports, so that he will be able to sell his produce for less than either foreign or Colonial goods would be sold for when the duty is added. Thus if you give a preference to the Colonial and protection to the British producer you must put on sufficient duties to increase the prices which the British consumer would have to pay for foreign produce. There was a time when ,Mr. Chamberlain had the courage to proclaim this doctrine in the House of Commons. There was a time when he was prepared to go into the houses of the working men and tell them that his scheme would cost them so much moreca week to live. But those brave days are past. .Now lie wants us to believe that by some wonderful scheme he can get us at one and the same time better prices for British manufacturers and farmers, cheaper food and goods for British workmen, and national revenue from the foreigLer I

div.head: EDUCATIONAL EXPENDITURE.
div.p: EDUCATIONAL EXPENDITURE.

The following letter was read from Mr. R. Potts, clerk to the Cheshire County Council re educa- cational expenditure :—" I am in receipt of your letter intimating that the Guardians of the Runcorn Union have passed a• resolution strongly approving of the resolution passed by the Wirral' Guardians and embodied in your letter. I think such resolution nisust have been passed under a misapprehension, as the County Council are not at the present time erecting any school build- ings. They have, however, given notice of their inten- tion to provide new schools in different parts of the county to meet the requirements of the Board of Education and of the different localities, and I think that your Guardians may rely that only such expendi- ture on their schools as is consistent with the require- ments of the Board will be incurred."

Mr. Collier said he thought it was under- stood that the County 'Council would charge only one half the cost of new schools on the lacalities in which they were built. He believed they had increased the charge on the localities to two thirds indiscriminately,vapart from the needs of any parish. That system would be very hard on parishes where rates were high,and he considered the county ought to bear half the expense. He proposed that the County Council be written to that effect.

Mr. Woodward asked if it'would be wise, in the ab- sence of information imparted to the local sub-com- mittee, to take the step suggested by Mr. Collier. It might be common knowledge through the medium of the Press, but it was not official knowledge. Until they had official information of the intention of the County Council, it would be a little premature to take steps in the matter.
The Board deferred action, pending official infor- mation.
THE COST OF PAUPER RELIEF.

The Swansea Union forwarded the following resolu- tion which had been adopted by them, and asked the Runcorn Board to pass a similar one :—"That in order to more equitably distribute the cost of pauper relief throughout the country, this Board is of opinion that grants in aid shOuld be made from the National Exchequer, as is already done for Education and as regards lunatics." The resolution was to be forwarded to the Local Government Board and the Association of Poor Law Unions. leFIM
The letter was referred to the Parliamentary Committee. •
HOLIDAY ALLOWANCE FOR BLIND CHILDREN.

A letter was received from Liverpool Hardman-street school for the blind intimating that all pupils had to leavefor vacation on the Ist September and asking the Board to forward expenses for two Runcorn inmates. The Council agreed to make the usual allowance. THE VALUATION BILL.

The Clerk said that at the last meeting the Chairman of the Assessment Committee and himself were appointed to attend a further meeting of Union Assessment Committees to be held in London withrefer- ence to to the Valuation Bill. He had received a let- ter stating that the date ha. 4 not yet been fixed, bet the committee were doing their best to prevent the Bill being passed. The Council were asked to contribute 15s. towards the expenses incurred. The Council sanctioned the contribution of 15s. THE WATER MAIN EXTENSION.

The Clerk said that at the iast meeting the Council sealed an agreement with ,Messrs. Timmins for the ex- tension of the water main to the Workhouse at a cost f £49 13s. 10d. There was now a recommendation from the Visiting Committee that the main be extended into the youngmen's yard, for fire extinguishing purposes, at a further cost of £l9 7s. Od.
The matter was referred to a special committee con- sisting of Messrs. Lea, Mountield, Morris, Pilling Broome, Taylor, Collier, H. Davies, and Woodwarc'.
I,THE SUGGESTED TELEPHONIC COMMUNICATION WITH
THE HOUSE.

The Clerk Teported that he met the Warrington Secre- tary of the National Telephone Company, along with Mr. C. E. Linaker, jun., and went into the matter of connecting the Workhouse and other properties in which Mr. Linaker was interested. The secretary sug - gested that the Council should allow the matter to stand over until it was decided by the Government whether they were going to take over the telephones from the company or not. The question should have been decided some time during June, and the secretary said that if the Government took over the telephones, as they had the trunk lines passing the Workhouse, the Council would probably be able to obtain the connec- tion at a cheaper rate than the company would be able to allow them if the Government dtd not take over the system. ,t,

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
NOTICE TO CORRESONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must mall oases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper andisent in, if possible,not later than Thursday.

div.head: Mr. Podmore's Denial.
div.p: Mr. Podmore's Denial.

Sir,—Your correspondent, Mr. E. Osborne, as usual ‘‘ wriggles " and tries to blind your readers by throw- ing verbal litter" into their eyes. There was no need for him to drag into this matter any reference to my remarks at the Trades Council ; but since he has, let me say that this remark was per- fectly justified in the circumstances under discussion, and would be endorsed by the delegates who were pre- sent at that meeting. As Mr. Osborne in trying to score a point at my expense has brought in this phrase, let him apply it to himself. His statements are abso- lute y untruthfal. 3 Your readers shall judge of him and his methods. The only time I have had any conversation with him, was when I was unfortunately introduped to him by a mutual friend at the close of a public meeting on the Chinese Labour Question, held in the Co-operative Hall some time ago. This conversation out of which—by the help of Mr. Osborne's fertile imagination—so much has come, lasted quite one minute ; and was of the most casual and desultory character. Daring that conversa- tion Mr. Crosfield's name tras never mentioned,. Nor was the Labour Representation Committee discussed.
Yours, &c.,
JOSEPFI PODMORE, junr., (President Trades and Labour Council).

Representation of Warrington Sir,—lt must he gratifying to the friends of freedom of election to hear that the front rank men of the labour nrvement have resolved to have no compromise with either of the two political parties. This is a wise and manly decision, seeing that the object of theLtberals iii desiring amalgamation was to secure the return of.therr pet candidate, Mr. Croslleld. Too long have the inter- ests of the working classes been sacrificed to the pride and ambition of those who ueithsr toil nor spin. It is to field labourers, miners, mechanics, millworkers, and men before the mast that the country owes all its wealth And the first and great object of a righteous government would be to protect these wealth producers against injus- tice and oppression, and secure tothem a fair and ample reward for their labours. The Miserable failure of all governments, Conservative and Liberal alike, to do this is producing all over the country a strong desire on the part of working men to secure justice to themselves by sending fellow workers to represent them in parliament Warrington I am glad to say, seems determined to share in this great and just movement. The working people of the town have an overwhelmintr majority of voters on the parliamentary register, and are therefore, in a posi- tion to command the seat whenever they will, and thus relieve the Borough from the incubus of partisan rule under which it has so long suffered. When the next _general election comes round if the workers will only be true to themselves their cause will be triumphant and the present Tory member will bt the last of his race in Warrington. Add when the time has arrived when Toryism is at a discount in "the good old town "the chances of Rad;cal:sm will have disappeared for ever. In commerce, the best and most valuable traveller is the one who has a thorough practical know- ledge of the business he represents;who knows the prices ofthe raw materials used, the cost of labour and the correct ratio of charges incidental to the production and sale of his wares. Such a representative would obtain and book an order for his principals while one depending on his price list would be fumbling for a quotation. In like manner, the man who would effec- tively represent the working classes in Parliament must himself be a worker, not a mere amateur and speechmaker. He must know by experience the toils, hardships, and privations of a life of labour, and be pre- pared, without fear or favour, to wage war against land and all other unjust privileges and monopolies which entail poverty and suffering upon millions of his fellow countrymen. Messrs. Pierpoint and Crosfield are, no doubt, upright and honourable men, having abilities up to the standard of '.he rank and file of Parliamentarians but they are absolute strangers to the qualifications just named. Belonging as they do to the idle and monied class their instincts and interests naturally compel them to take sides with that class, and all that the workers could reasonably expect from them, under the circumstances, would be some mild promises of reform in the future, when the nation would be ripe for it. To return either of these men fora working class constitu- ency would be a_mockery of repres _ _ _ e-
petition of the old partisan game of politics.—Yours truly, lONA.
Sine 1904

div.head: Social Problem. The Social Service League.
div.p: The Social Problem. The Social Service League.

Sir,—The constitution of the "Social Service League" (affiliated with the British Institute of Social Service) is now placed before your readers, and henceforth they will know exactly its aims and objects and the work it proposes to do. Like all new organizations it must of necessity learn to walk before it attempts to run, and your readers may rest assured that nothing of a revolu- tionary character will be attempted ; in fact, the "Social -Service League" is of the opinion that it is by way of evolution and not by revolution that permanent and lasting reform will be secured. I therefore invite friendly criticism, and shall be pleased to answer, to the best of my ability, all questions which may be asked. As stated in our constitution, the "League" is open to all persons irrespective of creed or party who are in sympathy with its avowed objects. Party government, is an accident, not an essential of our English form of government and the " Social Service League " will stand for principles and noVparties. Moreover in the opinion of the League " the State is not a mere utilitarian machine for protecting person and property, driven by the opposing forces of private interest on the one hand or public interest on the other. It looks upon the State as an ethical organisation rooted and grounded in those eternal principles of right and wrong which constitute the moral law,and its office is to unite the individuals who compose it (the State) by a moral and religious bond. May L now pass on to reply to the letter of your correspondent "One Interested." Upon all essential points your correspondent is at one with us and differ- ence of opinion upon details is.at the outset at any rate absolutely inevitable, in fact absolute agreement is by no means a thin(' to be desired even if it were possible. Evidently "One Interested" is either an agnostic or an atheist and as such has a right to his own opinion, but surely he is not in sober earnest when he suggests that every member of the "Social Service League" should pledge himself to eliminate the word" God" from his vocabulary. Such a proposal is both unreasonable and intolerant and I think that upon further consideration he will admit that I am right. The gospel of Jesus Christ is beyond doubt the finest ethic in the entire sphere of moral science and is therefore the best politi- cal enonomy. and although we consider it a part of our duty to co-operate with men who have imbibed its spirit without perceiving and acknoaledging His loftier claims yet we believe with Mazzini "that not till democracy becomes a religious movement can it hope to carry the victory." May I now reply to your correspondent P.B. As a sample of bad logic, narrow-mindedness, ignorance of each subject touched upon, the letter would be difficult to beat, but coming as it does from a member of a party which holds that it is capable of setting in order all things in heaven and on earth and whose adherents with a few exceptions look upon all other organizations as bitter rivals and upon all who hold aloof from their organizations with suspicion, one cannot even feign to be surprised. P. B. states that I have declared myself a" socialist" and have taken part in socialists' gather- ings, but P.B. omits what may be in the opinion of his party an unimportant adjective, but in my opinion a vital one, viz., 'Christian. Again and again T have stated, even at meetings of his own party, "that I was a Christian socialist,' and that in my opinion the only solution to the 'Social problem' was to be found in the teachings of Jesus." Now "Christian Socialism" is easily defined, it is neither complex nor-mysterious, and may be summed up in these words: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart and mind and soul and thy neighbour as thyself." Now will P.B. be good enough to give us a definition of the" Socialism "advocated by his own party and one which his party will abide by. P. B. asserts that the aims and objects of the "Social Service League" are identical with those of the "Independent Labour Party." If that is so why describe it as a "rival "and an "antagonistic" organization? Surely such an accusa- tion is unworthy of one not actuated by motives so frequently attributed to others. But are our aims iden- tical? I think not. The "Social Service League "as such, does not hold that the state should ()yin all means of production but that I understand is a fundamental principle of the Independent Labour Party. Again the " League " considers the Labour party just as much a class party seeking class interests as any other—in fact the class interest is more marked in the constitution of the Labour Representation Com- mittee than in the constitution of either the Conserva- tive or Liberal Parties, whereas the " League " does not recognise parties but principles. As stated in a previous letter the" Social Problem"can not be solved by any one party looking at its own particular interests but by all parties united by a common principle—and however enthusiastic one may be in the interests of labour it will be well to keen in mind that there are interests other than those of labour demanding our con- sideration. In these and other ways the "Social Ser- vice League " differs from the Independent Labour Party but the " League " is broad enough to include not only the members of the Independent Labour , Party but also those whom the Independent Labour Party are not allowed to admit. 'The" Social Service League " Mr. Editor has come to stay,it has also come to work, the measure of its success will be the measure of its support but you may rest assured of this that it will not waste its time in
discussing what is ideally the best but what is as a !natter of fact practicable.—Yours truly, HERBERT DUNNICO.

P.S. Inasmuch as the" Social Service League" does not seek to deprive its members of their individual liberty I fail to see why my connection with the Liberal party has been introduced into the discussion. lam not a party man—in the narrow sense of that word—and never will be, but I am prepared when occasion demands to state the reasons which have led me to fight the election—in this constituency—in the Liberal interest. When that occasion arises the, workingmen of Warring- ton will learn that the motives which have led me to join the Liberal orty are quite As honourable as those which have led P. B. and his friends to do otherwise.

div.head: IN AND AROUND WARRINGTON.
div.p: IN AND AROUND WARRINGTON.
The Electric Light Question in Stockton
Heath.
[BY THE FREE CRITIC.]

The people who dwell on one side of the Ship Canal in the place known as Stockton Heath have once more decided to have a tilt with the Warrington Corpora- tion. It is true it was only by a small majority, but being a majority of two it counted and sufficed. It is very strange how some of these Stockton Heath people love a fight,bat so sure as Warrington or any Company come- along With a scheme which is intended to be for the benefit of Warrington or the Company and Stockton Heath, theti some of the sprightly and leading spirits of the latter place suggest that Warrington or the Company should be fought or that terms should be "dictated " before Warrington or the Company should be allowed to come into the " sacred village." Of course all the residents of this rapidly-growing district are not so barbaric and enamoured of this policy of fighting. Some believe that there is a better and happier way. In fact their policy is one of "Welcome." At the present time if these leading or non-leading pugnacious spirits are allowed to prevail Warrington and Stockton Heath are eventually going tm be landed into a totally unnecessary legal fight. And even legal fighting is expensive at times. It has come about this way. Warrington having an Electric plant and believing that Stockton Heath which is ontsi.de their borough might eventually prove a good market for them have very naturally asked permission to enter and supply all or sundry who want the electric light. No—or words to that effect—says Stockton Heath,unless you further reduce the price of gas. I should imagine that the Warring- ton Corporation are rather staggered at the reply for they really thought they should not only be doing themselves a good turn—but the Stockton Heathens as well, seeing they were prepared to sell electricity in Stockton death on the same terms as to their own ratepayers. It passes, some people's comnrehension that the Stockton Heath Council should have, at this juncture raised the question about gas. The Warrington Cor- poration have only just reduced the price of gas 3d. per 1,000 culsic feet to all their consumers both inside and outside the borough, and in reducing it to those outside the Borough it is generally considered that the Corporation have done a most generous act. It war a generous act, for Warringten have power under an Act.of Parliament to charge 6d. per 1,000 cubic feet to outside consumers. • In fact there are many ratepayers in Warrington who consider that the Cor- poration ought never to have made the reduction to outsiders. -So it will easily be seen that some of the leading or misleading spirits are playing at a I dangerous game. Do they not themselves perceive that instead of making a further reduction of 3d. per 1,000 feet War- rington in a spirit of retaliation may put up the price] of as to its original finre ? If they did then there would be" weeping, wailing, and gnashing of teeth" in Stockton Heath. Stockton Heath is very much at the mercy of Warrington in the matter, as she is in others, for Warrington is supplying her with trams, gas, and water. In fact in most things Stockton Heath is dependent upon Warrington. Do not most of the residents in addition obtain their living in Warrington? This continued opposition to undertakings in Stockton Heath that would be a benefit to most con- cerned is doing a great deal of harm. Stockton Heath nearly lost the tramways by her foolish opposition and delay was occasioned. It was the same I under- stand with the Warrington and Northwich Light Railway, for Stockton Heath obstructed the scheme and here again she got much less by opplsing than would have been gained if she had assisted. The same story can be told of other matters. In fact look- ing at what occurred at last Monday night's meeting it is again considered by many that Stockton Heath blundered in raising the question of gas in connectibn with the electric light. What I have to suggest to the Stockton Heath Parish Council is—that instead of opposing schemes it would be a much better plan if they adopted and carried out a few themselves. It would be more sensible and more profitable. If they need a few hints I will give them some. A. market is badly I needed where tolls could be gathered in. When in I Stockton Heath, T have observed a large number ofl potato carts Bc.c., resting under the shadow of the "Mulberry Tree Inn." Then Stockton Heath needs new schools where children can 'be well educated and free from all sectarian teaching. Some improvement has already been made thanks to agitation in her midst but Stockton Heath is not up to the mark yet. Stockton Heath also will require shortly a Recreation ground. Are not these the kind of objects worthy of ,1 being'stri yen for? It appears to me that they are prefer- I able to a cantankerous dog-in-the-manger policy which does nobody any good and will very probably result in considerable harm.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. Business of the Next Meeting.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. Business of the Next Meeting.
A meeting of the Town Council will be held on Tues- day evening to transact the following among other business.
THE ALDERMANIC VACANCY.
There will be the election of an Alderman to fill the vacancy occasioned by the death of •Mr. Alderman Heaton, and election of Presiding klderman for the Fairfield Ward.

div.head: PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE
div.p: THE PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE
Resolved that Councillor Tinnion be appointed Chai- rman and Mr. Councillor Roberts the deputy chairman of this committee for the ensuing year.
FREE BATHING FOR SCHOOL CHILDREN.

At a Meeting of the Town Flail Parks and Baths Com- mittee a letter was read from the Education Committee requesting the free use of the second class swimming bath for children attending the elementary schools. After discussion the consideration of the matter was deferred until the neKt meeting. In the meantime the Town Clerk was to obtain information as to the free use of baths in other towns.
THE COAL TENDERS.

The Gas Committee has resolved, that the following tenders be accepted :—The Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company Limited, for the supply of 12,000 tons of Arley Slack. Cross, Tetley and Company Limited, for the supply of 10,009 tons of Arley Slack. Crompton and Shawcross Limited, for the supply of 10,000 tons of Arley Slack. Messrs. W. and J. Richard- son, for the supply of 2,000 tons of Cannel Chippings. Cross, Tetley and Company. Limited, for the vupnlv of 1,000 tons of Cannel Chippings. The Abram Coal Com- pany, Limited, for the supply of 1,000 tons of Cannel Chipnings. The Coed Talon Colliery Company, for the supply of 1,000 tons of Smooth Cannel. APPLETON RESERVOIR.

At a meeting of the Water Committee, the question of increasing the storage at the Appleton Reservoir by means of deepening the same was considered, and at the conclusion of the business the committee proceeded to Appleton to make an inspection of ,the works. THE TRAMWAYS.

The Electricity and Tramways Committee has resolved That the Town Clerk apply to the Board of Trade for a further prolongation of time for the construction of tramways in Padgate-lane and Manchester-road. The Tramways Manager was instructed to take the number of passengers in Orford-lane for one vibek from 6 am. to 11 p.m., the enumerators to statidat the end of Long- ford-street. Resolved also that the Borough Treasurer be requested to prepare a statement of the actual cost of each tramway route. Resolved, that the tender of Mr. J. A. Ewa.rt for the construction of the nermanent Light Railway No. 1 from Stafford-road to Victoria-square, Stockton Heath, at £2,935 15s. Bd. be accepted. Resolved,that the tender of Messrs.BAbcock and Wilcox Ltd. for the supply of 4 mechanical stokers at .£957 be accepted; resolved, that the tender of Messrs. Bell Bros. for the supply of water softening plant at 5.,'450 be accepted.
