div.head: AS, OTHERS SEE US. I AN OUTSIDE VIEW OF "WALKING
div.p: AS, OTHERS SEE US. I AN OUTSIDE VIEW OF "WALKING
BAY."

aR. H." writing in yesterday's " Liverppol Daily Post," makes the following comments on Warrington's ' Walking Dity:—Up and down this fair land of England there are to be found a number of objects which can lay no special claim to beauty, but about . the most forbidding of all is that black nightmare known as a Lancashire manufacturing town. After you have taken a walk through the principal streets, which are unlovely enough as a rule, you think you have reached the zero stage of depression, and wonder how people exist in such a place. Then, perhaps, you wander through some of the side streets, and get glimpses of the most appalling squalor and misery imaginable, and then—then you discontinue your subscriptions to the foreign missions. Such a town is Warrington, known amongst its neigh- bours as Sodom. The inhabitants will tell y?lti with pride that it is the home of thirty-one different indus- tries, and it looks it. When you come out of the Central Station you instinctively wonder what time the first train starts back to the place from whence you came. At the foot of the principal thoroughfare runs a Midianitish stream called the Mersey, of which, judg- ing from the smell that arises, the qtiality has not been strained. I think it would give the proud people of Liverpool something of a shock to see what their beloved river springs from. I am told the surroundings of Warrington are extremely pretty. That is as it may la,?. I walked out of the town in three different directions, and in each case I was stopped by an evil smelling canal. These canals, including Man- chester's bogey—the Ship—seem to surround Warring- ton on every side. However. it is only fair to say that Warringtonians are very proud of their town, and any odious comparisons are speedily put an end to by the stock assertion that "the old postal address of Liver- pool was in days gone by, 'Liverpool, near Warrington." But there is one day in the year when Warrington and its inhabitants come out of their shell; when the decorations are such that the puzzled stranger entering the town vainly endeavours to think what anniversary it is, and is not very much the wiser when he is told that it is "Walking Day." Essentially it is amhildren's day,and only to those per- sons who have the gift of retaining their own childish recollections can have any idea how the children look forward to this one day of the whole year; with what care the odd pennies and half-pennies have been hoarded up to buy some little adornment for them- selves - how anxiously for the past week have little faces been upturned to the sky with the prayer that for one day—just this one single day-might be fine; this day of days, which has been thought of and dreamt of ever since the last glorious occasion. It is an event of great importance to the maidens of the town, for by all the sacred laws of fashion it is not considered etiquette in Warrington to don one's new summer dress until Walking Day. Needless to say how this occasion comes to be looked forward to in this particular quarter, and how the overworked dressmakers have toiled incessantly for the past few week. Shortly after eight o'clock one begins to see straggling groups of children hurrying off to head- quarters to join their respective schools. At nine all traffic is stopped, the pathways on either side of the street being lined thick with spectators, many of whom care nothing for the procession in general. but care very much to see hoW their particular Mary Jane looks. We, who are interested spectators of everyone in general and nobody in particulat,take up a position where all have to pass on their way to the review ground—the Town Hall. Gracious, how the children do pont. out! One would scarcely have thought there were so many little mites in the whole of Lancashire. Every street and every alley seems to be one mass of gaily dressed children,all making for the one spot.as if they were under the influence of a modern "Pied Piper of Hamelin." On they come, each school headed by four sturdy urchins staggering under the weight of a huge banner. The bulk of the schools are the possess- ors of bands, and such bands ! However, one begins to get so interested in the children themselves that trifles like these pass unnoticed. Gazing at them, one won- ders which to admire most the plain simplicity of the Nonconformist children in their simple white frocks and sober sashes, or the dazzling brilliance of the little Catholic girls, dressed in all the colours of the rainbow carrying baskets of choice flowers procuredlfrom good- ness knows where, or else having in their hands long white wands decorated with dainty coloured ribbons. It makes one wonder how it is possible that such visions could come out of the squalid streets that most of them do come from. Some of the actors in the Procession do not seem to be altogether enjoying it. The little boys plodding along seem to be depressed by the unusual weight of cleanliness, and give one the impression that for them the happiness of the day does not begin until their nice white snits are blackened and disfigured, and they have pulled each others collars to bits. The grown- up scholars, those elderly wordlings from fifteen to eighteen years of age, show by their manner pretty plainly that the whole performance bores them, and that they would be much ibliged if yau would kindly take notice that they have no connection whatever with the children who are preceding them. The same afternoon any stranger who banpened to be in the outskirts of Warrington would wonder what such a number of children were doing playing in the fields, the truth being that the good-natured farmers in the district were in the habit every " walking " afternoon of placing at the dispo§al of the various Sunday schools fields for the children. Accordingly high carnival is held. Buns and milk are on tap all the afternoon, and all manner of sports indulged Their elders, bless von, who are too grown upr to take part in the "walking," are quite young enough for any sort of game that is going on. It develops by stages, from rounders to blind man's buff, thence, as the shyness begins to wear off, kiss-in-the-ring, and as the afternoon advances dancing on the green. Finally it ends in couples pairing off. But by this time the poor little souls who have been awake since early dawn are tired out. Accordingly, they are packed into carts and lurries, and it has to be seen to be believed how many children you can pick together. They have not room to budge an inch, even if they wanted to. which they don't. They are too tired, and more than half asleep. As the twilight deepens and the lights of Warrington come into view they are being slowly driven into the town, away from the fresh green fields where for the part o.f one whole happy day they have been free to roam. The thick, heavy atmosphere closes round them, and brings to an end the long-wished for claw, which for many of them is the only time from year's end to year's end when they have their faces clean, and when they do not play in the reeking, squalid streets where fate has cast their homes.

div.head: SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC. Report of the Medical Officer of Health.
div.p: THE SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC. Report of the Medical Officer of Health.

Inconsequence of 15 deaths from scarlet fever having occurred during the first quarter of this year, and the Local Government Board having asked for a renort on the recent prevalence of the disease, Dr. J. G.lGornall (medical officer of health) has furnished the members of the Health Committee with a report giving some de- tails of the cases and deaths that occurred during the first 13 weeks of the yaar. This report has now been printed. From this it apnears that of the 230 cases which were notified as scarlet fever, and which there was no reason to doubt had that disease, 205 were removed to hosnital. This was done within 24 hours of the receipt of the notification, with one or two exceptions. A case in New-road was. oia March 4, reported as doubtful scarlet fever. On visiting it the rash had entirely disappeared, and the child looked as if it were beginning measles. "Consequently, says the Medical Officer, left it at home, the mother promising to keep it in one room by itself. I instructed the Inspector o the district to visit twice weekly, so that I might know if my instructions were being carried out. The doctor in attendance subsequeatly reported that the child hall measles (March 7th). On the 16th March. being in the neighbourhood. I visited the place, and found the mother had taken the child into the kitchen to have dinner with the rest of the family, among whom were severll children. it, was peeling profusely from the:scarlet fever. I had it removed the same day and put in the ward where I had isolated the scarlet fever Patients with measles. We had had an outbreak of•the latter disease in Aikin-street hospital for some time." Twenty-six of the reported caseslwere left at home;of these2lbecause they were properly isolated,arrangernents for that purpose being made according to circumstances, e.g., in some instances there was only one child, in others the rest of the children were sent away, or per- sons living in the house were stopped from their em- ployment for the time or else got lodgings elsewhere. Of these 21, two died ; of the remaining five, all died. These latter would all have been removed to hospital (probably to their benefit) had circumstances permitted it. In ordinary uncomplicated cases four weeks was the usual period in hospital during the first two months of the year, frit, from the beginning of larch the Medical Officer raised this to five weeks, merely as a measure of precaution. This MIR done perhaps without any very well thought out reason, con'inues the Medical Officer, "and as far as T am aware its only result has been to make the accommodation question less easy to solve." In dismissing the present situation, Dr. Gornall says ;—There is no great fall in the number of cases. but they are certainly of a milder character. Cases are being taken first to a first ward, where they are kept until the abatement of acute svmptorns ; in a second ward they are kept until the disappearance of ear and nose discharges, for which the treatment started in the first ward is continued; in a third ward to which only clean cases are sent, and only after disinfection of clothes and body, the final week is spent, and here they receive the daily irrigation of nose and throat. Any case developing a discharge in the third ward is sent back to the second at once. There are great difficulties attending the carrying out of this plan—one is the tendency of overcrowding in the second stage ; and if there be an outbreak of enteric fever, as may well be feared, the system under trial must be abandoned if cases of that disease are to be taken into hospital.

div.head: SOCIAL SERMONETTES FOR WORKING MEN.
div.p: SOCIAL SERMONETTES FOR WORKING MEN.
BY JOHN TAYLOR. Author of Search Lights on Land, Labour and Social Problems."

div.head: DERELICT 'FARMS.
div.p: DERELICT 'FARMS.

"The land is mother of us all ; nourishes, shelters, gladdens, lovingly enriches us all. In how many ways, from our first awakening to our last sleep on her blessed mother-bosom, does she, as with blessed mother-arms enfold us all."—Carlylc. -- I have been spending a few days lately among the derelict farms, and declining villages of rural England, talking to our agricultural labourers, and trying to fathom the mysteries of low wages, and lack of employ- ment, and agricultural depression. Everywhere I find a great land hunger, and plenty of capable, industrious' labourers, anxious to secure some land, and become cultivators of the soil. And side by side with this land hunger, I have found plenty of land pining and hungering, and starving, and dying, for the labour that it cannot get. Here you have a big demand, and a big supply, and yet the ordinary laws of supply and demand will not settle these difficulties, because our dishonest system of land tenure, and our unjust land laws,set up an effec- tive barrier between them. So we have impoverished labourers, and derelict farms, existing side by side. We have an admitted evil, and a drastic remedy, and yet we refuse to deal with the evil because we think more of "vested interests," and the "rights of property," than we think of the rights of man, and the welfare of humanity.
L-A DERELICT FARM IS A NATIONALI MISFORTUNE.

Carlyle is right when he says that "the land is mother of us all," and that we draw all our food and nourish- ment from her. Bata mother can only supply the needs of her children while she is alive, and able to atteed to her maternal duties. A dead mother cannot feed, or clothe, or nourish anybody. So the land can only feed us when it is in a state of cultivation, and able to yield us bountiful harvests. If it is neglected, and abandoned and forsaken, it pines, and dies, and turns to corruption. Did you ever see a derelict farm? It is one of the ;saddest sights I know. The farm house is untenanted, and the windows are broken, and part of the roof has blown off, and the garden has become a desolation. The labourers cottages, and the barns, and stables, are all deserted, and fast going to rack and ruin. The hedges are untrimmed, and spreading out their branches on either side as wide as a street. The drains and water courses are choked with rubbish, and in wet weather the low lying land is under water and turned into a I filthy bog. I And what about the soil? If the last tenant did his duty by it. and farmed it well, it would make some show of life the first year after it was abandoned. With- out any effort or labour, it would yield a small crop of I self-sown wheat or oats, or barley, from the gleanings and droppings of the previous harvest. The second year it would yield no harvest worth reaping, for if you cease to plough and sow, you will mighty soon cease to reap. If you intend the land to feed and nourish you, it is certain that you will have to feed and cultivate it. If you starve and impoverish it, you know very well that it will starve and impoverish you. The third year after a farm has become derelict a destructive weed makes its appearance,and very quickly overruns the place. This weed resembles the plant that grows on land occasionally covered by the sea, and is known to our fishermen under the name of samphire. It is so objectionable that neither rabbits nor rats will eat it, and it is so persistent in its hold on the soil that it requires a good deal of effort to root it out, and destroy it. As you walk round this " dead man's farm "and take stock of its lonely, forlorn, and Godforsaken condition, I want you to realise how much mischief has been wrought by permitting it to go out of cultivation. In the first place, the landowner is badly hit by this misfortune. He not only loses the whole of his rent for all the years it has been lying derelict, but he will have to put the buildings into repair before any tenant sill take it. Then it will cost probably twenty pounds an acre to grub up the weeds, aud open the drains, and bring the land back to cultivation, and he will have to bear that expense,er he must allow a tenant to live on it rent free for ever so long, by way of com- pensation. In the second place, labour has suffered severely. The tenant farmer who occupied it last, put his labour and capital into it. and got nothing in return. The agri- cultural labourers employed by him lost their employ- ment, and had to abandon their homes, and find work elsewhere, or migrate to the towns, to compete with the unskilled labourers on the verge of starvation. In the third place. we are all of us impoverished when land goes out of cultivation. We have more than forty million mouths to feed every day in this country, and every rood of ground ought to maintain its man. When farms become derelict we are lessening our food supplies, and limiting the productiveness i.3f our own country, and increasing our dependence on the foreigner. Derelict farms pay neither rent, nor rates, nor taxes, and if the tax-gatherer can get nothing from uncultivated land, he will certainly take what he wants out of us, and increase our burdens. So you can take it from me that it does not pay to have uncultivated fields, and derelict farms multiplied. We must find some means of getting rid of them, or there will, be trouhle for everybody. IL—A DERELICT PAR.II IS USUALLY A PREVENTABLE EVIL.

It is one of those things that ought not to have happened, and need not have happened, with ordinary wisdom and prudence. If a ship loses her rudder, and becomes unmanageable. or shifts her ballast, and is thrown on her beam ends and lost, you can neither blame her captain or her owners for these misfortunes, because they are accidents beyond their control. But ,if a tenant farms his land badly, and takes out of the soil more than he puts into it, and utterly exhausts it before tho tenancy expires, that is not an accident. And if a tenant farms his land generously, and greatly improves it, ancf_then his landlord tries to raise his rent because of these improvements, and he raises a quarrel and a row instead, there can be nothing accidental about that business. Let me give you the history of one typical case. It is a large farm of five hundred acres, that was let for twenty eight shillings an acre,or.£7oo a vear,to a capable, enterprising and successful farmer. This man farmed 1. liberally, and wisely, and spent a good deal of money on fertilisers, and artificial manures. He sunk a large sum of money in raising the land to a very high state of cultivation, and he made it a model farm, and it be- came a financial success.

t His landlord saw he was making money, and thought he could afford to pay more rent, so he wanted a thou- sand a year for it, instead of seven hundred. Some of the tenant neighbours set their covetous eyes on that farm, and expressed their willingness to pay a. higher rent for it than he was paying. But times of depression came, and prices fell, and the shrewd farmer who had raised the land to such a high state of cultivation, saw that his own profits could not be maintained. Under the altered conditions of the market he refused to pay a higher rent, and asked for a reasonable reduction. Then came the inevitable quarrel, and the notice to quit, and the sale by auction, that ended his occupation of the farm. The aristocratic landowner who. has turned this good tenant out, fondly imagined that he could easily get another farmer to take it at a higher rent, but that is just where he made his mistake. The farmers in the neighbourhood said that the last tenant had been very badly treated by his landlord. He had made many val- uable improvements with his own money, and in spite of Agricultural Holdings Acts, he had not received due compensation for his outlay. An attempt had been made to raise his rent in consequence of his own im- provements, and because his landl6rd thought somebody else would pay him more rent for it, he had given a good tenant notice to quit. k When these things leaked out, nobody would take the farm at any, price, and as the landowner could not farm it himself, it became abandoned, and forsaken, and derelict. And the longer it remains in its present melancholy condition, and the more money it will cost to bring it back into profitable cultivation. If that landlord complains that he is losing seven hundred pounds a year in rent, and a great deal more in depre ciation of property, you can tell him that he richly de- serves all he gets, and his troubles are of his own seek- ing and making. We shall never have better land-laws till we have more tenant farmers, and fewer landowners in the House of Commons and the men who cultivate the soil will unite for their own protection. Sir Edward Verney some time ago compared the farmers to a rope of sand, and told them that "Agriculture is the only industry in this country that forbears to assert itself by combination in any form whatever." We want to see that the tenant farmer has every possible security that can be given him for valuable improvements which he makes with his own money, and yet every attempt to obtain this security ends disas- trously for the tenant. Mr. Fred Horne, a vice-Presi- dent of the Shropshire Chaniber of Agriculture, says : "The new Agricultural Holdings Act of 1900 cannot be. considered even a stet) in the right direction, and its passage in its present form is a gross breach of faith towards the a._griciilturists of this country." A practical intelligent farmer sums up the situation thus : "Bad land-laws, bad farming, ball education, and insu Mcient cottage accommodation, are the chief factors in the sum 'of agricultural depression, and consequent rural de-popnlation. Our present system of land tenure is an incentive to, and a premium on, bad farming."

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH AND THE CORPORATION.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH AND THE CORPORATION.
DISCUSSION ON THE PROPOSED ELECTRICITY SUPPLY. Parish Council's Action Approved. THE PRICE OF CAS.

To discuss the Warrington Corporation's proposals to supply electricity to Stockton fleath,a parish meeting was held in the church Institute, Stockton Heath, on Monday evening. There was a fair attendance, presided over by Mr. J. H. Clarke. Amongst those present were :—Messrs. J. Hallows, T. R. Westbrook, W. Mc Intyre, H. J. Westbrook, J. W. Bouchier, J. Warburton H. Isherwood, Frank Warburton, S. W. Dallow, E. England, G. J. Brown, F. Timperley,and E. Bradshaw, (clerk to the Parish council).

THE CHAIRMAN EXPLAINS. The Chairman detailed the negotiations which had taken place up to date. On receipt of the Corporation's proposal to supply electricity to the Parish, a sub-com- mittee was appointed, and on its recommendation the Parish Council resolved :—" That this Council is not opposed to the Warrington Corporation seeking powers to supply electricty within the area of this parish, pro- vided that the net price charged to all customers and users in the parish for all purposes for electricity and for gas shall never be more than is from time to time charged in Warrington for electricity and gas." A circular was distributed throughout the parish signed by the Warrington electrical engineer, in which the in- habitants were requested to answer certain questions. In his (Mr. Clarke's) opinion, the circular ought first to have been submitted to the Parish Council. To say the leasgof it,that would have been much more respectful.He therefore thought it his duty in the interests of the ratepayers to issue a circular suggesting that the ques- tions be not answered until a parish meeting had been held. It was now for the parishioners to say whether the resolution adopted by the Parish Council met with their approval or otherwise. He issued the circular solely out of consideration for the interests of the ratepayers. as he thought it was only right and fair that they should know the full details of the position before committing themselves to answering the questions. In a more recent letter the Town Clerk intimated that the Elec- tricity Committee were prepared to supply the district with electric light and energy at the same prices as were charged within the borough, but they were not prepared to consider, as it was outside their province, the question of a reduction in the price of gas. He (Mr. Clarke) would point out that the Parish Council was not dealing exclusively with theElectricityCommittee,but with the Corporation,and the Corporation as such could deal with both the gas and electricity questions. He did not wish thrt meeting to take it that he was com- mitting the Parish Council, because some of the members did not take exactly the same view that he took. It had been said that the Corporation had no power to reduce the price of gas to Stockton Heat 4. He had gone into the matter, and found that the Corporation had the power to reduce the charge to the same amount as was paid by Warrington people, if they thought fit. One of the old Acts certainly stated that the Corporation should supply gas to Stockton Heath at a higher price, but in a more recent Act it was stated that they "might" (not should) charge extra. Not only that, but the Warring- ton people had actually reduced the price of gas to suit a certain outlying district. In order to get hold of the custom for that place, they were allowing an extra discount of threepence, and Stockton Heath became participators in that benefit. He had no. wish to oppose the Corporation bringing electricity to Stockton Heath. There was no unfriendly feeling between the authorities. Some people thought they were at loggerheads, but there was nothing of the kind. The Corporation had to sell electricity, and they were very anxious for Stockton Heath to buy. He considered that an injustice was be- ing done to Stockton Heath, in charging them a higher price for gas than was paid by Warrington customers. If they agreed to support the Corporation in introducing electricity,they would have tied their hands for all time. Seeing that the Corporation would receive a privilege of that kind, it was the Parish Council's duty to make the best bargain they could. In answer to Mr. Nfoolhouse, the Chairman said he did not consider the Corporation were tied to charge one outlying district the same as another.

A RESOLUTION. Mr. Norman moved "That this meeting of parishioners fully approves of the terms of the reply of the Parish Council to the Town Clerk of Warrington, respecting the supply of electricity within the parish." In-as- much as the Corporation were offering them a commodity for sale, he considered it was their duty to make the best bargain they. possibly could.
Mr. Brown said that was no resolution to put before the meeting. It did not say whether they were going to have electricity or not, or upon what conditions they would have it.
Mr. Woolhouse: It commits the meeting to the resolution of the Council that a demand must be made for the price of gas to be altered in favour of Stockton Heath. •

The Chairman : It approves of the Council's action. If you disapp-ove of it, we want you to say so. Mr. H. J. Westbrook seconded the resolution. Mr. Brown said he did not like to propose an amend- ment condemning the action of the Parish Council, but to his mind there was nothing before the meeting to vote upon except a vote of censure on the Parish Conncil. He did not care to take up that attitude, but. in order to create discussion he would move that the meet- ing did not accept the ruling of the Parish Council. Mr. Woolhouse seconded. The Chairman: It does not need an amendment. say" No." nytimatedjthat ha would move an amend- mentcanßrown later. _ _ _

J. Westbrook said the question they had met to discuss that evening was a most serious one. This was not a question of supplying electricity nor of a reduction of threepence in the price of gas, but that the Warrington Corporation wanted a monopoly. They could not come into the parish unless they obtained Parliamentary Parliamentary powers, and when they Sought them the Parish Council, as a local authority, could oppose. The Town Clerk, before embarking on the expense of a Parliamentary Bill, wanted to know their views and what position they would take up if the Corporation decided to go to Parliament to seek those Powers. Were they prepared to give the Warrington Corporation another area of monopoly? That was how the matter presented itself to his mind, and before Stockton Heath granted power or acytiescei In thei▪ r relnest, terms ought to be made with the Corporati▪ on. They had a perfect right to say to the Corporation "We have no , objection to you seeking Parliamentary powers to come ' into this outside area on terms, and our terms are these, that with regard to electricity we are never charged , more than the people of Warrington, and also With regard to gas that we must have it reduced to the same price as is charged in Warrington." He did not think that was asking too much ; they were entitled to dictate their own terms. Those on the other side of the boundary might, of course take a different view of the situation, but on that side of the boundary he considered they would be wanting in their duty to the ratepayers if they acquiesced in the feeling letter of the Town Clerk about the terms. (Hear.hear). Were they going to give another monopoly without having something in return? That WAS the most important point to consider. It was not ridiculous to sup Pose that in the future other electric supplies might be forthcoming if light railways were constructed from Northwich, Knutsford, or Runcorn. If Stockton Heath people were tied hand and foot to Warrington, they would not be able to bargain at all. With regard to gas, Stockton Heath would have the power whenever the district was formed into an urban sanitary authority to buy out such of the Warrington undertaking as lay within the urban district. If they granted an electrical area of monopoly, they would have to do the same thing again. There was nothing to be ashamed of, and nothing unreasonable in Stockton Heath's demand. Were the ratepayers prepared to lose an opportunity of getting a reduction in the price of gas? He considered the Parish Council had asked for a very moderate quid pro quo in reply to the Corporation's request to come into that area with electricity.

div.head: AN AMENDMENT.
div.p: AN AMENDMENT.

Mr Brown moved the following amendment :—"That this meeting accepts th terms offered by the Warring- ton Corporation for the supply of electricity to Stock- ton Heath at the same price as to Warrington, and that the question of gas'he left over for further negotiation. With reference to Mr. Westbrook's remarks about their saddling themselves with conditions that it might be to get rid ot•he said he difficult for them ultimately would like to ask if it were not possible, if they accept- ed the terms of the Warrington Corporation for the supply of electricity, to make such terms as might safeguard Stoclsto? Heath and prevent their having to buy the Corporation out at some future date? Mr. Westbrook talked about the villarte of Stockton Heath dictating its own termsi to Warrington. That was sheer nonsense. He said t,of course.in all friendliness, but he wanted to be candid. He had heard nothing yet emanating from Stockton Heath which would warrant the ratepayers rejecting the proposals of the Warring- ton Corporation. (Hear. hear). If they had anything to go upon or any basis upon which they could object and dictate their terms, it would be another matter. (Hear, hear). As a Matter of fact they were not in a position to put down a gas plant and if they were they did not want it If the Warrington Corporation were willing to give them electricity on the same terms that they were mapplying it to their own ratepayers, who had to hear the burden of the Warrington rates, they were dealing with them in a vevy generous manner. (Applause.) If they were getting the Same terms, as the Warrington people were getting they had no need to grumble. As regarded the price charged for gas by the Corporation he did not think it unreasonable to ask him to pay a

little more than Warrington ratepayers. because he did not contribute anything towards the Warrington rates. There might be some gentlemen present who did con- tribute to the Warrington rates, but he was speaking personally. If at some future time they approached the Corporation with regard to a reduction in I the price of gas, they must not do it in a dictatorial manner. The Corporation had the whip hand of them. He would not pay more for gas than he could help, but in as much as Stockton Heath was in the unfortunate position of not being able to supply gas—and he took it that the bulk of the residents did not want to supply it from their own neighbourhood—he was perfectly willing, rather than have a gasometer and the smell of gas in the district, to pay a little more for the Warrington supply. Mr. J. Bouchier seconded, and alluded to a speech at the Parish Council meeting in which it was stated that negotiations with Warrington in the past had always been carried on in a friendly spirit, and that the Corporation had not been approached in a dictatorial manner. He wished to refer to the early negotiations with the Corporation about the tramway extension to Stockton Heath. He suggested that the Corporation were then approached in the same manner, he would not say the same spirit, as the Parish Council were now trying to approach them now on this question, and matters came almost to a dead lock. The Parish Council, fortunately for the parish he thought, modified tkeir manner at any rate, if not their demands,and approached the Corporation in a much more conciliatory manner than they had done up to then. The result was that they had the extension. He remembered going on one deputation to the Town Hall and they were met by the committee in a very gentlemanly manner. Their suggestions were all accepted, and the business was carried through without a hitch. He suggested that they might approach the Corporation upon the question before them in some- thing like the same spirit, and not say to the Corpora- tion : ."If you must supply us with electricity, we won't have it unless you are prepared to give us your gas at the same price as to the Warrington people." If they carried the amendment, he thought it would be an easy matter to approach the Corporation later, and negotiate upon the question of gas, and then they might bring the electricity question as an argument in favour of some concession from the Corporation. Mr. West- brook said that the time might come when they might through arbitration obtain control of the gas, and he (Mr. Bouchier) took it that they could similarly get control of the electricity, supposing they desired to make it themselves. He (the speaker) did not agree with Mr. Westbrook that there was such a tremendous danger in that so-called monopoly that he wished to put before them. Mr. Westbrook himself stated that they could arbitrate when they obtained urban powers and, in his (the speaker's) opinion, there was nothing a; all in the argument of monopoly. As regarded tit' water, he was perfectly satisfied, it was:as good as an-ye in the country; taking it altogether, he thought the benefits they had derived from the 'Warrington Corpora- tion were very great. (Applause.) He heartily sup- ported the amendment. if it was a question of paying threepence a thousand cubic feet more for gas than was paid by the Warrington ratepayers, he would rather pay it than have a nuisance caused in their own district by supplying it themselves. (Applause.) Mr. England said there might be a little danger regarding a monopoly by the Corporation of electric light but that danger could be safeguarded against. As regarded the question of gas, they could not expect to be supplied on exactly the same terms as Warrington ratepayers for the very reason that it cost more to supply outlying districts. (Hear, hear.) Owing to the leakage that took place it cost Warrinotonan additional twopence per thousand to supply Stockton Heath with gas, and thus they only made a penny out of the Stock- ton Heath ratepayers. The ratepayers of Stockton Heath had been very unfortunate in their negotiations with the Warrington Corporation. The tramways would I have been running in Stockton Heath had it not been for the Parish Council's opposition to the Warrington Corporation. The expense of the opposition had never yet been known, but it must have cost them a consider- able sum of money, and the parish had not got anything commensurate with the expenditure. The Parish Council on being approached by the Corporation in regard to any new scheme seemed to ask themselves : "What can we squ eze out of these persons ? " (Laughter.) By a spirit of that kind bad feeling would he engendered between the two neighbouring bodies. It was not in the interests of Stockton Heath to be continually running against a strong body like the IWarrington Corporation. (Hear, hear.) He thought it was in the interests of Stockton Heath to foster and engender a good spirit between themselves and the Warrington Corporation.
The Chairman: I want to shorten the number of your mis-statements. The expense in connection with the tramway extension would be covered by a live- pound note. _
Mr. England: That does not include the opposition to the Northwich light railway. Me Chairman: I don't say it includes the cost of opposition to that scheme.

"kr. England said he WM. referring to the cost of that opposition. Continuing, Mr. England said if they were going to oppose the scheme of the Warrington Corpora- tion with regard to the Electricity Bill when they brought it into Parliament, they would have to engage solicitors and counsel, who would have to thrash the matter out in London,and it would mean a great deal of expense. If the Parish Council went to London and said they were opposing the electricity scheme in order to get a threepenny reduction in the price of gas, the committee would simply laugh at them as they were being laughed at in Warrington and round about. There had been too much opposition to things that were far the benefit of the district. (Hear hear). Some people were under the impression that the Parish Council had succeeded in getting carried out the widening of London-road, but that was not so. The width of the road was specified by the Light Railway Commissioners. He was sorry that a bitter spirit existed between the Parish Council and the Corporation. He appealed to them to do all they could to create a good feeling between Warrington and Stockton Heath, because it was to their own interests ia the long run to do so. (Applause.) Mr. John Hallows said that in spite of everything, it was the Parish Council's duty to consider first what was beneficial to the ratepayers of Stockton Heath. Ever since he had been on the Parish Council, he bad never heard one word in opposition to the Warrington Corporation, and it was not right that there should be opposition. Warrington was their workshop, and War- rington's advancement was their advancement. (Applause). They would not have got the terms they had with the Warrington Corporation respecting the tramways had it not been for the Parish Council. The Parish Council was fighting the cause of the working- man in endeavouring to get a reduction for slot meters. He did not believe in the policy of shutting their eyes and opening tlieir mouths and seeing what the Corpora- tion would give them. (Laughter.)

, Mr. Dallo-w thought it was the duty of the Parish Council to meet the Corporation ina conciliatory spirit. If they did not the Corporation might retaliate, and he would like to know whether they had not power to charge an additional fare on the trams when the exten- sion was completed to the Square. The Corporation had met them in regard to several matters, one of which was the sewage question. - A Ratepayer: Who bore the expense of laying the pipes in Stockton Heath ? The Chairman: The original gas company. Mr. McDermott thought the Parish Council had acted in a strictly business spirit, and their action was to be commended. It seemed to be lost sight of that the Council were approached by the Warrington Corporation, and he saw nothing nasty in their replies. He con- sidered the action of the Parish Council worthy of the district it represented. (Applause.) The Parish Coun- cil ought to use the power it possessed in order to secure some reduction in regard to the price of gas. There was a tendency to under-estimate the district. The Corporation had not been such a paragon of excel- lence that they should lie down to it. He thought it was not an unreasonable request to ask that the parish should be supplied with gas at the same rate as War- rington.

The Chairman, in reply, said he did not want them to take it for granted that the letter embodied all the terms that the Parish Council wanted. They would certainly ask Warrington for power to purchase the electric plant in the same manner that they had power to purchase the gas plant. It was a well-known fact that unless they petitioned against a Bill they had no power to obtain any terms at all. To obtain their own points they must give notice of opposition. It was a matter of negotiation. One-of the speakers who had addressed the meeting that evening had made a remark to the effect that the way they went about their business was all "sheer nonsense," and that they must shut their eves,open their mouthe,and accept anything. (Laughter.) But he, as a parish , councillor, refused to accept that position. Stockton Heath was a good customer of War- rington, and he should like to know the profit that was made. Stockton Heath was a combined area. The Cor- poration had to go miles to supply gas one way and another, but here they were on the spot, and there was not an outlying district where the profits made any- thing apProaching the profits made from Stockton Heath. Ten thousand pounds had been made out of the Warrington gas during the past 12 months, so that the concern was not a losing One, and the people of Stockton Heath were paying an extra share towards the rates of Warrington. Mr. Hallow: We should be contributing towards the rates if the additional 3d. were knocked of the price of gas. Continuing, the Chairman said a good deal had been said about the kindness of Warrington, but he wished to mention the good turn that was done a few years ago when Warrington took in a district called Wilderspool. Some opposition was raised; he was sorry there was not more. But what was the position? Next year the Corporation would be taking from the district of Wilderspool £2,000 a year in rates into Warrington. that was to say that after next year they would be receiving from Wilderspool .£2,000 a year. It was very kind on the part of the Corporation of NVarr relieve them of <£2.000 a year. (Laughter.) ington to Mr. Bouchier : But you don't say that the Corpora- tion took charge of the sewage. • i The Chairman, continuing. said that if they took charge of the district where the sewage emptied itself, they had a right to expect them to look after the sewage. Mr. Timverley : They have taken your sewage. The Chairman (continuing) said he was surprised Mr.

England had taken up such a position with regard tO. cost of opposing the Corporation, especially as it ban been so low. He wished to correct one of his numerous mis-statements. The fact was that the widening of the road in Stockton Heath was obtained solely owing tc... the persistency of the Parish Council—(hear, hear, and applause)—who opposed the Warrington trarawaY scheme -Jail the widening was granted. If the tram! had come into the village with the road widened, it would have been a disgrace to concerned. But what had they now? A good roat_t, and it was owing to the persistency of the Parish_ Council in existence at the time. Now the people of Stockton Heath were proud of what they saw; thei only wished the improvement had been greater. ilet Council did their best and stood out until they got Wu' they thought was reasonable and right. As to the sug- gested twopenny tram fare to Victoria Square, all he, had to say was that if 2d. was charged the people neeq not use the cars. But that was an argument that would not hold water, because the trams were coming from Warrington with the object of paying, and not for the purpose of doing the people of Stockton Heath a your. The The Corporation lost £6lO on the tramway last year, but what would have been their loss if they hal not come to Wilderspool ? (Hoar, hear). , Hundreds o pounds a year more. The Wilderspool line was the only line that paid and when the line ran, to iVictoria square, it would be the finest PaVng line the Corporation had, and they knew it. And when' the time came to supply electricity it would pay them' also. Mr. Dallow : You have not answered my question. The Chairman : The Corporation may have power to charge an additional fare but they have commonsense to • know that it will not pay to increase thelare. THE AMENDMENT DEFEATE D.
MR. BROWN MOVES THAT A POLL BE TAKEN

On a vote being taken, the amendment was defeated, 14 voting for it and 16 against. Afterwards the resolution was put to the meetingrana there were 17 votes for and 12 against. Mr. Brown said that, as there bad been so much ex- traneous matter introduced, and• so many subjects dis; cussed which had tended to influence the voting,he woulc! move that, as that was not a representative meeting 01 the parish, a poll betaken. He did not consider by an means that that meeting represented Stockton ileatn,', The majority in favour of the resolution was so sate!: that he did not think they would be doing their duty they did not give every householder an opportunity' 01 recording a vote for oragainst the introduction of elec" trinity.

The Chairman said he hoped Mr. Brown did not pro- pose that seriously. There might come a time later when the proposition would have to be put before th! parishioners, and that was when the Town Council Wen' to Parliament. Still they hoped they would come t(). proper terms. He spoke seriously, and he hoped gr..; Brown would not put them to the expense, trouble, fie' inconvenience of a poll at the present time. Of course" the meeting had the power to demand a poll. Mr. Brown said he had no wish to put the Parish. Council to any expense,but from his reading of the roe' lotion it appeared that they had laid it down that theY would only accept the electricity on condition that the. Warrington Corporation reduced the price of gas. rAt the WarringtonCorporation sought for power to nrevj",e' Stockton Heath with electricity, the only th., ' o°l could do was to take other measures and 0p,,,J.e the Bill.

The Chairman: That is the time for a poll. - Mr. Brown said it was getting too serious when it got to that, and it might land them in far more exPense than they. expected. Mr. Isherwood said the resolution simply meant that. the action of the Parish Council Was confirmed up now, and that the Council be desired to procead ttb the negotiations with the Corporation.. The resolutio.n did not force the Council to in.ist upon a reduction In the pricip of gas. There was some further discussion, a member of the audience remarking that the Corporation's proposals din not seem to have aroused a great amount of interest, 115 the attendance was not at all 'representative of the - parish. Mr. Brown's motion that a poll be taken was !Int supported, and therefore fell to the ground.

'that statesman had set himself the task of captur- ting the Unionist party, and in the Cbertsey "division Lord Bingham, who has been put forward asa candidate, is warranted to go as far in the direction of" whole hoggery " as even the Tariff Reform League could desire. But the Unionist -Free Traders, who include many of the most influential residents in the constituency, have replied to his challenge by issuing a manifesto calling upon Unionists convinced of the dangers of Mr. Chamberlain's policy to vote against Lord Bingham. This action means a departure from the "passive attitude which the Free Traders within the Unionist party have hitherto adopted in the sChertsey division, and it markq, it may be hoped, Closer co-operation between Free Traders of both Parties. Davenport brings the list of constituencies Which have been polled on the Fiscal issue up to 'nineteen. At the last General Election the Union- ist candidates in these Parliamentary divisions Polled 86,442 votes, whereas at the by-elections this total fell to 81,457, a drop of 2,000. On the •Other hand, the Liberal vote has increased from 68,312 to 95,928, a gain of no fewer than 27,600 l'otes. In other words, while at the General Election the Tory majority was 16,115, this has .120 w been converced into a Liberal majority of 9,186. Nothing could attest more strongly the nclisastrons effects upon the Unionist party of Mr. •-iharnberlain's Protectionist proposals.
